(a) straight head of rectus femoris musc: The straight head of rectus femoris takes origin from the anterior inferior iliac spine just above the acetabular roof, while the iliofemoral ligament arises immediately below it and fans as an inverted Y across the front of the hip capsule to the intertrochanteric line.
11th rib (tip of): Second lowest rib, best identified by counting up from the 12th; like the 12th it is a floating rib whose anterior tip ends free in the abdominal wall without reaching the costal margin. Distinguish it from an elongated L1 transverse process, which arises from the vertebra itself rather than articulating at a costovertebral joint.
1st metacarpal: Shortest and broadest metacarpal, on the radial side and rotated out of the plane of the others, articulating proximally with the trapezium at the saddle joint. It lies proximal to the thumb MCP joint, unlike the thumb proximal phalanx.
1st metatarsal: Shortest and thickest of the metatarsals, lying most medially, articulating proximally with the medial cuneiform and distally with the proximal phalanx of the hallux; the paired sesamoids beneath its head confirm the identification.
1st metatarsophalangeal joint: Joint between the head of the first metatarsal and the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, with the two sesamoids lying beneath it; because the great toe has only two phalanges, the next joint distally is the interphalangeal joint.
1st rib: Shortest, broadest and most sharply curved rib, arising from T1 and arching anteromedially over the lung apex to the manubrium; a cervical rib arises one level higher from C7 and is usually much shorter and slimmer.
1st rib (anterior): Anterior end of the first rib sweeps steeply downwards and medially from its posterior origin at T1 towards the manubrium; its costal cartilage calcifies early, and the resulting irregular density over the upper zone is a classic mimic of a lung nodule.
2nd metatarsophalangeal joint: Joint between the head of the second metatarsal and the base of the proximal phalanx of the second toe, the ray immediately lateral to the great toe. The first metatarsal head is broader and carries the paired sesamoids beneath it.
4th metatarsal: Fourth ray counted from the great toe; its base articulates with the cuboid alongside the fifth, whereas the third metatarsal base lines up with the lateral cuneiform, a useful alignment check on the oblique view.
4th metatarsal (shaft): Tubular midportion of the fourth ray, counting from the great toe; its base articulates with the cuboid alongside the fifth, but unlike the fifth it lacks the flared proximal styloid tuberosity.
abdominal aorta: Begins at the diaphragmatic hiatus at T12 and runs just left of the midline directly in front of the vertebral bodies, bifurcating at about L4. On ultrasound it is thick-walled and pulsatile, unlike the thinner, compressible IVC lying to its right.
abductor pollicis longus tendon or (othe: First dorsal extensor compartment: the most radial pair of tendons, running together directly over the radial styloid; the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis of the second compartment lie just ulnar to them, closer to Lister's tubercle.
acetabular angle: Angle between Hilgenreiner's line, drawn horizontally through both triradiate cartilages, and a line along the sloping acetabular roof; a steeper (larger) angle indicates a shallow dysplastic acetabulum. It is a measurement, not a bone.
acetabular labrum: Echogenic triangle at the superolateral acetabular rim on infant hip ultrasound, extending laterally over the femoral head; the hyaline cartilaginous acetabular roof lying deep and medial to it is hypoechoic, and on MRI the labrum is a low-signal triangle at the bony rim.
acetabular roof: Dense curvilinear sclerotic band forming the superolateral weight-bearing cover of the femoral head; it is the top of the acetabulum, distinct from the fainter anterior and posterior wall lines that run inferiorly from it across the femoral head.
acetabulum: Cup-shaped socket on the lateral pelvis where ilium, ischium and pubis meet at the triradiate cartilage, receiving the femoral head. On a frontal radiograph identify it by the medial teardrop, the dense sclerotic roof and the overlapping anterior and posterior wall lines.
achilles tendon: Thick, uniformly wide vertical soft-tissue band on the lateral ankle radiograph descending to insert on the posterior calcaneal tuberosity, its anterior margin made visible by the lucent pre-Achilles (Kager) fat pad in front of it.
acromio-clavicular joint: Narrow lucent gap between the lateral end of the clavicle and the medial edge of the acromion, superolateral to the humeral head, with the inferior cortices of the two bones normally aligned. It lies above the subacromial space, not within the glenohumeral joint.
acromio-clavicular joint space: Thin lucent gap between the lateral end of the clavicle and the medial edge of the acromion at the top of the shoulder, with the cortical margins normally aligned. Do not confuse it with the wider subacromial space beneath the acromion.
acromioclavicular joint: Synovial joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the medial margin of the acromion, normally under 5 mm wide with the inferior cortices aligned. It lies well lateral to the coracoclavicular space, where clavicle and coracoid are tethered by ligaments rather than a joint.
acromion: Flat lateral continuation of the scapular spine that roofs the joint and meets the lateral end of the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint. On the scapular Y view it is the posterior fork of the Y; the coracoid is the anterior fork, closer to the ribs.
acromion of left scapula: Posterior fork of the Y, continuous with the scapular spine and running laterally to meet the distal clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint. The anterior fork, lying nearer the ribs, is the coracoid process.
acromion of left scapula – ossification: Late-ossifying secondary centre at the lateral tip of the acromion, seen as a separate corticated ossicle above the humeral head; because it fuses late, do not call it a fracture, and remember the unossified acromion makes the acromioclavicular joint hard to assess in children.
acromion of right scapula: Flattened lateral continuation of the scapular spine forming the bony roof above the humeral head and articulating with the distal clavicle; the coracoid is the beak-like process projecting anteriorly, seen more medially and inferiorly, overlying the upper glenoid.
acromion process: Flat lateral continuation of the scapular spine arching over the humeral head and meeting the lateral end of the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint; the coracoid process, its usual confusion, is a hook-like projection arising anteriorly from the scapular neck and lies anteroinferior and medial to it.
acromion process (of left scapula): Flat lateral continuation of the scapular spine forming the bony roof over the humeral head and articulating with the distal clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint; the coracoid, its usual mimic, projects anteriorly and lies medial and inferior, beneath the clavicle.
acromion process of scapula: Flat lateral projection continuous posteriorly with the scapular spine, arching over the humeral head and meeting the distal clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint. The coracoid is separate, more medial and inferior, and points anteriorly.
acromion process of the scapula: Flat lateral extension of the scapular spine forming the roof of the subacromial space above the supraspinatus tendon and articulating anteromedially with the distal clavicle; the coracoid is the anterior hook, lying lower and in front of the joint.
acromium: Posterior limb of the scapular Y, continuous with the scapular spine and arching laterally over the humeral head to reach the clavicle. The scapular blade is easily mistaken for the spine here; the spine lies more posteriorly and runs directly into the acromion.
adductor canal (hunter's canal, subsarto: Fascial tunnel in the middle third of the medial thigh bounded by vastus medialis anterolaterally, the adductors posteriorly and sartorius medially, running from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus and transmitting the femoral vessels and saphenous nerve.
adductor longus muscle: Most anterior muscle of the medial compartment on axial images, running from the pubis to the linea aspera with adductor brevis and magnus stacked behind it, and forming the medial border of the femoral triangle; gracilis is the thin strap at the extreme medial subcutaneous margin.
adductor magnus muscle: On a radiograph it is located by its tendinous insertion onto the adductor tubercle, the small bump at the top of the medial femoral epicondyle. The medial head of gastrocnemius arises just posterior and inferior to that on the condyle.
adductor tubercle: Small bony protuberance at the most superior aspect of the medial femoral epicondyle, at the end of the medial supracondylar line, giving insertion to adductor magnus. It sits just above and behind the medial epicondyle proper, which is broader and more distal.
adductor tubercle of the right femur: Small bony bump at the distal end of the medial supracondylar ridge, immediately above the medial femoral epicondyle, into which the tendinous part of adductor magnus inserts; if the prominence is on the joint side of that ridge it is the epicondyle instead.
alpha angle: Angle between the baseline drawn along the straight lateral wall of the ilium and the line of the bony acetabular roof, measuring acetabular depth and normally greater than 60 degrees; the beta angle instead uses the cartilaginous roof and labrum line.
anatomical neck of humerus: Shallow groove immediately around the articular margin of the humeral head, separating it from the tuberosities and marking the line of capsular attachment; the surgical neck is further distal, below the tuberosities, where the axillary nerve is at risk.
anatomical neck of right humerus: Oblique groove immediately distal to the articular surface of the humeral head, separating the head from the greater and lesser tuberosities; the surgical neck is the narrower segment of shaft lying below the tuberosities.
anatomical neck of the humerus: Slight constriction encircling the humerus immediately distal to the articular surface of the head and proximal to the tuberosities, marking the capsular attachment; the surgical neck is lower, at the proximal diaphysis just below the tuberosities, and is the common fracture site.
anatomical neck of the right humerus: Oblique groove immediately distal to the articular surface of the humeral head, separating it from the greater and lesser tubercles and giving attachment to the joint capsule. The surgical neck lies further distal, below the tubercles at the head-shaft junction.
anconeus: Small triangular muscle at the posterolateral elbow running from the lateral epicondyle to the olecranon and proximal posterior ulna. On axial images it hugs the posterolateral ulnar cortex deep to the extensor group, unlike the more superficial extensor carpi ulnaris.
anconeus muscle: Small triangular muscle at the posterolateral elbow running from the lateral epicondyle to the lateral olecranon and proximal ulna, the most posterior muscle overlying the ulna on axial images just distal to the triceps insertion.
angle of mandible: The posteroinferior corner where the vertical ramus turns into the horizontal body, just behind and below the last molar, seen as a smoothly corticated curve on an OPG or lateral view. It lies well posterior to the midline mental symphysis where the hemimandibles fuse.
angle of the mandible: Corner where the posterior border of the vertical ramus turns forwards into the lower border of the tooth-bearing body, giving attachment to masseter laterally and medial pterygoid medially. Trace the smooth lower cortex backwards until it turns upwards.
angle of the mandible (not possible to s: Corner where the posterior border of the ramus turns forwards into the lower border of the body. On a true lateral projection the two sides are superimposed, so the angle cannot be assigned to right or left.
angle of the mandible (right): Point where the posterior border of the ramus turns forwards into the lower border of the tooth-bearing body; follow the continuous lower mandibular cortex backwards on the orthopantomogram until it sweeps upwards towards the condyle.
angle of the right mandible: Corner between the posterior border of the ramus and the lower border of the body of the mandible. On a lateral oblique sialogram the submandibular gland and duct lie just below and medial to it, while the parotid lies behind the ramus.
annular ligament: Encircles the radial head like a collar, attached to the anterior and posterior margins of the radial notch of the ulna and allowing the head to spin in pronation and supination. Its level is the radial head, not the radial tuberosity further distally.
annulus fibrosis of l4/l5 disc: Tough outer ring of the L4/5 disc, dark on every sequence, encircling the brighter central nucleus and anchored to the vertebral rim; defects in it are the route through which nucleus herniates.
anterior and posterior interosseous arte: Branches of the common interosseous artery, itself arising from the ulnar artery just distal to its origin; they run distally on the front and back of the interosseous membrane, so on angiography they lie centrally between the laterally placed radial and medially placed ulnar arteries.
anterior arch of atlas: Small oval bony density immediately in front of the dens at the craniocervical junction on the lateral view, just below the tip of the clivus; it is far smaller than the C2 body, which lies below and behind the peg.
anterior arch of c1: Small rounded bony density lying immediately anterior to the odontoid peg on the lateral view, forming the front of the atlas ring; the gap between it and the peg is the atlanto-dental interval, normally under 3 mm in adults. Do not mistake it for the body of C2, which lies below and is continuous with the peg.
anterior arch of c1 vertebra: Small oval ring of bone lying immediately anterior to the dens on the lateral view, taking the place of the absent C1 body; the posterior arch with its small posterior tubercle lies behind the spinal canal.
anterior arch of c1 vertebra (atlas): Small oval ring of bone lying immediately in front of the dens on the lateral view, the atlas having no vertebral body. The predental space between arch and dens should not exceed about 3 mm in an adult.
anterior arch of cricoid cartilage: Short anterior band of the complete cricoid ring at the lower larynx, lying just below the thyroid cartilage at about C6 on the lateral view; the cricoid's posterior lamina is much taller, and the thyroid cartilage is larger and sits above it.
anterior arch of the atlas: Small rounded or oval bone lying immediately in front of the odontoid peg at the top of the lateral cervical film; C1 has no vertebral body, so this is the only anterior bone at that level. The gap between it and the dens should measure under 3 mm in an adult.
anterior arch of the atlas (c1): Small oval bony density lying immediately in front of the dens at the craniocervical junction, separated from it by the atlantodental interval (under 3 mm in adults); it is much smaller than the C2 body, which lies lower and behind.
anterior clinoid process: Backward-pointing bony spur at the medial end of the lesser wing of sphenoid forming the anterosuperior lip of the pituitary fossa on a lateral skull film; the posterior clinoids project forwards from the top of the dorsum sellae behind the fossa.
anterior corner of the distal metaphysis: On the lateral wrist, the volar corner of the flared distal radial metaphysis just proximal to the articular surface; the volar side is identified by the pisiform, which projects anterior to the capitate and scaphoid. The dorsal corner is the opposite, posterior margin.
anterior epidural fat pad: Fat signal tissue lying between the posterior vertebral body and posterior longitudinal ligament in front and the thecal sac behind, bright on T1 and suppressing on fat saturated sequences. That fat signal separates it from disc material, which follows disc signal and is centred at the disc level.
anterior fat pad: Thin lucent triangle lying flat against the anterior cortex of the distal humerus in the coronoid fossa on a true lateral elbow radiograph, and normally visible. With an effusion it is lifted into a sail shape and the posterior fat pad, normally hidden in the olecranon fossa, becomes visible.
anterior first rib: Highest rib, arching from T1 downward and forward to the manubrium, its short broad anterior end lying at the very top of the frontal film medial to the clavicle. Its costal cartilage calcifies early and commonly mimics a lung nodule; trace continuity with the rib.
anterior fontanelle: Diamond-shaped lucent gap at the vertex where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet, normally closed by around 18 months; the posterior fontanelle is smaller and triangular, at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures.
anterior glenoid labrum: Small low-signal triangle capping the anterior bony rim of the glenoid on axial MRI, sitting deep to the subscapularis tendon. Distinguish it from the middle glenohumeral ligament, a separate band lying free within joint fluid rather than attached to the glenoid rim.
anterior humeral line: Line drawn down the anterior cortex of the humerus on a true lateral elbow; normally it crosses the middle third of the capitellum. If the capitellum lies behind the line, suspect a supracondylar fracture.
anterior inferior iliac spine: Rounded anterior prominence of the ilium sitting just above the acetabular roof, below and behind the anterior superior spine; it is the origin of the straight head of rectus femoris and a classic adolescent avulsion site.
anterior interosseous artery: Runs distally on the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane, deep between flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus with its nerve; the ulnar artery is more superficial and medial, hugging the ulna alongside the ulnar nerve.
anterior junction line: Thin line formed where both lungs meet in the midline in front of the great vessels; on the frontal film it runs obliquely downwards and to the left below the level of the aortic arch, and never extends above the clavicles.
anterior longitudinal ligament: Thin continuous low-signal band running along the anterior surface of the vertebral bodies and discs on sagittal MRI, blending with the periosteum. Its position in front of the bodies separates it from the posterior longitudinal ligament, which lines the posterior vertebral surface inside the canal.
anterior process of calcaneum: Beak-like anterosuperior projection of the calcaneus seen on the lateral or oblique ankle radiograph immediately behind the calcaneocuboid joint, a classic avulsion fracture site. An os calcaneus secundarius is distinguished by smooth, complete cortication all round.
anterior superior acetabular labrum: Triangular low-signal fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the bony acetabular margin, profiled anterosuperiorly on oblique axial and sagittal MR arthrogram slices. This quadrant is the commonest site of tear, so compare it with the smooth triangular posterior labrum.
anterior superior iliac spine: Bony prominence at the anterior end of the iliac crest, the attachment of the inguinal ligament and sartorius; the anterior inferior iliac spine lies below it, separated by a notch, and sits much closer to the acetabular roof.
anterior tibial artery: Passes through the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment and runs down to become the dorsalis pedis at the ankle.
anterior tubercle of the atlas: Small midline bump on the front of the thin ring-like anterior arch of C1, seen directly in front of the dens on axial or midline sagittal CT; the dens is the rounded bone behind the arch, held there by the transverse ligament.
anterior tubercle of the left transverse: Anterior of the two bony prominences at the tip of a cervical transverse process, lying in front of the foramen transversarium; the posterior tubercle sits behind the foramen, the two joined by the intertubercular lamella.
anterior tubercle of transverse process: Anterior lip of the C5 transverse process, bounding the foramen transversarium in front and therefore lying in front of the vertebral artery. The posterior tubercle sits behind the foramen and projects further laterally and posteriorly.
anterior vertebral line: Smooth curved line traced along the anterior margins of the vertebral bodies on the lateral view, one of the four alignment lines with the posterior vertebral, spinolaminar and spinous tip lines; any step or break in its gentle lordotic curve indicates injury.
antero-inferior glenoid rim: Lower anterior margin of the pear-shaped glenoid, best appreciated on an en-face or 3D CT of the scapula; it anchors the anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament and is the site of a bony Bankart avulsion.
aorta: Pulsatile, thick-walled anechoic tube lying just left of the midline directly on the vertebral bodies and giving anterior branches such as the coeliac axis and superior mesenteric artery; the inferior vena cava lies to its right, is thinner walled, compressible and changes calibre with respiration.
aortic arch: Rounded convexity, the aortic knuckle, forming the left upper mediastinal contour and continuous inferiorly with the descending aorta; the smaller bulge immediately below it is the pulmonary trunk and left pulmonary artery, with the left atrial appendage lower still.
aortic knuckle: Convex bulge on the upper left mediastinal border at about the T4 and sternal angle level, sitting just above the concave aorto-pulmonary window and continuing inferiorly as the straight lateral edge of the descending aorta.
aortic knuckle or arch: Rounded prominence forming the upper left mediastinal contour, produced by the distal arch turning backwards; below it the contour indents at the aortopulmonary window before the pulmonary trunk and left hilum, which distinguishes it from a left upper zone mass.
aorto-pulmonary angle or aorto-pulmonary: Concavity on the left mediastinal border between the aortic knuckle above and the left pulmonary artery below, at about the level of the left main bronchus. It should be straight or concave; a convex bulge here means nodal or other mass.
aorto-pulmonary window: Concave notch on the left mediastinal contour between the aortic knuckle above and the left pulmonary artery below, containing the ligamentum arteriosum and left recurrent laryngeal nerve. Convexity here indicates nodal enlargement or mass.
aortopulmonary window: Concave segment of the left mediastinal contour between the aortic knuckle above and the left pulmonary artery below; it should never bulge outwards, and a convex margin there means mediastinal nodes or mass.
appendix: Blind-ending tubular structure arising from the caecal base near the ileocaecal junction, with gut signature layers, compressible, aperistaltic and under 6 mm in maximum diameter. Terminal ileum looks similar but is not blind-ending and shows peristalsis.
arch of aorta: Arches over the left main bronchus and left pulmonary artery at about the T4 level; on the frontal film it is the convex left superior mediastinal contour, the aortic knuckle, continuing down as the straight edge of the descending aorta.
arch of aorta (aortic knuckle): Convex bulge on the upper left mediastinal border at about T4 and the sternal angle, sitting immediately above the concave aorto-pulmonary window; the pulmonary trunk lies below that window, and the straight edge of the descending aorta continues inferiorly.
articular pillar: Column of bone at the junction of pedicle and lamina bearing the superior and inferior facets, lying posterolateral to the foramen transversarium; unlike the transverse process it contains no foramen, and unlike the lamina it lies lateral rather than posteromedial.
atlantoaxial joint: Paired lateral articulation between the inferior facet of the C1 lateral mass and the superior facet of C2, seen on the open-mouth peg view as the horizontal joint space on each side of the odontoid. Overlying teeth and hard palate can mimic fracture lines here.
atlas: C1 is a ring with no vertebral body; its posterior arch is seen as a thin corticated line high on the lateral cervical view, just below the occiput.
atrial appendage: Short segment of the left heart border lying between the pulmonary trunk above and the left ventricle below, normally straight or slightly concave. A convex bulge at this point signals left atrial enlargement, as in mitral valve disease.
atrial border: Gently convex contour forming the lower part of the right mediastinal border, lying between the straighter, more vertical SVC line above and the right cardiophrenic angle below.
atrium: On the frontal chest radiograph the right atrium forms the lower right heart border, a smooth convexity between the superior vena cava above and the right cardiophrenic angle below. The left atrium sits posteriorly, showing as a double density with an appendage bulge on the left border.
atrium (left atrial appendage): Contributes a short segment of the left heart border between the pulmonary trunk above and the left ventricle below, normally straight or slightly concave; a convex bulge here is the classic sign of left atrial enlargement in mitral valve disease.
atrium (right heart border): Forms the lower right heart border as a smooth convex arc rising from the right cardiophrenic angle; the superior vena cava takes over above it as a straighter, more vertical edge, and the carina lies directly above the left atrium, not this chamber.
axillary artery: Continuation of the subclavian artery beyond the outer border of the first rib, crossing the axilla behind pectoralis minor and giving chest wall and shoulder branches before becoming the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major. Proximal to the first rib it is the subclavian.
axillary fold: Curved soft-tissue edge over the lateral chest wall formed by the skin fold and the lateral border of pectoralis major. Lung markings continue lateral to it and it runs off the ribcage into the axilla, which excludes a pneumothorax line.
axillary neurovascular bundle: Cluster of axillary artery, vein and brachial plexus cords embedded in fat at the apex of the axilla, deep to pectoralis minor and anterior to subscapularis; vessels show flow void with small round nerve bundles alongside.
axillary vein: Continuation of the basilic vein from the lower border of teres major, running through the axilla medial and superficial to the axillary artery and becoming the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib; the cephalic vein joins it near the shoulder.
axillary, radial, ulnar, median and musc: The five terminal branches of the brachial plexus, small round bundles in fat around the axillary artery: musculocutaneous entering coracobrachialis, median anterior to the artery, ulnar medial, radial posterior, axillary passing back through the quadrangular space.
axis: C2 is identified by the odontoid peg projecting upwards from its body into the C1 ring.
azygo-oesophageal line: Interface between the right lower lobe and the azygo-oesophageal recess: a near-vertical line running up from the diaphragm just right of the midline behind the heart, indented gently to the left at the level of the left atrium. Focal convexity suggests subcarinal nodes.
azygo-oesophageal recess: Gently curved interface running down the right side of the vertebral column from the azygos arch to the diaphragm, created where aerated right lower lobe contacts the mediastinum beside the azygos vein and oesophagus; focal convexity or distortion points to subcarinal disease.
azygos fissure: Fine curvilinear line arcing down through the right upper zone from the apex to a teardrop-shaped opacity, the azygos vein, at the right tracheobronchial angle, and containing four pleural layers; the minor fissure instead runs horizontally at the fourth rib.
azygos lobe/fissure: Thin curvilinear line in the right upper zone sweeping from near the apex downwards and medially to end in a teardrop-shaped density, the azygos vein itself. Four pleural layers make it thicker than a normal fissure, and lung markings lie on both sides, unlike a pneumothorax edge.
azygos vein: Small oval or teardrop opacity in the right tracheobronchial angle, where the vein arches forwards over the right main bronchus to enter the superior vena cava. Unlike a lymph node it varies with posture and Valsalva, enlarging when supine.
base of 5th metatarsal: Proximal end of the lateral-most metatarsal, articulating with the cuboid and bearing the laterally projecting tuberosity into which peroneus brevis inserts; the separate rounded os peroneum lies further proximal and lateral within the peroneus longus tendon.
base of fifth metacarpal: Most ulnar metacarpal base, articulating with the hamate across the carpometacarpal joint line and receiving the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon on its dorsal aspect. The hamate lies proximal to that joint line and carries the volar hook.
base of little finger metacarpal: Proximal end of the fifth metacarpal, articulating with the hamate at the ulnar edge of the distal carpal row; the fourth metacarpal base also meets the hamate but lies radial to it, in line with the ring finger.
base of right fifth metatarsal: Proximal end of the lateral-most metatarsal, carrying the tuberosity that projects proximolaterally beyond the cuboid articulation and receiving the peroneus brevis tendon. Distinguish from the os peroneum, a separate rounded ossicle lying lateral to the cuboid within the peroneus longus tendon.
base of right little finger metacarpal: Proximal end of the shortest, most ulnar of the four finger metacarpals, articulating with the hamate at the fifth carpometacarpal joint and carrying the extensor carpi ulnaris insertion; the fourth metacarpal base lies immediately radial to it and also abuts the hamate.
base of right thumb metacarpal: Proximal end of the shortest and most radial metacarpal, forming the saddle-shaped first carpometacarpal joint with the trapezium and the site of a Bennett fracture-dislocation. The head is the rounded distal end at the MCP joint; the thumb ray has only two phalanges.
base of the fifth right metatarsal: The proximal, laterally flared end of the fifth metatarsal articulating with the cuboid, its tuberosity projecting backwards as the peroneus brevis insertion. In children the normal apophysis here is a thin ossicle oriented parallel to the shaft, whereas an avulsion fracture line runs transversely.
base of the metacarpal of the thumb: Proximal end of the shortest and most radial metacarpal, articulating with the trapezium at the saddle-shaped first carpometacarpal joint; the thumb ray is confirmed by having only two phalanges. The index metacarpal base instead articulates mainly with the trapezoid.
base of the patella: Flatter superior aspect of the patella receiving the quadriceps tendon; patellar parts are named by shape rather than position, so the base lies on top and the pointed apex inferiorly, giving origin to the patellar ligament.
base of the right 5th metatarsal: Expanded proximal end of the fifth metatarsal bearing the laterally projecting styloid tuberosity and articulating with the cuboid; the cuboid lies proximal to that joint line, and an avulsion fracture through the base runs transversely.
base of the right fourth metacarpal (rin: Proximal end of the ring-finger metacarpal, articulating with the hamate at the carpometacarpal joint; orientate using the hamate and pisiform on the ulnar side and count in from the little finger. The head is the opposite, rounded distal end at the MCP joint.
base of the second metatarsal: The proximal end recessed backwards into the mortise between the medial and lateral cuneiforms, articulating with the shorter intermediate cuneiform; it is the keystone of the Lisfranc joint. Its medial cortex should align with the medial border of the intermediate cuneiform on dorsoplantar views.
base of the third metacarpal: Bone articulating with the capitate, and on a sagittal wrist image the most distal element of the straight line radius, lunate, capitate, third metacarpal; loss of that alignment indicates lunate or perilunate dislocation.
base of third metacarpal: The distal end of the straight sagittal line radius, lunate, capitate, third metacarpal, articulating with the capitate; disruption of that alignment indicates a lunate or perilunate dislocation.
base of third metacarpal bone: Sits just distal to the carpometacarpal joint line and articulates with the capitate; its dorsoradial styloid process is characteristic. The capitate is the rounded bone immediately proximal to that joint line, within the distal carpal row.
base of thumb epiphysis: Look at the proximal end: in the thumb the secondary ossification centre lies at the base, separated from the shaft by a lucent physis, the thumb metacarpal being unique among metacarpals in this and matching the phalanges. The index to little finger metacarpals ossify from a centre at the head instead.
base of tongue: Soft-tissue mass filling the oropharynx behind the mandible and above the epiglottis on the lateral neck radiograph, its posterior surface forming the front wall of the oropharyngeal air column; the air-filled valleculae separate it from the epiglottis below.
basilic vein: Superficial vein on the medial or ulnar side of the forearm and arm which pierces the deep fascia in mid-arm to join the brachial veins as the axillary vein; the cephalic vein is its lateral counterpart, entering the axillary vein at the deltopectoral groove.
basivertebral vein: Midline vein lying within the horizontal channel through the centre of the vertebral body and draining posteriorly into the internal vertebral (epidural) plexus; linear, high signal on T2, and it may enhance strikingly with gadolinium.
basivertebral vein of l3: Vein running in the horizontal channel through the middle of the L3 body and opening posteriorly into the epidural plexus; prominent enhancement after gadolinium is normal here and does not indicate a lesion.
belly of infraspinatus: Muscle filling the infraspinous fossa on the back of the scapula below the spine, lying posterior to the glenoid on axial sections; supraspinatus appears only on higher slices above the spine, and teres minor is the smaller muscle below.
belly of supraspinatus: Feathered muscle filling the supraspinous fossa above the scapular spine and medial to the acromion; distal to it the uniformly dark tendon is the part that passes through the subacromial space, so belly and tendon must not be interchanged.
biceps: Superficial anterior arm muscle with two heads converging on a single distal tendon that dives posteriorly to the radial tuberosity; brachialis, its usual mimic, lies deep to it, plastered on the anterior distal humerus, and inserts on the ulna.
biceps brachii and brachialis: Bulk of the anterior humeral compartment lying in front of the distal humeral shaft on a lateral elbow view; these are the principal elbow flexors, biceps crossing to the radial tuberosity and brachialis lying deeper and inserting on the ulnar coronoid, aided by brachioradialis in mid-pronation.
biceps brachii muscle: Superficial muscle of the anterior arm lying directly in front of brachialis, with the long head tendon in the intertubercular groove and a distal tendon to the radial tuberosity plus an aponeurosis over the antecubital fossa; brachialis lies deep to it and inserts on the ulnar coronoid.
biceps brachii muscle tendon (long head): Round, uniformly dark tendon sitting in the intertubercular (bicipital) groove between greater and lesser tuberosities on axial images, traceable proximally over the humeral head to the supraglenoid tubercle; the subscapularis tendon lies medial to it, heading for the lesser tuberosity.
biceps brachii tendon: At the shoulder this is the long head: a small round low-signal structure lying in the intertubercular groove or arching over the humeral head towards the supraglenoid tubercle; the short head tendon lies medially with coracobrachialis on the coracoid.
biceps brachii tendon (long head, in bic: Small round black tendon lying in the groove between the greater and lesser tuberosities on axial images, roofed by the transverse humeral ligament; the subscapularis tendon is the broader striated structure medial to it, running to the lesser tuberosity.
biceps femoris: Posterolateral hamstring running from the ischial tuberosity (long head) and linea aspera (short head) to the fibular head; on axial images it is the lateral-most posterior compartment muscle, whereas semimembranosus and semitendinosus lie posteromedially.
biceps femoris muscle: Posterolateral muscle of the sciatic-innervated posterior compartment, arising with the other hamstrings from the ischial tuberosity and running laterally towards the fibular head; semitendinosus and semimembranosus lie medial to it and vastus lateralis lies anterior across the intermuscular septum.
biceps tendon: Thick dark cord running obliquely and posterolaterally from the muscle across the antecubital fossa to insert on the radial tuberosity; brachialis, its deeper neighbour, remains muscular at this level and attaches to the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity.
bicipital groove: Vertical sulcus on the anterior proximal humerus between the greater tuberosity laterally and the lesser tuberosity medially, transmitting the long head of biceps tendon; it is profiled as a notch on a tangential view and lies proximal to the surgical neck.
bifid spinous process: Posterior midline process split into two prongs, the usual appearance of the mid-cervical vertebrae; C7, the vertebra prominens, instead has a single long non-bifid process, useful for confirming level.
bifid spinous process of c4 vertebra: Seen end-on in the midline of the frontal cervical radiograph as a paired or notched double density, the normal bifid form of the mid-cervical spinous processes; establish the level by counting up from the rib-bearing T1.
bipartite hallucal sesamoid bone: Sesamoid beneath the first metatarsal head split into two fragments with smooth rounded corticated margins, the combined bone often appearing larger than its partner; usually the medial (tibial) sesamoid and frequently bilateral. A fracture instead shows sharp, uncorticated fragments that reconstitute a normal-sized sesamoid.
bipartite patella: Accessory ossification centre at the superolateral corner of the patella, separated by a smooth lucency, with rounded corticated margins on both fragments and often bilateral. A fracture has sharp uncorticated edges, fragments that fit together exactly, and usually an accompanying effusion.
blade of left scapula: Flat thin plate of bone forming the vertical stem of the Y, projected over ribs and lung with faint cortical margins. Unlike the humeral shaft beside it, it has no medullary canal or thick parallel cortices.
blade of scapula: Thin triangular flat bone projected over the upper posterior thorax, relatively lucent and bounded by a dense thick lateral border descending to the inferior angle; on the swimmer's view it lies behind the raised humerus, which is denser and tubular.
body of c2 vertebra: Block of bone directly beneath the dens, from whose upper surface the peg arises, with the large bifid spinous process behind; C1 above has no body at all, only a small anterior arch.
body of corpus callosum: Arching band immediately above the cavum septum pellucidum on the midline sagittal view, relatively hypoechoic with brighter margins and the pericallosal artery along its upper surface; the body is the flat middle part between genu and splenium.
body of hyoid bone: Anterior midline bar of the U-shaped hyoid, seen on the lateral neck film as a short dense horizontal stripe at about the C3 level above the thyroid cartilage. It has no bony articulation, lying suspended above and separate from the thyroid cartilage below.
body of mandible: Horizontal tooth-bearing part of the mandible running from the midline symphysis back to the angle, where it turns upwards into the ramus; the ramus is the vertical portion carrying the condylar and coronoid processes.
body of pancreas: Mid-portion of the gland crossing the midline on transverse epigastric ultrasound, immediately deep to the left lobe of liver and stomach and lying anterior to the splenic vein and superior mesenteric artery. The splenic vein along its posterior surface is the key identifying landmark.
body of pubic bone: The flat, squarer medial portion of the pubis abutting the symphysis, from which the superior ramus runs superolaterally to the acetabulum and the inferior ramus descends to meet the ischium. It forms the medial boundary of the obturator foramen.
body of right zygoma: Quadrilateral mass of the cheekbone lateral to the maxillary antrum, forming the inferolateral orbital rim; on Water's view it is the elephant's face, with the temporal process running back as the trunk (zygomatic arch) and the frontal process rising to the orbital margin.
body of scapula: Flat triangular blade lying against the posterior chest wall, forming the vertically descending limb of the Y on the lateral scapular projection. Do not mistake the blade for the scapular spine, which lies more posteriorly and runs out into the acromion.
body of sphenoid: Central block of bone at the skull base between the greater wings, hollowed by the sphenoid sinus and carrying the pituitary fossa on its upper surface; the greater wing is the plate spreading laterally to form the lateral orbital wall.
body of sternum: Middle and longest part of the sternum, seen on the lateral chest film as the flat plate below the manubrium. Its junction with the manubrium is the sternal angle at the second costal cartilage, and the small xiphoid process continues below it.
body of the c1 vertebra (anterior arch): C1 has no true body; its equivalent is the anterior arch, seen as a small oval ring of bone directly in front of the dens on the lateral view, with the predental space between them normally under about 3 mm in adults.
body of the c2 vertebra: Block of bone directly beneath the dens, which rises from its upper surface, and above the C2/C3 disc; the incomplete Harris ring is projected over it on the lateral. Unlike C1 above, C2 has a true vertebral body.
body of the hyoid bone: Midline transverse bar of bone lying anterior to the airway at about the C3 level, with the greater cornua sweeping backwards from each end; calcified thyroid cartilage lies lower and is broader.
body of the left hemimandible: Horizontal tooth-bearing part of the mandible, running obliquely across the lower part of the open-mouth view; it lies anterior to the angle, unlike the ramus, which ascends vertically from the angle to the condyle and carries no teeth.
brachial artery: Continuation of the axillary artery from the lower border of teres major, running down the medial then anterior arm with the median nerve and crossing the cubital fossa medial to the biceps tendon. It divides at the radial neck into radial and ulnar arteries.
brachial vein: Deep vein of the upper arm, usually paired and running either side of the brachial artery within the medial neurovascular bundle. The basilic vein it is confused with lies superficially in the subcutaneous fat medially until it pierces the deep fascia.
brachialis: Broad muscle lying deep to biceps directly on the anterior surface of the distal humerus, crossing the joint to insert on the ulnar tuberosity and coronoid. Biceps is superficial to it and its tendon crosses laterally to the radial tuberosity.
brachialis muscle: Flat muscle applied directly to the anterior surface of the distal humerus, deep to biceps, running to the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity; biceps lies superficial to it and its tendon passes to the radial tuberosity.
brachiocephalic (innominate) vein: Long, almost horizontal vein sweeping across the superior mediastinum anterior to the arch branches, formed behind the left sternoclavicular joint by the left subclavian and internal jugular veins; the right brachiocephalic is short and nearly vertical.
brachiocephalic vein: Crosses the midline obliquely behind the manubrium from left to right to join its fellow and form the superior vena cava; its interface with lung fades above the clavicles as the vein runs more anteriorly and merges with the chest wall shadow.
brachioradialis: Most lateral (radial) muscle of the proximal anterior forearm, arising from the lateral supracondylar ridge and forming the superficial bulge along the radial border; extensor carpi radialis longus lies just deep and posterior to it.
brachioradialis muscle: Most lateral muscle of the proximal forearm anteriorly, arising from the lateral supracondylar ridge and lying superficial along the radial border; flexor carpi ulnaris is the corresponding most medial muscle.
branch of right portal vein: Intrahepatic vessel within the right lobe with bright, clearly echogenic walls from the surrounding fibrofatty Glisson sheath, traceable back to the porta hepatis; hepatic veins are the usual confusion and have thin, imperceptible walls and course towards the IVC.
bregma: Midline point in the anterior vault where the coronal sutures meet the sagittal suture, corresponding to the diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle in the infant. The lambda is the equivalent posterior junction of sagittal and lambdoid sutures.
bronchus intermedius: Air column continuing down from the right main bronchus once the upper lobe bronchus has left, ending at the middle lobe origin; the interlobar artery lies immediately lateral to it, and its posterior wall can be seen as a thin line on the lateral film.
c2 vertebral body: Body of the axis, identified by the odontoid peg projecting upward from its superior surface and by the large bifid spinous process behind. It lies immediately below C1, which is distinguished by having a ring with lateral masses and no vertebral body at all.
c2–3 interspace: First true intervertebral disc space, a horizontal lucent gap at the bottom of the open-mouth view below the C2 body; the atlantoaxial joints above it are synovial facet joints lying laterally, not disc spaces.
c3/c4 facet joint: Lucent line in the articular pillar column between the descending inferior articular process of C3 and the ascending superior articular process of C4; count down from C2, whose body carries the dens. The joints slope posteroinferiorly and should overlap when not rotated.
c3–c4 facet joint: Zygapophyseal joint between the inferior articular process of C3 and the superior articular process of C4, seen on the lateral view as a thin lucent line between the shingled articular pillars, behind the vertebral bodies and in front of the spinous processes.
c4 nerve root: Exits through the C3/4 intervertebral foramen, above the pedicle of C4 — cervical roots leave above their numbered vertebra, so the foramen one level higher than the named body is the one to point to (only C8 exits below C7).
c7 spinous process: Longest and most prominent cervical spinous process, typically not bifid, at the base of the neck; confirm the level by counting up from T1, the first vertebra bearing a full-length rib.
c7 vertebra: Last cervical vertebra, identified on the frontal film as the one immediately above T1, the first to carry a full-length rib; a cervical rib may arise from C7 but is much shorter and thinner than a true first rib.
c7/t1 intervertebral disc space: Lowest cervical disc space, which must be seen for the lateral radiograph to be adequate and is often obscured by the shoulders. Identify C7 by its long non-bifid spinous process and downward-pointing transverse processes, with T1 below bearing the first rib.
c7/t1 joint (interspace): Disc space at the cervicothoracic junction, immediately above the first rib-bearing vertebra; it is the level most often hidden by overlapping shoulders on the lateral film, which is exactly why the swimmer's view is performed.
caecum: Wide-calibre gas- and faeces-filled bowel in the right iliac fossa continuing upwards as the ascending colon; its haustral folds are thick and do not cross the full lumen, unlike the fine complete valvulae conniventes of small bowel.
calcaneal tuberosity: The posterior prominence of the calcaneus forming the heel, seen as the posteroinferior corner on a lateral view; the Achilles tendon inserts on its posterior surface and the plantar fascia arises from its plantar (medial) process. Distinguish from the anterior process, which abuts the cuboid.
calcaneocuboid joint: Articulation between the anterior surface of the calcaneus and the proximal cuboid, forming the lateral half of the midtarsal joint; on the oblique view it should align with the medially placed talonavicular joint in a smooth continuous arc.
calcaneous: Largest tarsal bone, forming the heel: posteroinferior in the hindfoot, articulating with the talus above at the subtalar joint and the cuboid in front. Distinguish from the talus, which sits above it and alone articulates with the tibia.
calcaneum: Largest tarsal bone, forming the heel below and behind the talus and articulating anteriorly with the cuboid; it is ossified at birth, unlike most tarsals. The talus, its neighbour, lies above it and articulates with the tibia in the ankle mortise.
calcaneus: Largest tarsal bone forming the heel, seen on the lateral view as the elongated posteroinferior bone carrying the talus on its upper surface. In an infant foot it is one of the few tarsals already ossified, and is the longest and most posterior of them.
calcification within laryngeal cartilage: Irregular, often asymmetric dense flecks or plaques within the thyroid, cricoid and arytenoid cartilages lying anterior to the C4–C6 bodies; their expected anatomical position and increasing frequency with age distinguish them from a swallowed radio-opaque foreign body.
calcified stylohyoid ligament: Thin vertical ossified band running downwards and forwards from the styloid process just anteroinferior to the mastoid towards the lesser horn of the hyoid, often crossing the mandibular ramus on an orthopantomogram. Continuity with the skull base separates it from an unrelated calcified node.
capital femoral epiphysis: Rounded ossification centre capping the femoral neck above the growth plate and seated in the acetabulum; in a slip it looks shorter, the physis widens, and a line drawn along the superior femoral neck no longer intersects it.
capitate: Largest carpal bone, occupying the centre of the distal row with its rounded head seated in the concavity of the lunate and its distal surface meeting the base of the third metacarpal. Distinguish from the hamate, which lies ulnar to it and carries the hook.
capitate. this is the largest carpal bon: Largest, centrally placed carpal bone whose rounded proximal head sits in the distal concavity of the lunate, aligned with the third metacarpal; the hamate lies ulnar to it and carries the volar hook.
capitellum: Rounded lateral articular surface of the distal humerus, facing the radial head; the first ossification centre to appear, within the first year. Distinguish from the trochlea, the spool-shaped medial surface taking the ulna, which ossifies around nine years.
capitellum epiphysis: First elbow centre to ossify, within the first year: a rounded nucleus capping the lateral articular surface of the distal humerus and facing the radial head directly. A line drawn along the radial neck should pass through it on every projection.
capitellum left humerus: Rounded lateral condyle of the distal humerus that articulates with the radial head, with the radiocapitellar line passing through it on every view; the trochlea lies medially, is grooved like a spool and takes the trochlear notch of the ulna.
capitellum of humerus: Rounded lateral articular surface of the distal humerus, articulating with the radial head; the first elbow ossification centre to appear. A line drawn along the radial neck should pass through it, and the trochlea is its spool-shaped medial neighbour taking the ulna.
capitellum of right humerus: Rounded lateral condyle of the distal humerus articulating with the radial head, through which the anterior humeral line should pass on a true lateral; the trochlea, its mimic, lies medially, is spool-shaped with a central groove, and articulates with the ulna.
capitellum of the left humerus: Rounded lateral portion of the distal humeral articular surface, always aligned with and articulating with the radial head. The trochlea is the medial spool-shaped surface that takes the trochlear notch of the ulna.
capitulum: Rounded lateral articular condyle of the distal humerus which receives the radial head; a line drawn along the radial neck should pass through it on every projection. The trochlea is medial and spool-shaped, articulating with the ulna instead.
capitulum of distal humerus: Smooth rounded lateral articular surface of the distal humerus, articulating only with the radial head; the trochlea is its medial, spool-shaped neighbour which takes the ulna. On any view a line along the radial neck must pass through the capitulum.
capitulum of humerus: Rounded lateral articular condyle of the distal humerus receiving the radial head, so a line drawn along the radial neck should pass through it in every projection; the trochlea is the medial, spool-shaped surface articulating with the ulna.
capitulum of the humerus: Rounded lateral articular knuckle of the distal humerus capped by cartilage and articulating with the shallow concave head of the radius; the trochlea is medial, grooved like a pulley, and articulates with the ulna.
capitulum ossification centre: First elbow ossification centre to appear, seen as a small density at the lateral aspect of the distal humeral metaphysis. Unlike the radial head centre it sits on the humeral side of the joint, and the radial shaft line should point directly at it.
cardiophrenic recess: The acute angle where the right heart border meets the right hemidiaphragm, often occupied by a triangular fat pad. Do not confuse it with the costophrenic angle, which is the lateral recess between the chest wall and the diaphragm.
carina: Point where the tracheal air column divides into the two main bronchi, the left more horizontal and the right more vertical. Use it as the reference for endotracheal tube tip position; the aortic arch lies above it, indenting the trachea from the left.
carpo-metacarpal joint of the thumb. thi: Saddle-shaped joint between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal at the radial base of the thenar eminence; the scaphotrapezial joint lies immediately proximal to it, on the other side of the trapezium.
cartilaginous acetabular roof: Hypoechoic band continuing laterally from the bony acetabular margin and curving over the unossified femoral head, tipped by the small echogenic triangular labrum; it provides the roof line for the beta angle, whereas the brightly echogenic bony roof defines alpha.
cauda equina: Bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots descending within the thecal sac below the conus medullaris, seen as multiple discrete dots on axial T2 (dependent posteriorly when supine) or as fine parallel strands on sagittal images, in contrast to the single continuous tubular cord above.
cauda equina in the thecal sac: Cluster of punctate low-signal dots suspended in the bright CSF of the thecal sac on axial T2, gravitating to the dependent posterior part of the sac below the conus at L1/L2.
caudate lobe of liver: Segment 1, seen on the sagittal epigastric view as the wedge of liver lying between the left lobe anteriorly, separated by the echogenic fissure for the ligamentum venosum, and the inferior vena cava posteriorly.
caudate nucleus head: Rounded mass forming the floor and lateral wall of the frontal horn of the lateral ventricle on the coronal view, separated from the thalamus behind by the caudothalamic groove, the site scrutinised for germinal matrix haemorrhage.
cavum septum pellucidum: Anechoic fluid-filled box in the midline between the frontal horns, roofed by the corpus callosum and bounded below by the fornices, a normal finding in preterm infants; the third ventricle is the narrower slit lower down between the thalami.
central incisor: Midline-most tooth of the dental arch, with a dense enamel-capped crown and a single tapering root, projected over the dens on the open-mouth peg view; the transverse lucency at its neck is a classic mimic of an odontoid fracture.
cephalic vein: Superficial vein running up the radial side of the forearm and the lateral aspect of the arm, ascending in the deltopectoral groove to join the axillary vein near the shoulder; it lies outside the deep fascia, unlike the paired brachial veins that flank the brachial artery.
cerebellum: Rounded, distinctly echogenic mass in the posterior fossa below the tentorium on midline sagittal neonatal ultrasound, the vermis being the brightest structure on the image. It sits behind and below the brainstem, separating it from the supratentorial occipital lobe above the tentorium.
cervical rib: Extra rib arising from the C7 transverse process above the first rib; C7's transverse process points inferolaterally whereas T1's points superolaterally, which is the reliable way to separate a cervical rib from a hypoplastic first rib.
channel for basivertebral veins: Horizontal, sometimes Y-shaped cleft through the middle of the vertebral body reaching a small notch in the posterior cortex; it carries the vein and marrow fat and should not be read as a fracture line.
choroid plexus: Echogenic, smooth-outlined tissue lining the lateral ventricle on neonatal cranial ultrasound, tapering anteriorly and never extending in front of the caudothalamic groove. Bulky irregular echogenicity anterior to that groove is germinal matrix haemorrhage, not normal plexus.
cingulate gyrus: Gyrus arching immediately above and around the corpus callosum on the midline sagittal view, separated from it by the echogenic pericallosal sulcus carrying the pericallosal artery, and bounded superiorly by the cingulate sulcus.
circumflex humeral artery: Anterior and posterior branches of the third part of the axillary artery that curve around the surgical neck of the humerus, seen encircling the proximal humeral metaphysis; the circumflex scapular, by contrast, arises from the subscapular artery and turns backwards to the lateral scapular border.
clavicle: S-shaped bone crossing the top of the thorax from the sternoclavicular joint medially to the acromion laterally. On a frontal chest film its medial ends should sit equidistant from the spinous processes, which is how adequacy of rotation is judged.
clavicle (lateral part): Lateral third of the clavicle is flattened and concave forwards as it runs out to meet the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint; trace the long S-shaped tubular bone from the sternum. The acromion, by contrast, is the broad flat continuation of the scapular spine.
clivus: Sloping bar of dense bone running downwards and backwards from the dorsum sellae to the anterior margin of the foramen magnum on the lateral skull view; the dorsum sellae above it is the short vertical wall forming the back of the pituitary fossa.
coalition of lunate and triquetral: Loss of the normal joint space between the lunate and triquetral in the proximal carpal row, with trabeculae running continuously across so the two form one ulnar-sided block; identify each carpal in turn and the absent interval becomes obvious.
coccyx: Small triangular terminal segment of the spine, three to five rudimentary fused vertebrae hanging below the sacral apex and curving anteriorly on the lateral view, separated from the last sacral segment by the sacrococcygeal joint.
coeliac axis: Short anterior branch of the aorta arising immediately below the diaphragmatic hiatus and dividing into splenic artery to the left and common hepatic artery to the right, giving the seagull appearance on transverse ultrasound. The SMA arises just below it and runs caudally parallel to the aorta.
common bile duct: Thin anechoic tube running anterior to the portal vein at the porta hepatis, forming the anterolateral element of the portal triad; the hepatic artery, its main mimic, crosses between duct and portal vein and fills on colour Doppler while the duct does not.
common carotid artery: On an arch angiogram the left common carotid is the second arch branch, arising directly from the arch and ascending vertically in the neck without branching until the bifurcation. The subclavian, by contrast, courses laterally towards the arm; on ultrasound the carotid is round, pulsatile and non-compressible.
common extensor tendon: Low-signal tendon arising from the lateral epicondyle and continuing into the extensor muscles of the forearm; its counterpart, the common flexor tendon, arises from the medial epicondyle, so laterality on the image settles which is which.
common extensor tendon (lateral epicondy: Low-signal tendon on the lateral epicondyle, mirror image of the common flexor tendon, continuing into the extensor muscle bellies of the posterior forearm; the radial collateral ligament lies deep to it and blends with the annular ligament around the radial head.
common extensor tendon insertion: Short dark tendon attached to the lateral epicondyle, the origin of the superficial extensors and the site of tennis elbow; the lateral collateral ligament complex lies deeper, running to the annular ligament and ulna, with the flexor tendon medially.
common femoral vein (cfv): Thin-walled, readily compressible vessel lying medial to the common femoral artery in the groin and receiving the great saphenous vein at the saphenofemoral junction; compressibility, absence of pulsation and phasic rather than pulsatile flow separate it from the artery.
common flexor tendon: Conjoined tendon arising from the anterior aspect of the medial epicondyle, the non-articular prominence on the ulnar side of the distal humerus, giving origin to pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis. The common extensor tendon mirrors it from the lateral epicondyle.
common flexor tendon (medial epicondyle: Short low-signal tendon arising from the medial epicondyle, giving origin to pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis and ulnaris, palmaris longus and flexor digitorum superficialis; the ulnar collateral ligament lies deeper and passes to the ulna rather than into muscle.
common flexor tendon insertion: Short dark tendon anchored to the medial epicondyle of the humerus, the origin of the superficial flexor-pronator group; deep to it the ulnar collateral ligament runs to the sublime tubercle of the ulna, and the common extensor tendon lies on the lateral side.
common iliac artery: Arises at the aortic bifurcation around the L4 level and runs inferolaterally across the sacroiliac joint before dividing into external and internal iliac arteries. It lies proximal to that division, whereas the external iliac continues on to become the femoral artery beneath the inguinal ligament.
common peroneal nerve: Terminal division of the sciatic nerve that runs along the lateral border of the popliteal fossa and then winds subcutaneously around the fibular neck, so it is localised to that bony landmark; the tibial nerve instead continues vertically down the middle of the fossa.
companion shadow of left clavicle: Thin soft-tissue line running parallel to and hugging the upper border of the clavicle, produced by skin and subcutaneous tissue seen tangentially. It follows the bone exactly, unlike an apical pleural cap or pneumothorax line, which follows the lung contour.
condylar process of the mandible: Posterior of the two projections from the top of the mandibular ramus, made up of a narrow neck and a rounded head that forms the mandibular side of the temporomandibular joint. The coronoid process in front of it is flat and pointed and articulates with nothing.
condyle of mandible: Rounded articular head capping the neck at the posterosuperior corner of the mandibular ramus, seated in the mandibular fossa just in front of the external auditory canal. It is the posterior of the two upper ramus projections; the pointed coronoid process lies anteriorly.
confluence of splenic vein and superior: The rounded head of the transverse epigastric tadpole, with the splenic vein forming the tail running to the left; it lies behind the pancreatic neck and in front of the IVC, and marks where the portal vein begins.
confluence of the radial and ulnar veins: Point in the proximal forearm where the paired deep radial and ulnar venae comitantes unite to form the brachial veins, lying deep and flanking the brachial artery; the cephalic and basilic veins are the separate, more peripheral subcutaneous channels.
conoid tubercle: Bony prominence on the posteroinferior surface of the lateral third of the clavicle, giving attachment to the conoid part of the coracoclavicular ligament; the trapezoid line runs anterolaterally from it towards the acromial end.
conus medullaris: Tapered caudal tip of the spinal cord, normally ending at the L1/L2 level, below which the cauda equina roots descend as separate strands; distinguish it from the filum terminale, a single thin midline strand continuing caudally from its apex.
coraco-acromial ligament (cal): Strong band running from the lateral edge of the coracoid process to the undersurface of the acromion, completing the arch that roofs the supraspinatus tendon; the coracoclavicular ligaments instead run upwards from the coracoid to the clavicle.
coracoclavicular, coracoacromial and cor: All three radiate from the coracoid process, so the labelled point is the coracoid: coracoclavicular to the undersurface of the lateral clavicle, coracoacromial to the acromion, coracohumeral to the humeral tubercles. None is visible as a density itself.
coracoid process: Beak-like anterior projection from the upper scapular neck, projected medial to and overlapping the glenoid on a frontal shoulder film. On the scapular Y view it is the anterior fork of the Y, lying closest to the ribs; the acromion is the posterior fork.
coracoid process of left scapula: Short hooked process projecting anteriorly from the upper scapula, forming the anterior limb of the Y on the lateral scapular view; it always points forwards. The acromion is the posterior limb, continuous with the scapular spine and reaching the clavicle.
coracoid process of scapula: Short anteriorly directed hook from the anterosuperior scapula, projected on the chest radiograph as a well-defined density over the humeral head or upper lung zone medial to the acromion; pectoralis minor and the conjoint tendon attach to it.
coracoid process of the left scapula: Beak-like process arising from the upper scapula just medial to the glenoid and projecting anterolaterally, so on an AP it is seen obliquely below and medial to the acromion. The acromion is more lateral and meets the clavicle.
coracoid process of the right scapula: Beak-like process projecting anteriorly from the superolateral scapula; on a frontal chest film it is the rounded density over the upper lateral chest just below and medial to the acromioclavicular joint, while the acromion lies further laterally, capping the humeral head.
coracoid process of the scapula: Most anterior part of the scapula, projecting forwards and laterally just anterior to the glenoid with pectoralis minor and the conjoint tendon attached; the acromion lies posterosuperiorly, roofing the humeral head.
coronal suture: Serrated lucency running obliquely downwards and forwards from bregma on each side, separating the frontal bone in front from the parietal bone behind. On a lateral skull film it is the anterior of the two large curving sutures; the lambdoid lies posteriorly.
coronoid fossa of the humerus: Shallow hollow on the anterior surface of the distal humerus just above the trochlea, receiving the ulnar coronoid process in full flexion; the olecranon fossa is the deeper counterpart on the posterior surface, and the radial fossa lies anteriorly above the capitulum.
coronoid process: In the mandible, the pointed triangular process at the front of the top of the ramus, separated by the mandibular notch from the rounded condyle behind, which is the part that articulates and translates forward on opening. In the elbow, the anterior beak of the proximal ulna forming the front of the trochlear notch.
coronoid process mandible: Anterior, triangular and pointed of the two upward projections of the mandibular ramus, separated from the rounded posterior condylar process by the mandibular notch; on a 3D lateral view it disappears deep to the zygomatic arch.
coronoid process of mandible: Triangular, upward-pointing anterior projection from the top of the mandibular ramus giving attachment to temporalis; separated by the mandibular (sigmoid) notch from the rounded condylar head, which is the posterior projection articulating at the temporomandibular joint.
coronoid process of right mandible: Pointed triangular process rising from the front of the mandibular ramus for temporalis attachment; on the occipitomental view it is projected over the lower maxillary antrum and can mimic sinus opacity. The condyle is the rounded process further posteriorly at the temporomandibular joint.
coronoid process of right ulna: Triangular anterior beak of the proximal ulna forming the anterior/distal lip of the trochlear notch, best profiled on the lateral view where it sits just below the trochlea; the olecranon is the opposite, posterosuperior lip of the same notch.
coronoid process of the left ulna: Anterior triangular beak of the proximal ulna forming the front lip of the trochlear notch, received into the coronoid fossa in flexion. The olecranon is the larger posterior process behind it.
coronoid process of the mandible: Pointed triangular projection from the anterosuperior ramus of the mandible, the insertion of temporalis, which passes medial to the zygomatic arch to reach it; it is separated by the mandibular notch from the rounded condylar head lying posteriorly at the temporomandibular joint.
coronoid process of the ulna: Triangular anterior beak of the proximal ulna forming the lower lip of the trochlear notch and lying beneath the trochlea on the lateral view. The olecranon is the opposite, posterosuperior projection forming the upper lip of the same notch.
coronoid process of the ulna (left): Anterior triangular beak of the proximal ulna forming the anterior lip of the trochlear notch, seen on the lateral view projecting forwards beneath the trochlea; the olecranon is the larger posterior process of the same notch.
coronoid process of ulna: Triangular anterior beak of the proximal ulna forming the front lip of the trochlear notch and received into the coronoid fossa of the humerus on flexion. On the lateral elbow it is the anterior projection lying beneath the anterior fat pad; the olecranon is the posterior beak.
corpus callosum: Curved midline band arching over the cavum septi pellucidi and third ventricle on the midsagittal view, hypoechoic with bright upper and lower margins, thickened anteriorly as the genu and posteriorly as the splenium; the cingulate gyrus lies just above it beyond the pericallosal sulcus.
costophrenic angle: Sharp acute recess where the lateral hemidiaphragm meets the ribs on the frontal film, crisp and pointed when normal and blunted by pleural fluid; the cardiophrenic angle is the corresponding medial recess beside the heart.
costotransverse joint: Small posterolateral articulation between the tubercle of the rib and the anterior surface of the transverse process. Distinguish it from the costovertebral joint, which lies more anteromedially between the rib head and the vertebral body and disc.
costovertebral joint: Anteromedial articulation between the head of the rib and the vertebral body and adjacent disc. The costotransverse joint lies more laterally and posteriorly, between the rib tubercle and the transverse process.
crista galli: Diamond-shaped midline bony density at the level of the superior orbits on a frontal skull radiograph, projecting up from the cribriform plate of the ethmoid as the anterior attachment of the falx; below it the midline density continues as the nasal septum.
crown of unerupted right inferior third: Dense enamel-capped crown lying below the level of the alveolar crest in the posterior mandible near the anterior border of the ramus, with no part projecting into the mouth and roots often incompletely formed.
crown, neck and root: Crown is the dense enamel-capped portion projecting above the gum line, the neck the constriction at the alveolar margin, and the root the tapering part within the socket, outlined by the thin lucent periodontal ligament space and its adjacent lamina dura.
cuboid: Lateral midfoot bone wedged between the anterior surface of the calcaneus behind and the bases of the fourth and fifth metatarsals in front. Confused with the navicular, which lies medially between the talar head and the three cuneiforms.
deep artery of the thigh (profunda femor: On axial CT, the vessel that peels off the common femoral artery and runs posterolaterally deep to the superficial femoral artery, passing behind adductor longus to give circumflex femoral branches; the SFA stays anterior and superficial with the femoral vein.

Large branch leaving the posterolateral aspect of the common femoral artery a few centimetres below the inguinal ligament and coursing deep and laterally to give circumflex femoral and perforating branches; the superficial femoral artery is the vessel continuing vertically down the thigh without significant branches.
deep brachial artery (profunda brachii): First and largest branch of the brachial artery, arising just below the lower border of teres major and passing posterolaterally with the radial nerve into the spiral groove behind the humerus; the superior ulnar collateral is smaller and descends medially instead.
deep brachial veins: Paired venae comitantes running either side of the brachial artery deep to the fascia in the medial arm, appearing as two parallel channels with frequent cross-connections; the basilic vein is a single larger superficial channel that pierces the deep fascia in mid-arm to join them.
deltoid: Thick muscle forming the rounded contour of the shoulder, sweeping from clavicle, acromion and scapular spine over the humeral head to the deltoid tuberosity. On axial MRI it is the outermost muscle layer, separated from the rotator cuff by the subdeltoid fat plane.
deltoid muscle: Thick muscle capping the shoulder and forming the outermost layer on axial images, wrapping the humeral head superficial to the subacromial bursa and rotator cuff. It arises from the lateral clavicle, acromion and scapular spine and converges onto the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.
deltoid tuberosity of humerus: Roughened V-shaped cortical thickening on the anterolateral surface of the humerus about halfway down the shaft, marking the deltoid insertion; it blends smoothly with normal cortex and lacks a lucent cleft, unlike periosteal reaction or a fracture line.
dens: Solid vertical peg rising from the top of the C2 body in the midline, articulating anteriorly with the arch of C1 and held by the transverse ligament. On the frontal open-mouth view it sits centrally between the C1 lateral masses with symmetrical gaps either side.
dens (odontoid peg): Vertical peg continuous inferiorly with the superior surface of the C2 body, its tip pointing towards the basion; unlike an overlying tooth root it has no enamel cap and merges seamlessly into the vertebral body below.
dens (odontoid peg) of c2: Central vertical peg on the open-mouth view with equal gaps to each C1 lateral mass, arising from and continuous with the C2 body below; the overlying incisors and occiput create horizontal lucent lines that must not be called a fracture.
dens/ odontoid peg: Peg-shaped process rising vertically from the body of C2 and sitting midway between the lateral masses of C1 on the open-mouth view; overlying incisor teeth and the hard palate cast horizontal lucent lines across it that mimic fracture.
dentine: Bulk of the tooth deep to the enamel, of intermediate density, surrounding the lucent pulp chamber and continuing down into the root. It appears greyer than the very white enamel cap, which covers only the crown and stops at the neck.
descending colon: Gas- and faeces-containing bowel running vertically in the left flank, peripheral and fixed because it is retroperitoneal, surrounded by fat that outlines it. Haustra, mottled faecal gas and peripheral position separate it from centrally placed small bowel.
descending thoracic aorta: Straight, near-vertical interface descending from the aortic knuckle just left of the vertebral bodies, traceable through the cardiac shadow down to the diaphragm; the paraspinal line is fainter and hugs the vertebral margins more closely.
diaphragm: Bright curvilinear echogenic line capping the liver and spleen, moving with respiration, forming the interface with aerated lung; a mirror-image duplication of liver above it is characteristic and confirms you are at the diaphragm rather than a fissure.
diaphysis of the left fifth metatarsal: Long slender tubular midshaft of the lateral-most metatarsal, between the flared tuberosity at its base and the head distally; count metatarsals from the hallux to confirm, and do not confuse it with the base region where the apophysis and avulsion fractures occur.
diaphysis of the proximal phalanx of the: Shaft of the most proximal of the three phalanges of the second toe, articulating with the second metatarsal head at the metatarsophalangeal joint; proximal phalanges are the longest and most slender in each toe, whereas the middle phalanx is short and squat.
diaphysis of the right fibula: Slender tubular shaft of much smaller calibre than the tibia, running along its posterolateral side; on the lateral knee radiograph it projects behind the tibia below the expanded fibular head and neck.
diaphysis tibia: Long tubular midshaft between the flared metaphyses, with thick cortex, a narrow medullary canal and a subcutaneous anterior border; the tibia is the larger medial bone of the leg, the slender lateral one being the fibula.
diploic layer: Cancellous marrow-containing layer sandwiched between the inner and outer tables of the vault, seen as a slightly lucent band with fine trabeculation; the branching vascular channels within it have corticated, undulating margins, unlike the sharp lucent line of a fracture.
distal diaphysis of the humerus: Humeral shaft just proximal to the supracondylar flare and the coronoid and olecranon fossae; on the lateral view the anterior humeral line drawn down its anterior cortex should cross the middle third of the capitellum. Distal to it the bone widens and thins into the supracondylar region.
distal end of clavicle: Flattened lateral end of the S-shaped clavicle seen superomedially on coronal oblique shoulder images, meeting the acromion across the narrow acromioclavicular joint; the acromion is the lateral component, continuing posteriorly as the scapular spine.
