distal epiphyseal scar of the right tibi: Dense transverse line across the distal tibial metaphysis in the adult, marking the site of the fused growth plate; its smooth uniform transverse course across the full width of bone separates it from a fracture line.
distal femoral diaphysis: The tubular shaft above the knee with parallel cortices and a narrow medullary canal, proximal to the point where the bone flares into the metaphysis and condyles. If the cortex is diverging and the trabeculae are coarse, you are already in the metaphysis, not the diaphysis.
distal femoral epiphyseal (growth) plate: Transverse lucent band separating the ossified distal femoral epiphysis from the flared metaphysis above; do not mistake it for the joint space, which lies below the epiphysis between the femoral and tibial articular surfaces.
distal femoral epiphysis: Ossification centre at the far end of the femur, present at birth and separated from the flared metaphysis by a lucent physis; it lies above the knee joint, the proximal tibial epiphysis being the corresponding centre below.
distal fibula: Lateral of the two leg bones at the ankle; its lower end forms the lateral malleolus, which descends further and lies more posteriorly than the medial malleolus, abutting the lateral talus and bound to the tibia by the syndesmosis.
distal fibular epiphysis: Separate ossification centre at the lower end of the fibula, lateral to the distal tibial epiphysis and extending further distally, destined to become the lateral malleolus; the lucent line separating it from the metaphysis is the physis, not a fracture.
distal left clavicle: Lateral end of the S-shaped clavicle, flatter and broader than its shaft, ending at the acromioclavicular joint. Traced medially it heads towards the sternum, unlike the acromion, which continues backwards from the scapular spine.
distal phalanx of a parent's finger: Unexpected finger projecting into the field on a child's film, recognised by fully mature corticated adult bone and a soft-tissue outline that runs off the edge of the image; it belongs to whoever is holding the child still.
distal phalanx of the left great toe: Terminal broad segment of the hallux with an expanded distal tuft; the great toe has only two phalanges, so the bone distal to the interphalangeal joint is the distal phalanx, unlike the three-segment lesser toes.
distal pole of the scaphoid: Radial and volar end of the scaphoid, including its tubercle, articulating with trapezium and trapezoid near the thumb metacarpal base and lying anteriorly on the lateral view. The proximal pole is the opposite end, abutting the radius, and is the part at risk of avascular necrosis.
distal radial epiphysis: Ossific centre at the distal end of the radius, separated from the metaphysis by the lucent physis and lying between it and the carpus. In a toddler it is the only forearm epiphysis present, the distal ulnar centre appearing several years later.
distal radio-ulnar joint (druj): Narrow vertical space between the ulnar notch of the distal radius and the head of the ulna, just proximal to the radiocarpal joint; widening or malalignment indicates DRUJ disruption. The radiocarpal joint is the more distal curved space between radius and the scaphoid and lunate.
distal radioulnar joint: Narrow vertical lucency between the ulnar notch on the medial side of the distal radius and the head of the ulna, proximal to the triangular fibrocartilage. The radiocarpal joint is the transverse space distal to it, against scaphoid and lunate.
distal radius: Proximal element of the sagittal radius, lunate, capitate, third metacarpal line, with a concave articular surface facing the lunate and slight volar tilt; the ulna sits on the opposite side of the wrist and does not articulate with the lunate directly.
distal right fibular physis: Smooth transverse lucent band crossing the distal fibula just above the lateral malleolus, bordered by a dense zone of provisional calcification; its uniform width and intact adjacent cortex separate it from a Salter-Harris fracture, and it sits lateral to the wider tibial physis.
distal right radio-ulnar joint: Narrow vertical lucency between the ulnar notch of the distal radius and the head of the ulna, lying just proximal to the radiocarpal joint. The radiocarpal joint is the more distal curved space separating the radius from scaphoid and lunate.
distal tibial metaphysis: Flared segment of tibia immediately above the distal physis, wider than the diaphysis with thinner cortex and prominent trabeculae; the epiphysis is the separate ossified block on the joint side of the physeal lucency.
distal tibial physeal line: Smooth transverse lucency crossing the distal tibia a few millimetres above the plafond, parallel to the joint and bordered by a dense zone of provisional calcification; unlike a Salter-Harris fracture it is uniform in width and uninterrupted.
distal tibiofibular joint: Fibrous syndesmosis between the medial surface of the distal fibula and the fibular notch of the tibia, seen just above the ankle joint; assessed by tibiofibular overlap and clear space, and distinct from the mortise joint line below it.
distal tibiofibular syndesmosis: The fibrous articulation where the distal fibula sits in the fibular notch of the tibia, just above the level of the ankle joint; judged by the tibiofibular clear space and overlap on mortise views. It lies above, not within, the tibiotalar joint line.
distal ulna: The smaller, medially placed forearm bone whose rounded head sits in the sigmoid notch of the radius at the distal radioulnar joint and bears the styloid; the radius is bulkier, articulates with the carpus, and carries the dorsal Lister's tubercle.
dome of diaphragm: Smooth curved interface at the lung base, on the right normally the higher of the two and visible along its whole length because aerated lung lies above and liver below. On the lateral film, the hemidiaphragm whose anterior contour is effaced by the heart is the left.
dome of right talus: The convex superior surface of the talar body articulating with the tibial plafond within the ankle mortise, bounded by the malleoli on either side. Trace anteriorly across the narrower talar neck to reach the head, which meets the navicular.
dome of the right talus: The convex superior articular surface of the talar body that sits under the tibial plafond and forms the roof of the ankle joint, flanked by the malleoli. The head, further anterior beyond the neck, is the part that meets the navicular.
dome of the right talus (trochlear surfa: Convex superior articular surface of the talar body sitting directly under the tibial plafond within the mortise, with the malleoli gripping it on either side; the rounded anterior talar head lies further forward against the navicular.
dorsal nerve root: Sensory root formed by rootlets from the posterolateral surface of the cord that joins the ventral root to make the spinal nerve; within the sac and foramen it lies posterior to the motor root and carries the dorsal root ganglion.
dorsal sacroiliac ligament: Superficial posterior band running from the lateral sacral crest to the posterior superior iliac spine, behind the joint; the interosseous ligament lies deeper, wedged directly between the sacral and iliac tuberosities.
dorsal tubercle of radius/ lister's tube: Small cortical prominence on the dorsal surface of the distal radius, best appreciated on axial images; extensor pollicis longus hooks around its ulnar side while extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis run in the groove radial to it. Use it as the landmark dividing the second from the third extensor compartment.
dorsalis pedis artery: Direct continuation of the anterior tibial artery beyond the ankle joint, running on the dorsum of the foot over the tarsal bones just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon before diving into the first web space to complete the plantar arch.
dorsum sellae: Squared block of bone forming the back wall of the pituitary fossa, carrying the posterior clinoid processes at its upper corners and continuous below with the clivus; the anterior clinoids lie on the opposite side of the fossa.
duodenum (d1/d2): Gas- or fluid-containing tube with layered gut signature and peristalsis: D1 passes posterolaterally from the pylorus, D2 descends vertically hugging the right border of the pancreatic head, anterior to the IVC and right renal hilum. The pancreatic head itself is solid and uniformly echogenic.
dura mater: Outermost echogenic line bounding the thecal sac on neonatal spinal ultrasound, separated from the cord surface by anechoic CSF. The bright line hugging the hypoechoic cord itself is the pia-arachnoid; the dura is the more superficial of the two.
enamel: Densest, whitest layer on a dental radiograph, forming a thin cap over the crown alone and ending at the neck of the tooth. Below and deep to it the slightly less dense dentine continues down the root around the lucent pulp.
epidural fat: Fat inside the spinal canal but outside the dura, brightest on T1, filling the posterior canal and the neural foramina and outlining the nerve roots; CSF within the thecal sac shows the opposite pattern, dark on T1 and bright on T2.
epiglottis: Leaf-shaped cartilage of soft tissue density arising from the laryngeal pharynx and projecting upwards into the oropharynx behind the tongue base, above the hyoid. Normally thin and curved on the lateral film, it becomes thickened and thumb-like when inflamed.
epiphyseal line (fused): Thin dark undulating line crossing the proximal humerus at the head-neck junction, the scar of the fused physis; unlike a fracture there is no cortical break, no step and no surrounding marrow oedema.
epiphysis for the middle phalynx of the: Separate ossific centre at the proximal end (base) of the middle phalanx of the second digit. All phalangeal epiphyses lie proximally, whereas the finger metacarpals carry theirs at the distal head.
epiphysis of 1st metatarsal: Separate ossification centre at the proximal end (base) of the great toe metatarsal; the first metatarsal is unique in having a proximal epiphysis, whereas metatarsals two to five ossify distally at the head, so do not read this smooth transverse lucency as a fracture.
epiphysis of capitulum: First elbow centre to ossify, at about one year — a rounded ossific nucleus at the lateral aspect of the distal humerus, always aligned with and articulating with the radial head.
epiphysis of distal phalanx of great toe: In the immature foot, the separate ossification centre at the proximal end of the terminal hallucal phalanx, divided from the shaft by a lucent physis; phalangeal epiphyses in the foot are always proximal. The smooth transverse lucency is a growth plate, not a fracture.
epiphysis of distal radius: Ossific plate capping the distal radius, separated from the shaft by a transverse lucent physis and lying on the thumb side of the wrist; it carries the radial styloid. Carpal bones are separate rounded ossicles further distal, beyond the radiocarpal joint.
epiphysis of lateral epicondyle: Last centre to appear, around eleven years — a small, often fragmented ossicle at the lateral margin of the distal humerus, just proximal and lateral to the much larger capitellar centre.
epiphysis of medial epicondyle: Ossifies at about five years on the medial side of the distal humerus, outside the articular surface. If it is absent while the trochlear centre has appeared, suspect avulsion with the fragment displaced into the joint.
epiphysis of radial head: Thin disc-like ossific centre capping the radial neck, second to appear at around three years. It belongs to the radius, distal to the joint; the capitellar centre it articulates with is larger and part of the distal humerus.
epiphysis of right humeral head: Rounded ossification centre of the proximal humerus at the top of the hemithorax lateral to the glenoid, separated from the metaphysis by a lucent physeal line. Its bony density and position outside the ribcage distinguish it from an apical lung opacity.
epiphysis of the left thumb metacarpal: Ossification centre at the base, the proximal end, of the thumb metacarpal — the reverse of the other metacarpals, whose epiphyses lie distally at the head. This proximal position identifies the first ray.
epiphysis of thumb metacarpal: Ossific centre at the base of the first metacarpal adjacent to the trapezium, separated by a thin lucent physis and nearly adult in size in an adolescent; the thumb metacarpal alone ossifies proximally, whereas metacarpals two to five have distal epiphyses.
epiploic foramen: Slit-like communication between greater and lesser sacs, bounded anteriorly by the free edge of the lesser omentum carrying portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, posteriorly by the IVC, above by the caudate lobe and below by the first part of duodenum.
erector spinae: Bulky paraspinal muscle mass filling the gutter behind the transverse processes on either side of the spinous processes; psoas lies anterolateral to the vertebral body and quadratus lumborum between the two, in front of the transverse processes.
erector spinae muscle: Bulky paired paraspinal muscle column filling the groove between the spinous processes and the transverse processes, seen on axial images posterolateral to the vertebral body; multifidus lies deeper and more medially in the same groove, and psoas lies in front of the transverse processes.
ethmoid sinus: Honeycomb of small air cells in the midline upper nasal region between the medial orbital walls, lying beneath the anterior cranial fossa; the maxillary antra are the much larger pyramidal lucencies lateral and below.
ethmoidal air cells: Cluster of small honeycomb lucencies in the midline between the orbits, above the nasal cavity and medial to the thin lamina papyracea; the sphenoid sinus is a single larger cavity lying further back beneath the sella.
extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon: Ulnar member of the second-compartment pair, sitting immediately radial to Lister's tubercle and passing to the base of the third metacarpal; extensor pollicis longus lies on the ulnar side of the tubercle in the third compartment.
extensor carpi radialis longus tendon: Radial of the two second-compartment tendons on the dorsum of the distal radius, lying radial to Lister's tubercle and running to the base of the second metacarpal; the first-compartment tendons lie further radially over the radial styloid.
extensor carpi ulnaris tendon: Round dark tendon sitting in its own shallow groove on the dorsal-ulnar aspect of the distal ulna (sixth extensor compartment), just superficial to the TFCC; flexor carpi ulnaris is its volar counterpart, running to the pisiform.
extensor indicis tendon: Runs in the fourth extensor compartment ulnar to Lister's tubercle alongside the extensor digitorum tendons; at wrist level it is the deeper and more ulnar tendon of that group. Its position ulnar and deep to the index EDC tendon separates it from the digitorum tendons themselves.
external acoustic meatus: Rounded lucency in the temporal bone immediately behind the mandibular condyle and its fossa; it stays fixed when the mouth opens while the condyle glides forwards. Mastoid air cells lie further posteroinferiorly as multiple small lucencies.
external acoustic meatus of temporal bon: Rounded canal opening in the tympanic temporal bone directly behind the mandibular condyle and temporomandibular joint, below the root of the zygomatic arch and above the mastoid tip; the TMJ lies immediately anterior to it on a 3D reconstruction.
external auditory canal: Rounded lucency in the petrous temporal bone lying just behind and below the mandibular condyle on the lateral skull film, with both sides superimposed on a true lateral. Its position immediately posterior to the temporomandibular joint separates it from the mastoid air cells further back.
external auditory meatus: Rounded lucency in the temporal bone lying just behind the mandibular condyle, with mastoid air cells immediately posterior to it; the internal acoustic meatus lies deeper and medially and is not resolved on plain films.
external iliac artery: Continues anterolaterally from the common iliac bifurcation along the medial border of psoas on the pelvic brim, becoming the common femoral artery at the inguinal ligament; the internal iliac is the branch that dives posteromedially into the pelvis.
external occipital protuberance: Midline bony bump on the outer surface of the squamous occipital bone at the back of the skull, giving attachment to the nuchal ligament and trapezius. On a lateral neck film it is the posterior prominence at the top of the image, well above the posterior arch of C1.
fabella: Small, smoothly corticated round ossicle within the lateral head of gastrocnemius, projected on the lateral radiograph just behind the posterior margin of the lateral femoral condyle; its complete smooth cortex distinguishes it from a loose body or avulsed fragment.
facet joint: Synovial joint between the inferior articular process of the vertebra above and the superior articular process of the one below, seen on axial lumbar CT as a curved, near-sagittally oriented lucency behind the neural foramen.
facet joint (zygapophysial): Posterolateral synovial joint between adjacent articular processes, a thin curved line of fluid signal between dark cortical margins; it lies immediately behind the lateral recess, with the neural foramen anterior to it.
facet joint between l3 and l4: Lucent line between the downward projecting inferior articular process of L3 and the upward projecting superior articular process of L4, lying behind the L3/4 neural foramen. Count up from the L5-S1 level to confirm which facet joint is marked.
facet joint c4/c5: Thin lucent line within the articular pillar column between the inferior articular process of C4 and the superior articular process of C5, sloping posteroinferiorly; count down from the C2 body. In a non-rotated lateral the left and right joints overlap or lie closely parallel.
falx cerebri: Thin bright linear midline echo running in the interhemispheric fissure and separating the two cerebral hemispheres, extending downwards from the superior sagittal sinus. Do not confuse it with the corpus callosum, a horizontally orientated band lying beneath it.
femoral artery: Continuation of the external iliac artery below the inguinal ligament, lying lateral to the femoral vein in the femoral triangle. On ultrasound it is the round, thick-walled, pulsatile and non-compressible vessel, whereas the thin-walled vein flattens under gentle probe pressure.
femoral canal: Small fat-containing space forming the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, immediately medial to the common femoral vein, bounded anteriorly by the inguinal ligament and medially by the lacunar ligament; it contains Cloquet's node and is the neck of a femoral hernia.
femoral capital epiphyseal plate or phys: Lucent transverse line between the femoral head epiphysis and the femoral neck metaphysis; widening or irregularity here with posterior slip of the epiphysis on the frog lateral indicates SCFE. Do not confuse it with the separate greater trochanteric apophyseal line laterally.
femoral capital epiphysis: Ossified centre of the femoral head sitting above the physis within the acetabulum; on ultrasound it is the echogenic focus inside the otherwise hypoechoic cartilaginous head, and on the frog-leg lateral a slip shows posteromedial displacement with a widened physis.
femoral condyle: Rounded expanded articular mass at the distal femur above the joint line, one on each side of the intercondylar notch, the medial extending slightly further distally; the tibial condyles are the corresponding surfaces below the joint line.
femoral diaphysis: Tubular shaft of the femur with thick parallel cortices and a narrow medullary canal, between the flared metaphyses at either end; the widening trabecular bone near the knee is metaphysis, not diaphysis.
femoral head: Rounded epiphysis seated within the acetabulum, showing a small medial fovea and fatty marrow on MRI; in the infant it is the unossified, spherical, hypoechoic ball with fine internal echoes resting against the echogenic iliac line.
femoral head (unossified): Rounded, uniformly low-reflectivity sphere with fine stippled internal echoes seated in the acetabular concavity; once the ossific nucleus appears a bright central focus with posterior shadowing develops. Its spherical outline separates it from the adjacent hypoechoic cartilaginous roof.
femoral nerve: Oval, hyperechoic, honeycomb-fascicular structure lying LATERAL to the femoral artery in the groin (mnemonic NAVY), sitting in the groove between iliacus and psoas deep to the fascia iliaca. Unlike the adjacent vessels it shows no colour Doppler flow.
femur: Single long bone of the thigh, with a rounded head in the acetabulum, angled neck and greater trochanter proximally and condyles distally; on axial images it is the central cortical ring with fatty marrow surrounded by the thigh muscle compartments.
fibula: Slender lateral bone of the lower leg, far thinner than the tibia, its head sitting just below the lateral tibial plateau; distally it forms the lateral malleolus, which lies more posteriorly and extends further down than the medial malleolus.
fibular (common peroneal) artery: Middle vessel of the three-vessel run-off, arising from the tibioperoneal trunk and descending closely applied to the medial side of the fibula; it stays lateral to the posterior tibial and, unlike the anterior tibial, remains in the posterior compartment.
fibular (or common peroneal) artery: Branch of the tibioperoneal trunk descending in the posterior compartment closely applied to the medial border of the fibula, deep to flexor hallucis longus; it is the middle of the three run-off vessels, whereas the posterior tibial runs medially against the tibia.
fibular head: Expanded knob-like proximal end of the fibula lying lateral and slightly posterior to the lateral tibial condyle across the proximal tibiofibular joint; it marks the level at which the popliteal artery divides into anterior tibial and tibioperoneal trunk.
fibular head/ lateral malleolus: Two ends of the fibula: the head is the knob just below and lateral to the lateral tibial condyle at the knee, the lateral malleolus the distal expansion forming the lateral ankle mortise and descending lower than the medial malleolus.
fibular metaphysis: Flared portion of the distal fibula lying immediately proximal to the physeal lucency and distal to the narrow tubular shaft; the separate ossified fragment beyond the physis is the lateral malleolar epiphysis.
fifth metacarpal: Shortest and most ulnar of the four finger metacarpals, its base articulating with the hamate and its shaft lying furthest from the thumb; the fourth is longer and lies immediately radial to it, so compare relative length and the carpal articulation.
fifth metatarsal: Most lateral metatarsal, recognised by the prominent tuberosity projecting proximolaterally from its base towards the cuboid; the adjacent fourth metatarsal has a plain unexpanded base and no such lateral spur.
fifth proximal phalanx epiphysis: Ossific centre at the base (proximal end) of the proximal phalanx of the little finger, separated from the shaft by a lucent physis. Phalangeal epiphyses always sit at the base, whereas the neighbouring fifth metacarpal centre lies at its head, across the MCP joint.
filum terminale: Single fine midline strand of pia continuing from the tip of the conus (usually L1/2) down through the cauda equina to insert on the coccyx; the cauda equina roots are multiple and lie dependently, whereas the filum is solitary and central.
first (or thumb) metacarpal bone: Shortest and stoutest metacarpal, lying anterior (volar) and radial to the other four and rotated out of their plane, so on axial images it appears as an isolated bone set apart. Trace it proximally to its saddle joint with the trapezium.
first metacarpal epiphysis: Ossific centre at the base of the thumb metacarpal, unique among metacarpals, whose second to fifth centres lie at the head. Identify the thumb as the shortest, most radial ray with only two phalanges and a saddle joint with the trapezium.
first metatarsal: Shortest and thickest metatarsal, on the medial side of the forefoot, its base articulating with the medial cuneiform and its head carrying the two sesamoids on the plantar surface; the second metatarsal is longer with its base recessed between the cuneiforms.
first metatarso-phalangeal joint: The joint between the head of the first metatarsal, identified by the two sesamoids projected beneath it, and the base of the hallucal proximal phalanx. The interphalangeal joint of the great toe lies one level further distally and has no sesamoids.
first rib: Short, broad, sharply curved uppermost rib arising from T1 and running almost horizontally, its anterior costal cartilage often calcified and mistaken for a lung nodule; the clavicle crosses above it but is S-shaped and continues to the acromion.
first upper incisor: Central incisor, the tooth immediately beside the midline in the upper jaw, with a broad chisel-shaped crown and a single conical root; on a frontal view it lies just lateral to the nasal septum. The lateral incisor is the narrower tooth next to it.
flexor carpi radialis: Superficial anterior forearm muscle arising from the common flexor origin, lying immediately medial (ulnar) to pronator teres and lateral to palmaris longus on axial images; pronator teres is the more lateral and obliquely oriented belly crossing towards the radius.
flexor carpi ulnaris: Most medial of the superficial forearm flexors, arising from the common flexor origin and the olecranon and lying along the ulnar border, with the ulnar nerve and artery immediately deep to it, running to the pisiform. Flexor digitorum superficialis lies more centrally and has multiple tendons.
flexor digitorum longus: Deep posterior compartment muscle lying directly against the posteromedial surface of the tibia, medial to tibialis posterior and smaller than flexor hallucis longus, which occupies the corresponding position against the fibula.
flexor digitorum profundus tendons: Deepest row of flexor tendons in the carpal tunnel, lying directly volar to the carpal bones and dorsal to the superficialis tendons; the median nerve is more superficial and radial, flatter and slightly brighter than these uniformly dark tendons.
flexor digitorum superficialis tendon: Volar flexor tendon at the wrist lying superficial to the profundus tendon and deep to the flexor retinaculum; on the volar aspect there is more soft tissue padding than dorsally, so count tendon layers from the skin inwards.
flexor hallucis longus muscle: Deep posterior compartment muscle applied to the posterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane, deep to soleus; it is the deep muscle on the fibular side, whereas flexor digitorum longus lies against the tibia and tibialis posterior sits deepest between the two bones.
flexor hallucis longus tendon: Most posterior tendon of the medial ankle group (Harry in Tom, Dick and Very Nervous Harry), running in the groove between the posterior talar tubercles and under the sustentaculum tali towards the great toe; flexor digitorum longus lies anterior to the tibial vessels and nerve.
flexor muscles of the forearm: Soft tissue bulk along the volar and medial side of the proximal forearm, arising from the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle. The extensor group lies dorsolaterally and arises from the lateral epicondyle.
flexor pollicis longus (fpl): Deep forearm flexor arising from the volar surface of the radial shaft and adjacent interosseous membrane, its tendon passing through the carpal tunnel to the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. It alone flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint, unlike flexor pollicis brevis in the thenar eminence.
flexor pollicis longus tendon: Single tendon lying at the radial margin of the carpal tunnel in the same deep plane as the four profundus tendons, deep to the superficialis group and deep to the flexor retinaculum; it is the only unpaired tendon there.
flexor retinaculum: Thick low-signal band arching across the palmar carpus, anchored to the pisiform and hook of hamate medially and to the scaphoid and trapezial tubercles laterally; it roofs the carpal tunnel, so the median nerve lies immediately deep to it.
floor of anterior cranial fossa: Curved lines running forwards from the anterior clinoids to the frontal bone on the lateral view, formed by the orbital roofs and often appearing doubled because left and right are superimposed; it separates frontal lobes from orbits.
foramen ovale: Oval skull-base opening in the greater wing of sphenoid transmitting the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve; the foramen spinosum is smaller, rounder and sits just posterolateral to it, and foramen lacerum lies more medially.
foramen rotundum: Round channel in the sphenoid running from the middle cranial fossa to the pterygopalatine fossa, carrying the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve. On a frontal skull view it is the small circular lucency just below the medial end of the elongated superior orbital fissure.
foramen transversarium of the axis: Round hole within the transverse process of C2, lateral to the body and anterior to the articular process, transmitting the vertebral artery; the vertebral canal carrying the cord lies medial and posterior to it.
fourth metatarsophalangeal joint: Joint between the head of the fourth metatarsal and the base of its proximal phalanx; count rays from the great toe medially, remembering the fifth is the one bearing the flared proximal tuberosity. Do not mistake it for the more distal interphalangeal joints of the same toe.
fourth ventricle: Small anechoic triangle on the midline sagittal neonatal image, wedged between the pons and brainstem in front and the bright cerebellar vermis behind. Do not confuse it with the cisterna magna, which lies below and behind the vermis rather than in front of it.
fovea capitis: Shallow pit in the medial part of the femoral head, slightly below its centre, where the ligamentum teres attaches; a smooth corticated margin distinguishes this normal depression from an erosion or focal lucent lesion.
fovea capitis of femur: Small shallow notch or lucent depression in the medial cortical contour of the femoral head, just below and medial to its centre, giving attachment to the ligamentum teres. A normal variant, not a subchondral lesion or fracture.
fovea capitis of the left femur: Small notch or cortical indentation on the medial aspect of the femoral head just below its centre, marking attachment of the ligamentum teres; its smooth corticated margin identifies it as a normal depression rather than an osteochondral defect.
frontal bone (outer table of skull vault: Outer of the two dense parallel cortical lines of the frontal vault, following the scalp contour and separated from the inner table by the lucent diploic space; the inner table is the deeper line facing the frontal lobes.
frontal process of left zygoma: Upward-pointing limb of the zygoma forming the lower part of the lateral orbital rim; the frontozygomatic suture interrupts that rim, and the bone above the suture belongs to the frontal bone.
frontal process of right zygoma: Upward projection of the zygoma forming the lateral orbital rim as it ascends to meet the frontal bone at the frontozygomatic suture; on the Waters view it is the elephant's forehead. The temporal process running backward into the zygomatic arch forms the trunk.
frontal process of the right zygomatic b: Upward limb of the cheekbone forming the lateral orbital rim below the frontozygomatic suture, continuous inferiorly with the body of the zygoma at the cheek prominence. The bone above the suture belongs to the frontal bone.
frontal process of the zygomatic bone: Upward projecting limb of the cheekbone forming the lower part of the lateral orbital rim, meeting the frontal bone at the frontozygomatic suture; on Water's view it is the elephant's forehead. Above the suture the bone is frontal, not zygomatic.
frontal sinus: Air-filled lucency within the frontal bone above and medial to the orbital roof, either side of a midline septum, with a scalloped lobulated upper margin. Do not confuse it with the ethmoid air cells, which lie lower down between the orbits.
fronto-zygomatic suture: Lucent line crossing the superolateral orbital rim where the zygomatic bone meets the frontal bone, a key site of diastasis in zygomatic (tripod) fractures; do not confuse it with the innominate line, a vertical density projected across the orbit itself.
frontozygomatic suture: Short lucent line crossing the superolateral orbital margin where the zygomatic process of the frontal bone meets the frontal process of the zygoma. One of the classic sites to check for widening in a tripod fracture; unlike the innominate line it does not run down inside the orbit.
fused growth plate, proximal tibia: Transverse sclerotic line crossing the proximal tibial metaphysis a short distance below the plateau — the residual physeal scar in a mature knee. It is dense and continuous with the cortices, unlike a lucent fracture line.
gallbladder: Anechoic pear-shaped sac with a thin echogenic wall on the undersurface of the right liver lobe, linked to the right portal vein by the bright main lobar fissure; unlike fluid-filled duodenum it contains no gas or debris and does not peristalse.
gap of triradiate cartilage: Hypoechoic gap at the deepest part of the bony acetabulum where the ilium meets the ischium and pubis; identifying it along with a straight iliac line and the labrum confirms an adequate standard coronal plane for angle measurement.
gas in colon/splenic flexure: Lucency beneath the left hemidiaphragm showing haustral markings and often mottled faecal content, lying below and lateral to the smooth gastric air bubble. Free intraperitoneal gas differs, being a featureless crescent under the diaphragm with no bowel wall.
gas in vocal cord: Lucency of the laryngeal air column at cord level on the lateral neck film, framed by the thyroid cartilage laminae and lying immediately above the cricoid ring; below this the airway becomes the smooth uniform subglottic column.
gastric antrum: Distal stomach lying transversely across the epigastrium, anterior to the pancreas and behind the left lobe of liver, with a layered wall and visible peristalsis leading into the pylorus. In pyloric stenosis it stays distended with feed while the pylorus does not open.
gastric fundus: Rounded gas collection lying immediately beneath the left hemidiaphragm on an erect film, often with a smooth air-fluid level; colonic gas at the splenic flexure is distinguished by haustral folds and a more lateral, inferior position.
gastrocnemius muscle: Largest and most superficial muscle of the posterior calf, arising by two heads from the back of the femoral condyles so that it crosses the knee; soleus lies deep to it and arises below the knee from the tibia and fibula.
gastroduodenal artery: Branches from the common hepatic artery and descends between the duodenum and pancreatic head; its origin marks where the common hepatic artery becomes the proper hepatic artery.
glenohumeral joint: Curvilinear lucency between the convex humeral head and the shallow concave glenoid of the scapula, seen free of overlap only on a true AP (Grashey) view. The acromioclavicular joint is the separate small gap above, between lateral clavicle and acromion.
glenoid: Shallow pear-shaped socket at the lateral angle of the scapula receiving the humeral head; on a frontal radiograph its anterior and posterior rims project as two roughly parallel vertical lines. On the scapular Y view it lies at the centre of the Y where the three limbs meet.
glenoid cavity: Shallow articular concavity at the lateral angle of the scapula, at the point where coracoid, body and spine converge — the centre of the Y on a trans-scapular view — with the humeral head normally projected centrally over it.
glenoid fossa: Shallow pear-shaped articular surface at the lateral angle of the scapula, seen on AP as the vertically oriented curved line overlapped by the humeral head; the coracoid, the most anterior scapular process, projects anteriorly above it and should not be confused with the glenoid rim.
glenoid fossa of left scapula: Shallow articular surface at the lateral angle of the scapula, seen on AP as the vertical curved line overlapped by the humeral head, lying below the coracoid and medial to the humeral articular surface.
glenoid fossa of the left scapula: Shallow articular surface at the lateral angle of the scapula facing the humeral head; its anterior and posterior rims project as two closely spaced vertical lines overlapping the head on a standard AP. The acromion lies above it.
glenoid fossa of the left temporal bone: Concavity on the undersurface of the squamous temporal bone that receives the mandibular condyle, lying immediately anterior to the external acoustic meatus; the convex bump in front of it is the articular eminence.
glenoid labrum: Dark triangular fibrocartilaginous rim seated on the bony glenoid margin, deepening the socket; glenoid articular cartilage is intermediate in signal and lines the joint surface, whereas the capsule and glenohumeral ligaments extend away from the rim.
glenoid of scapula: Shallow pear-shaped articular fossa at the lateral angle of the scapula facing the humeral head, seen end-on as paired anterior and posterior rims on the axial view. It is continuous medially with the scapular neck and body, unlike the free-standing coracoid.
glenoid of shoulder: Shallow concave articular surface at the lateral angle of the scapula, continuous medially with the scapular neck and body and capped at its edges by labrum; opposite it the humeral head is a much larger convex sphere.
gluteal muscles: Layered soft tissue mass superficial (lateral) to the femoral head and greater trochanter on the coronal infant hip view, lying between skin and joint capsule, with a thin bright fascial line separating gluteus medius from the deeper gluteus minimus.
gluteus maximus muscle: The largest, most superficial gluteal muscle forming the bulk of the buttock; a thick quadrangular sheet from the posterior ilium, sacrum and coccyx passing inferolaterally to the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity, lying superficial to medius, minimus and the short external rotators.
gluteus medius: Fan-shaped muscle covering the outer table of the iliac wing, the middle of the three gluteal layers on axial MRI: deep to the bulky gluteus maximus, superficial to gluteus minimus, converging on the greater trochanter.
gluteus medius muscle: Runs from the outer iliac wing to insert on the lateral facet of the greater trochanter, so on a pelvic radiograph it is indicated at the lateral aspect of the trochanter; obturator externus and the gemelli attach medially, in the trochanteric fossa.
gluteus medius or minimus muscle: Soft tissue bulk lateral to the outer table of the iliac wing and above the greater trochanter, arising from the gluteal surface of the ilium and inserting on the trochanter as the hip abductors. Iliopsoas, by contrast, lies medially and descends over the pelvic brim to the lesser trochanter.
gluteus medius tendon: Thick low-signal tendon converging on the lateral and superoposterior facets of the greater trochanter, deep to gluteus maximus and the iliotibial band. The gluteus minimus tendon lies deeper and more anterior, inserting on the anterior facet.
gluteus minimus: Deepest and most anterior gluteal muscle, applied directly to the outer table of the ilium beneath gluteus medius, converging on the anterior facet of the greater trochanter. Medius is the thicker muscle superficial to it, inserting on the lateral/superoposterior facets.
gracilis muscle: Thin strap muscle at the medial margin of the thigh running from the pubis to the pes anserinus; on axial images it is the flat sliver at the innermost edge, superficial to adductor magnus. Sartorius, its rival, begins anterolaterally and only becomes medial lower down.
great (long) saphenous vein: Superficial vein lying in the subcutaneous fat of the medial thigh outside the deep fascia, ascending from in front of the medial malleolus to pierce the cribriform fascia and join the femoral vein; the femoral vein itself lies deep to the fascia beside the artery.
greater trochanter: Large quadrangular prominence at the lateral junction of femoral neck and shaft, projecting laterally and upwards and receiving gluteus medius and minimus; contrast with the lesser trochanter, a small cone pointing medially at the base of the neck.
greater trochanter of left femur: Prominent lateral projection at the base of the femoral neck, roughly level with the centre of the femoral head, with a separate apophysis and irregular lucent physis in children; the lesser trochanter is the small medial beak lower down.
greater trochanter of the femur: Large lateral bony prominence at the junction of femoral neck and shaft, lying roughly level with the centre of the femoral head and giving insertion to gluteus medius and minimus; the lesser trochanter is smaller and points posteromedially.
greater trochanter of the right femur: The large lateral prominence at the junction of the femoral neck and shaft, projecting superolaterally and receiving gluteus medius and minimus. The lesser trochanter is the smaller posteromedial cone at the inferior neck taking iliopsoas.
greater tuberosity: The lateral prominence of the proximal humerus giving attachment to supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor — the lesser tuberosity lies anteromedially and takes subscapularis.
greater tuberosity of the humerus: Lateral bony prominence of the proximal humerus, lying lateral to the bicipital groove and just above the surgical neck, carrying the supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insertions. The lesser tuberosity lies on the medial side of the groove and faces anteriorly.
greater tuberosity of the left humerus: Lateral prominence of the proximal humerus, lateral to the bicipital groove, receiving supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor; it is profiled laterally with the arm externally rotated. The lesser tuberosity is the anterior, medial prominence.
greater tuberosity of the right humerus: Lateral prominence of the proximal humerus lying lateral to the bicipital groove and profiled on the external rotation view; it carries the supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor footprints. The lesser tuberosity lies medial to the groove and faces anteriorly.
greater wing of sphenoid: Dense line crossing that of the lesser wing in the superolateral part of the orbit on a frontal facial view; it forms the posterolateral orbital wall and the inferolateral boundary of the superior orbital fissure, the tubular lucency lying between the two wings.
greater wing of the right sphenoid bone: Dense vertical line projected through the lateral part of the orbit on a frontal facial view, produced by the beam passing tangentially along the greater sphenoid wing. It lies within the orbital outline, unlike the lateral orbital rim, which forms the orbit's outer bony margin.
grooves for middle meningeal artery bran: Fine branching lucent lines sweeping upwards and backwards across the temporoparietal vault; unlike a fracture they taper, divide, curve gently and have slightly sclerotic margins, whereas a fracture line is sharper, blacker and does not branch.
hamate: Most ulnar bone of the distal carpal row, articulating with the bases of the fourth and fifth metacarpals; its hook projects palmarly and is seen end-on as a cortical ring over the body on the PA view. The capitate lies immediately radial to it.
hamate. this bone occupies the distal ca: Most ulnar bone of the distal carpal row, articulating with the fourth and fifth metacarpal bases and recognised by the hook projecting from its volar surface; the pisiform is a separate rounded bone lying volar to the triquetral in the proximal row.
hard palate: Dense horizontal bony plate forming the roof of the mouth and floor of the nasal cavity, made up of the palatine processes of the maxillae with the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind. On a lateral view it is the straight dense line ending where the soft palate continues backwards.
harris' ring: Incomplete oval ring of cortical density projected over the body of C2 on the lateral cervical radiograph, produced by superimposition of the cortical margins of the body and its posterior elements. A break or disruption of its contour suggests an occult C2 or dens fracture.
head of 2nd metatarsal: Rounded distal articular end of the second metatarsal, usually the longest ray, meeting the base of the second proximal phalanx; check carefully whether the marker sits on bone or on the joint space, and count rays from the great toe.
head of fibula: Expanded knob at the top of the fibula, posterolateral to and slightly below the level of the lateral tibial plateau, its apex receiving biceps femoris and the lateral collateral ligament; the common peroneal nerve winds around the neck just below it.
head of humerus: Rounded articular surface of the proximal humerus facing superomedially towards the glenoid, separated from the tuberosities by the anatomical neck; the greater tuberosity, often mislabelled, is the lateral bony prominence beyond that neck bearing the supraspinatus insertion.
head of left clavicle: Rounded medial (sternal) end of the clavicle articulating with the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint, sitting close to the midline either side of the spinous processes on a frontal view. The first rib arcs upwards and laterally behind it.
head of left fibula: The expanded proximal end of the slender lateral bone, overlapping the lateral tibial metaphysis on the frontal view and articulating with the posterolateral tibial condyle below the knee joint line. Its upward pointed tip is the styloid process.
head of left humerus: Rounded, uniformly dense hemisphere projected over the centre of the Y where the scapular limbs converge at the glenoid. The coracoid is the anterior fork of the Y, closest to the ribs, and is beak-shaped rather than spherical.
head of left talus: The rounded anteromedial end of the talus that articulates with the navicular at the talonavicular joint, separated from the body by the narrower neck. The dome/body is the part covered by the tibial plafond superiorly, so trace forwards from the ankle joint to reach the head.
head of mandible: Rounded condylar head at the top of the posterior process of the ramus, seated in the mandibular fossa just in front of the external acoustic meatus; the coronoid process is the anterior, pointed projection separated from it by the mandibular notch.
head of pancreas: Rounded right-sided portion of the gland cradled in the duodenal C-loop, lying anterior to the IVC and to the right of the superior mesenteric vein, with the uncinate process hooking behind that vein; the body is the part crossing the midline in front of the aorta and SMA.
head of radius: Disc-shaped proximal end of the radius articulating with the capitellum above and, at its rim, with the radial notch of the ulna; the radiocapitellar line drawn along the radial neck must pass through the capitellum in any projection.
head of right fibula: Expanded proximal end of the fibula lying lateral and slightly posterior to the lateral tibial condyle across the proximal tibiofibular joint, with the styloid process superiorly; the common peroneal nerve wraps around the neck just distal to it.
head of right talus: The rounded anterior end of the talus articulating with the navicular, separated from the body by the talar neck. Unlike the dome, it has no contact with the tibia, so identify the ankle joint first and then follow the bone forwards.
head of talus: Rounded anterior end of the talus capped by the concave navicular, separated from the body by the narrower neck; the body is the block-like portion held in the ankle mortise, so the rounded contour pointing towards the first metatarsal line is the head.
head of the fibula: Expanded knob of proximal fibula sitting lateral to and just below the lateral tibial condyle, articulating with it at the proximal tibiofibular joint; the pointed styloid rises from its top and the narrowed neck lies immediately beneath.
head of the left humerus: Rounded hemispherical articular mass facing superomedially towards the glenoid and clearly larger than the glenoid surface it meets. The tubercles lie lateral and distal to it, separated from the head by the anatomical neck.
head of the right talus: Rounded forward-facing end of the talus, joined to the body by the narrower neck and seated in the concave proximal surface of the navicular; the navicular itself lies distal to that joint line.
head of the talus: Rounded forward-facing end of the talus, separated from the body by the narrower neck and sitting in the cup of the proximal navicular; the navicular lies beyond that joint line and is flatter and crescentic.
head of thumb metacarpal: Rounded distal end of the shortest, most radial metacarpal, meeting the proximal phalanx of the thumb at the MCP joint, where paired sesamoids often overlie it. The base is the opposite, proximal end articulating with the trapezium; the thumb has only two phalanges.
hemidiaphragm: Smooth dome-shaped interface separating aerated lung from abdomen; the right sits higher because of the liver and its undersurface is silhouetted by liver, whereas the left has gastric or colonic gas immediately beneath it.
hepatic artery: Small tubular vessel crossing the anterior aspect of the portal vein at the porta hepatis, completing the Mickey Mouse appearance with the bile duct. Colour Doppler settles the distinction: the artery shows pulsatile flow, the adjacent common duct none.
hepatic portal vein: Formed behind the pancreatic neck by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins and running in the free edge of the lesser omentum to the porta hepatis, with characteristically bright echogenic walls from periportal fibrofatty tissue. Hepatic veins have thin imperceptible walls and drain into the IVC.
hepatic vein: Vein running in an interlobar plane between hepatic segments and converging towards the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, its walls barely visible on ultrasound; portal vein branches, the main mimic, have bright echogenic walls and run within portal triads towards the porta.
hilar point: The V-shaped angle on the lateral hilar border where the descending upper lobe vein crosses the superolateral aspect of the interlobar (descending) pulmonary artery; the right hilar point normally sits slightly lower than the left.
hilum or hilar point: V-shaped point where the descending upper lobe vein crosses the superolateral aspect of the interlobar pulmonary artery, the two meeting at an angle of about 120 degrees; the right hilar point normally lies lower than the left.
hoffa's fat pad: Triangular lucency on the lateral knee radiograph bounded in front by the patellar tendon, above by the patellar apex and behind by the joint and femoral condyles; being fat it is dark on radiographs but bright on both T1 and T2.
hook of hamate: Palmar hook of the hamate, seen end-on on a PA wrist radiograph as a corticated dense ring overlying the hamate body and profiled on a carpal tunnel view; the pisiform is more proximal and ulnar, overlying the triquetral.
hook of right hamate: Projected end-on over the body of the hamate on the PA view as a well-defined cortical ring on the ulnar side of the distal carpal row; loss or blurring of that ring suggests a hook fracture, confirmed on a carpal tunnel view.
hook of the hamate: Palmar bony projection from the hamate seen end-on as a dense cortical ring superimposed on the hamate on a PA radiograph, and forming the ulnar wall of the carpal tunnel. On axial images it is the anterior spur ulnar to the flexor tendons, with the ulnar nerve and artery superficial to it.
hook of the right hamate: Curved bony spur projecting volarly from the hamate, forming the ulnar wall of the carpal tunnel and the radial wall of Guyon's canal; the pisiform is a separate rounded bone lying more proximally and ulnar to it, volar to the triquetral.
humerus: Single long bone of the arm, with a rounded head facing the glenoid, greater tuberosity laterally and condyles distally; on a swimmer's view the humeral heads are the large rounded densities deliberately projected clear of the cervicothoracic junction.
humerus head: Rounded dense hemisphere that should sit centrally over the middle of the Y, where scapular body, acromion and coracoid meet at the glenoid. The coracoid, the anterior fork nearer the ribs, is beak-shaped rather than round.
hyoid bone: A U-shaped bone suspended in the anterior neck at about C3, the only bone with no direct articulation with another bone.
hyoid bone (body of): Anterior horizontal bar of the U-shaped hyoid, seen in the upper neck around C3 level below the mandible and above the thyroid cartilage; it has no bony articulation, and the thyroid cartilage below it is much larger and often calcified.
hypothenar eminence: Muscle bulk on the ulnar side of the palm overlying the fifth metacarpal, made of abductor, flexor and opponens digiti minimi and lying superficial to the pisiform and hook of hamate; the thenar eminence is the corresponding radial mass at the thumb base.
ileum: Straight vertical echogenic cortical line of the iliac wing running alongside the femoral head (the label here means ilium, not small bowel); it is the baseline from which both alpha and beta angles are drawn and must appear perfectly straight for a valid coronal plane.
iliac crest: Curved superior border of the iliac wing running from the anterior superior to the posterior superior iliac spine, its highest point lying at about the L4 level and serving as a counting landmark on abdominal and lumbar films; in adolescents its apophysis appears as a separate curvilinear ossification.
iliacus: Fan-shaped muscle lining the inner surface of the iliac wing and filling the iliac fossa, blending at the pelvic brim with psoas, which lies medial to it, to form iliopsoas inserting on the lesser trochanter; psoas is the rounded paravertebral muscle.
iliacus muscle: Fills the concave inner surface of the iliac fossa, lateral to the lower part of psoas major, and joins the psoas tendon to form iliopsoas passing anterior to the hip to the lesser trochanter; psoas is the rounder muscle lying medially against the lumbar vertebrae.
ilioischial line: Kohler's line on the AP pelvis: a smooth curve running from the medial border of the ilium down the medial cortex of the ischium, representing the posterior column and quadrilateral plate. The iliopectineal line, which runs to the pubis, marks the anterior column.
iliopectineal line: Smooth curved cortical line sweeping from the sacroiliac region along the pelvic brim onto the superior pubic ramus, marking the anterior acetabular column; the ilioischial line is more medial and vertical and represents the posterior column.
iliopsoas muscle: Soft tissue band running along the medial aspect of the ilium and over the pelvic brim, crossing anterior to the hip joint to insert on the lesser trochanter as the main hip flexor. Its medial, anterior course separates it from the gluteal muscles, which lie lateral to the iliac wing.
iliotibial band (itb) or tract: Thin, uniformly low-signal linear fascial band in the lateral subcutaneous plane, superficial to the greater trochanter and vastus lateralis, formed by tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus and running to Gerdy's tubercle. Its position outside the muscle bulk separates it from any tendon.
ilium: Broad fan-shaped upper part of the innominate bone whose crest curves from the anterior superior to the posterior superior iliac spine and whose lower part forms the acetabular roof; on infant hip ultrasound it is the straight echogenic line lateral to the unossified femoral head from which the alpha angle is measured.
inferior alveolar canal: Thin lucent tube with fine corticated margins running forwards through the mandibular ramus and body from the mandibular foramen to the mental foramen below the premolars, carrying the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle; a contrast-filled salivary duct, by contrast, lies in soft tissue outside the bone.
inferior angle of the right scapula: Pointed lowermost apex of the scapula where the medial and lateral borders converge, projected over the posterolateral chest wall around the seventh or eighth rib; follow the medial border downwards to it rather than confusing it with the lateral border or a rib.
inferior articular facet of l2: Process descending from the junction of the L2 lamina and pars to form the upper half of the L2-L3 facet joint, lying behind the L2/3 neural foramen. The upward pointing process forming the other half of that joint belongs to L3.
inferior articular facet of l4: Process descending from the L4 lamina to form the posteromedial half of the L4/5 facet joint; the L5 superior articular process is the component lying in front of and lateral to it.
inferior articular facet of l5 vertebra: Process descending from the L5 lamina to form the upper half of the L5-S1 facet joint, articulating with the superior articular process of S1 below it. The pars interarticularis, the site of spondylolysis, lies immediately above it.
inferior articular process (facet) of l2: On the oblique view this is the front leg of the Scotty dog, descending from the junction of the L2 lamina and pars to form the upper half of the L2-L3 facet joint. The dog's ear at the same level is the superior articular process.
inferior articular process of c4: Bony process descending posteriorly from the C4 articular pillar to meet the superior articular process of C5 at the facet joint. It always lies behind the process it articulates with; the facet joints slope posteroinferiorly and should overlap on a non-rotated lateral.
inferior articular process of l3: Process descending from the junction of the L3 lamina and pars to form the upper half of the L3-L4 facet joint; the upward projecting process it meets belongs to L4. On oblique views it is the front leg of the Scotty dog.
inferior articular process of l4 vertebr: Process descending from the junction of lamina and pars of L4 to form the posteromedial half of the L4/5 facet joint; the superior articular process of L5 is the anterolateral component it sits against.
inferior articular process of the verteb: Process descending from the lamina of the vertebra above to form the posteromedial half of the facet joint; the superior articular process of the vertebra below is the anterolateral component curving around it.
inferior end plate of c5: Lower dense cortical margin of the C5 vertebral body, forming the roof of the C5/6 disc space; the parallel line on the far side of that disc space is the superior end plate of C6.
inferior epigastric artery: Arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament and runs superomedially on the deep surface of rectus abdominis within the rectus sheath; find it with colour Doppler hugging the back of the muscle. It separates direct (medial) from indirect (lateral) inguinal hernias.
inferior facet of c4: Downward-facing articular surface at the lower posterior corner of the C4 articular pillar, articulating with the superior facet of C5 to form the shingled facet joint line behind the vertebral bodies on the lateral view.
inferior glenoid labrum: Dark triangular fibrocartilage capping the lower glenoid rim on coronal oblique images, bounding the axillary recess; glenoid articular cartilage is thinner and brighter, and the superior labrum sits at the opposite pole with the biceps anchor.
inferior nasal concha (or turbinate): Curved bony shelf projecting medially from the lower part of the lateral nasal wall into the nasal cavity either side of the septum; the middle concha, part of the ethmoid, is smaller and lies above it.
inferior pubic ramus: Thin bar of bone sweeping inferolaterally from the pubic body to meet the ischial ramus, forming the lower border of the obturator foramen; the superior pubic ramus forms the upper border and runs laterally towards the acetabulum.
inferior ramus of pubic bone: The slender bar descending posterolaterally from the pubic body to fuse with the ischial ramus, forming the inferomedial margin of the obturator foramen. The superior ramus is the one running upwards and laterally from the body towards the acetabulum, roofing the same foramen.
inferior vena cava: Thin-walled, compressible vessel lying to the right of the aorta, passing behind the caudate lobe and through the liver to the right atrium, with calibre that varies through the respiratory cycle. The aorta is the left-sided, thick-walled, pulsatile vessel.
inferior vena cava (ivc): Thin-walled vein running vertically just to the right of the aorta, indenting the bare area of the liver behind the caudate lobe before entering the right atrium; unlike the aorta it is compressible, varies in calibre with respiration and gives no anterior visceral branches.
inferior vertebral notch of l2 (exit for: Deep concavity on the undersurface of the L2 pedicle, forming the roof of the L2-L3 intervertebral foramen through which the L2 root exits. It is much deeper than the shallow superior vertebral notch of L3, which forms the floor of the same foramen.
infraorbital foramen: Small round corticated lucency in the anterior maxilla a short distance below the inferior orbital rim, transmitting the infraorbital nerve and vessels; its smooth cortical margin separates it from a fracture line, and it lies above the much larger maxillary antrum.
infrapatellar (hoffa's) fat pad: Triangular lucency on the lateral knee radiograph bounded by the patellar tendon in front, the distal femur/tibial plateau behind and the inferior patellar pole above. Distinguish from the suprapatellar recess and its fat, which lie above the patella behind the quadriceps tendon.
infrapinatus muscle: Fills the infraspinous fossa on the dorsal scapula below the scapular spine, its tendon crossing behind the humeral head to the middle facet of the greater tuberosity; supraspinatus lies above the spine on higher sections and teres minor below.
infraspinatus: Muscle filling the infraspinous fossa on the posterior scapula below the scapular spine, its tendon inserting on the middle facet of the greater tuberosity. Supraspinatus lies above the spine and teres minor below infraspinatus along the lateral scapular border.
infraspinatus muscle: Fills the infraspinous fossa on the dorsal surface of the scapula below the scapular spine, its tendon inserting on the greater tuberosity as an external rotator. Supraspinatus lies above the spine, and teres minor is the smaller muscle below it along the lateral scapular border.
inner dural layer: Deeper of the two dural layers, lying against the arachnoid; it is the layer that folds inwards to form the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, while the outer layer remains applied to the skull.
innominate line: Vertical linear density projected over the lateral part of the orbit on a frontal facial view, produced by the beam passing tangentially along the greater wing of sphenoid; it is a normal line, not a fracture, and lies medial to the lateral orbital rim.
innominate line/ greater wing of sphenoi: Vertical curvilinear white line running down the lateral part of the orbit on a frontal skull view, produced by the beam passing tangentially along the temporal surface of the greater wing of sphenoid. The lateral orbital rim is the separate bony margin further laterally.
insular cortex: Cortex lining the depth of the Sylvian fissure on the lateral part of the coronal view, identified by the pulsating middle cerebral artery running in the fissure beside it, deep to the overlying opercula.
intercondylar fossa: Deep notch on the posteroinferior aspect of the distal femur separating the two condyles and containing the cruciate ligament attachments, shown best on the tunnel view; it is distinct from the trochlear groove, which lies anteriorly and receives the patella.
intercondylar fossa (left): Arch-shaped lucency between the two femoral condyles on the frontal or tunnel view, housing the cruciate ligaments; it lies above the joint line, whereas the tibial spines project upwards into it from below.
intercondylar fossa of the right femur: Deep notch between the two femoral condyles housing the cruciate ligaments, seen on an AP film as the arched lucency directly above the tibial spines; on the lateral view its roof forms the dense Blumensaat's line.
intercondylar notch of the left femur: The lucent gap between the medial and lateral femoral condyles on the frontal knee radiograph, housing the cruciate ligaments; depending on beam angle the inferior patellar pole may be projected over it. It is a gap between condyles, not the joint space below them.
interhemispheric fissure containing falx: Bright continuous echogenic stripe running in the midline between the two hemispheres, formed by the double dural fold of the falx; beneath it the corpus callosum crosses the midline as a darker transverse band.
interlobar artery: Tubular vertical opacity making up the lower part of the hilum, running immediately alongside the bronchial air column of bronchus intermedius before dividing into lower lobe branches; arteries always accompany bronchi, whereas veins run separately towards the left atrium.
interlobar artery (right lower lobe arte: Vertical tubular opacity forming the lower right hilum, lying immediately lateral to the air column of bronchus intermedius and continuing into the lower lobe branches. Its tubular shape and sharp lateral margin separate it from a hilar mass.
interlobar pulmonary artery: Vertically oriented vascular band forming the inferior limb of the right hilar point, lying immediately lateral to the air-filled bronchus intermedius which outlines it; it is the continuation of the right pulmonary artery beyond the upper lobe branch.
intermediate (middle) cuneiform: Smallest of the three cuneiforms, wedged between the medial and lateral cuneiforms in the distal tarsal row; it is recessed proximally so the second metatarsal base keys into a mortise, unlike the much larger medial cuneiform which meets the first metatarsal.
intermediate cuneiform: Middle and shortest of the three wedge-shaped cuneiforms, lying between the medial and lateral cuneiforms and articulating distally with the recessed base of the second metatarsal; the medial cuneiform is the largest and takes the first metatarsal.
intermediate cuneiform bone: The middle of the three cuneiforms, between the medial and lateral cuneiforms, articulating with the navicular behind and the second metatarsal base in front. It is the shortest, so the second metatarsal base is recessed into a mortise between its neighbours.
internal carotid artery: Enhancing round vessel within the carotid canal of the petrous temporal bone, ascending vertically then turning anteromedially above the foramen lacerum towards the cavernous sinus; the jugular foramen and vein lie posterolateral and are larger with irregular margins.
internal iliac artery: Smaller posteromedial division of the common iliac artery at the sacroiliac joint, turning back into the pelvis towards the greater sciatic foramen and giving visceral and gluteal branches; the external iliac continues anterolaterally along the pelvic brim.
internal jugular vein: Thin-walled, easily compressible vessel lateral to the common carotid artery and deep to sternocleidomastoid, often oval or triangular and varying in calibre with respiration. The carotid alongside it is round, thick-walled, pulsatile and does not compress.
internal occipital protuberance: Midline bony prominence on the inner table of the occipital squama where the grooves for the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses converge; on a frontal or Towne's view it lies in the midline above the foramen magnum, distinct from the external protuberance on the outer table.
interosseous artery: Short common interosseous trunk arising from the ulnar artery just below the elbow and passing back to the gap between radius and ulna before dividing into anterior and posterior branches; the radial and ulnar arteries instead track the shafts of their named bones.
interosseous membrane: Thin fibrous sheet spanning the interosseous borders of radius and ulna, or tibia and fibula, seen on axial MRI as a low-signal band bridging the shafts and dividing anterior from posterior compartments; on radiographs only the lucent interval between the bones is seen.
interosseous sacroiliac ligament: Short, very strong low-signal fibres filling the gap between the roughened sacral and iliac tuberosities above and behind the synovial joint space; it lies deeper than the more superficial dorsal sacro-iliac ligament.
interphalangeal joint of great toe: The single interphalangeal joint of the hallux, which has only two phalanges, lying distal to the first metatarsophalangeal joint. The lesser toes each have three phalanges and therefore both a proximal and a distal interphalangeal joint.
interspinous ligament: Fills the interval between adjacent spinous processes, seen on sagittal MRI as a low-signal band deep to the supraspinous ligament which runs along the spinous tips; the ligamentum flavum lies further anteriorly, between adjacent laminae.
intertubercular groove: Vertical lucent channel on the anterior proximal humerus between the greater tubercle laterally and the lesser tubercle medially, transmitting the long head of biceps tendon and profiled on an axial or bicipital groove view. The anatomical neck is the oblique line separating head from tubercles.
intervertebral disc: Soft-tissue layer between adjacent thoracic vertebral bodies, thinner than a lumbar disc, with a brighter T2 nucleus inside a dark annulus and bordered above and below by the low-signal endplates.
intervertebral disc (nucleus pulposus): Central part of the disc, of higher T2 signal than the dark surrounding annulus, lying between adjacent endplates; on an axial slice through the disc space it forms the anterior wall of the vertebral canal.
intervertebral disc c7-t1: Lowest cervical disc, lying between the C7 body and T1, the first rib bearing vertebra. Count down from the C2 dens to be certain; the disc immediately above it is C6/7.
intraglandular duct: Fine branching ducts arising within the gland substance beyond the hilum, tapering peripherally into an arborising tree on sialography; on ultrasound they appear as small linear hypoechoic stripes. The main duct is single, larger and lies outside the gland.
intrahepatic segment of inferior vena ca: Large thin-walled vessel in the posterior liver receiving the three hepatic veins just before it pierces the diaphragm to reach the right atrium. Unlike the aorta it lies to the right of midline, is compressible and varies in calibre with respiration.
ischial ramus: Bar of bone passing forwards and medially from the ischial tuberosity to join the inferior pubic ramus, forming the lateral part of the lower border of the obturator foramen; the medial half of that lower ring is the inferior pubic ramus.
ischial spine: Small triangular bony projection from the posterior ischium pointing medially into the pelvis, lying between the greater sciatic notch above and the lesser sciatic notch below and giving attachment to the sacrospinous ligament; the ischial tuberosity is the much bulkier mass further inferiorly.
ischial tuberosity: Rounded bony prominence at the inferolateral corner of the obturator ring, projected just lateral to the inferior pubic ramus on an AP pelvis though truly posterior, and the common hamstring origin. The ischial spine is a smaller pointed projection sitting higher on the medial pelvic margin.
ischioanal fossa: Wedge-shaped fat-filled space lateral to the anal canal and below levator ani, bounded laterally by obturator internus and the ischium; recognise it by uniform high T1 fat signal with no muscle bulk, unlike the adjacent striated levator sling.
ischiopubic ramus: Bar of bone forming the inferior margin of the obturator foramen, running from the symphysis inferolaterally to the ischial tuberosity; it is the fused inferior pubic and ischial rami, so do not label the whole structure inferior pubic ramus.
ischiopubic synchondrosis: Cartilaginous junction of the inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus in the lower part of the obturator ring; in children it is often bulbous, lucent and asymmetric, a normal appearance mistaken for fracture or lesion, and it lies well below the triradiate cartilage.
ischiopubic syndesmosis: Bulbous, sometimes irregular or asymmetric expansion at the inferomedial corner of the obturator ring where the inferior pubic and ischial rami meet in children; a normal synchondrosis that fuses in later childhood, not a healing fracture or lesion.
ischium: Posteroinferior part of the innominate bone, comprising the tuberosity, spine and ramus; it forms the lateral half of the lower obturator ring, the medial half being the inferior pubic ramus, so do not label the whole ring as pubic ramus.
joint capsule: Thin dark layer passing from the glenoid rim and labrum to the anatomical neck of the humerus, enclosing the joint and blending with the cuff tendons; the labrum is the denser triangular wedge sitting directly on the bony glenoid rim.
joint capsule of the left hip: On arthrography the injected contrast outlines the capsule as a sleeve extending from the acetabular margin along the femoral neck to the intertrochanteric line, waisted at the zona orbicularis and forming recesses at the neck base. Amorphous contrast that does not conform to this outline is extracapsular extravasation.
kidney: Bean-shaped structure outlined by perirenal fat on the plain film, lying lateral to the psoas margin around T12 to L2; on ultrasound it shows an echogenic central sinus with cortex slightly less echogenic than adjacent liver or spleen, and the left sits marginally higher than the right.
l1 pedicle: Bar of bone connecting the L1 body to its posterior elements, seen end on as the oval cortical ring lateral to the midline in the upper part of the body on frontal films. Confirm the level by counting down from T12, the last rib bearing vertebra.
l1/l2 facet joint: Joint between the inferior articular process of L1 and the superior articular process of L2. Because lumbar facets are near sagittal it appears as a vertical lucent line lateral to the spinous process on the frontal view and behind the neural foramen on the lateral.
l2 nerve root: Occupies the upper part of the L2-L3 intervertebral foramen, immediately beneath the L2 pedicle, because each lumbar root exits under the pedicle of its own numbered vertebra. A root seen in the L3/4 foramen would therefore be L3, not L4.
l3 neural exit foramen: Fat-filled gap bounded above by the L3 pedicle, below by the L4 pedicle, in front by the L3 body and L3/4 disc and behind by the facet joint; the exiting L3 root sits in its upper part.
l3/4 intervertebral disc: Fibrocartilaginous joint between the L3 and L4 bodies, the second disc above L5/S1. A normal disc shows a bright nucleus pulposus with a dark surrounding annulus and a thin horizontal intranuclear cleft on T2.
l3/l4 intervertebral disc: Disc between the L3 and L4 bodies, two spaces above the lumbosacral disc; identify it by counting up from the sacral promontory, and note the low-signal annulus enclosing the brighter nucleus.
l3–l4 intervertebral disc space: Lucent gap between the inferior endplate of L3 and the superior endplate of L4; the disc itself is not visible on radiographs, only the space it occupies. Count up from the lumbosacral junction: L5/S1, then L4/5, then this level.
l4 exiting nerve root: Root leaving beneath the L4 pedicle in the upper part of the L4/5 foramen, surrounded by fat and above the disc level; the root seen more medially in the lateral recess at this level is the traversing L5.
l4 nerve root: Oval nerve of low signal hugging the undersurface of the L4 pedicle in the top of the L4/5 foramen, outlined by bright foraminal fat; in the thoracolumbar spine roots exit below their own numbered pedicle.
l4-l5 intervertebral disc: Disc between the L4 and L5 bodies, the second space above the sacrum; count up from the sloping S1 endplate rather than down from the top, and note the dark annulus surrounding the brighter nucleus.
l5 nerve: Root that has already left the L5/S1 exit foramen and lies lateral to the disc, above and lateral to the descending S1 root; it is the nerve threatened by a far lateral (extraforaminal) L5/S1 disc herniation.
l5 nerve root: Exits beneath the L5 pedicle through the L5/S1 foramen, sitting high in the foramen surrounded by fat; on myelography it is a filling defect leaving the thecal sac anterolaterally, whereas the S1 root traverses the lateral recess at that disc level.
l5 transverse process: The short, stout wing of bone projecting laterally from the last lumbar vertebra at the top of a pelvic radiograph, giving attachment to the iliolumbar ligament. Unlike the sacral ala, which is a continuous triangular mass fused to the sacrum, it is a discrete process with cortex on all sides.
l5/s1 joint (or interspace): Lowest disc space, the lucency between the L5 vertebral body and the sacral promontory at the top of the sacrum; it is more obliquely angled than the more horizontal spaces above, which separates it from L4/5.
labrum: On the coronal infant hip ultrasound, the small echogenic triangle at the outer tip of the acetabular roof, sitting over the unossified femoral head and marking the outer limit of the joint. It appears bright, unlike the echo-poor hyaline cartilage of the acetabular roof.
lambda: Point at the back of the vault where the sagittal suture meets the lambdoid suture, the site of the posterior fontanelle in infancy; the bregma is the equivalent anterior point where sagittal and coronal sutures meet.
lambdoid suture: Serrated lucent line running obliquely down and outwards from the lambda across the back of the skull, separating the parietal bones from the occipital bone and commonly containing wormian bones. The coronal suture is its anterior counterpart, in front of the vertex.
lamina: Flat plate of the vertebral arch running posteromedially from the facet and pedicle to the spinous process; on axial CT the pair meet in the midline as a V pointing back at the spinous process, whereas pedicles are the short bars joining arch to body.
lamina dura: Dense white line of cortical bone lining the tooth socket and outlining the whole root, with the thin radiolucent periodontal ligament space between it and the root surface. Its loss is a classic sign of hyperparathyroidism.
lamina of l5 vertebra: Flat plate of bone running posteromedially from the facet towards the spinous process and completing the back wall of the canal; the pedicle is the shorter, thicker strut in front of it joining arch to vertebral body.
lamina papyracea: Paper-thin medial orbital wall formed by the orbital plate of the ethmoid, separating orbital fat from the ethmoid air cells; with the orbital floor it is the commonest site of blow-out fracture, with fat or medial rectus herniating into the ethmoids.
