lateral border of the right atrium: Gently convex arc forming the lower half of the right heart border, running up from the right cardiophrenic angle; above it the straighter, more vertical edge of the superior vena cava continues towards the thoracic inlet.
lateral border of the sternum: Faint bony edge just lateral to the midline in the upper mediastinum, running down and slightly medially from the sternoclavicular joint as the manubrium narrows. The paratracheal stripe lies more medially, applied directly to the tracheal air column.
lateral circumflex femoral artery: Courses laterally across the front of the thigh at the level of the femoral neck, usually from profunda femoris, dividing into ascending, transverse and descending branches; the medial circumflex instead runs medially and posteriorly around the femoral neck.
lateral condyle of left femur: The distal femoral condyle on the same side as the fibula, i.e. directly above the fibular head on the frontal knee radiograph. The medial condyle is the one on the side of the tibial shaft's medial cortex and typically projects slightly further distally.
lateral condyle of the right femur: On the lateral knee radiograph the smaller, less inferiorly projecting of the two overlapping condylar outlines, recognised by the shallow condylopatellar notch on its anterior articular surface; on an AP view it is the condyle on the fibular side.
lateral cuneiform: Third cuneiform, articulating with the navicular proximally, the cuboid laterally and the base of the third metatarsal distally; it is the first cuneiform to ossify, so in a toddler's foot it may be the only cuneiform visible, unlike the more medial intermediate cuneiform that lines up with the second metatarsal.
lateral epicondyle: Small non-articular prominence on the radial side of the distal humerus just proximal to the capitellum, giving origin to the common extensor tendon; the last elbow centre to ossify, about thirteen years. The capitellum is larger, articular and faces the radial head.
lateral epicondyle apophysis: Small ossific fleck on the radial side of the distal humeral metaphysis, just proximal and lateral to the capitellum; the last CRITOL centre to appear, around thirteen years. Unlike the capitellum it is non-articular and does not face the radial head.
lateral epicondyle of humerus: Small non-articular prominence on the radial side of the distal humerus, just proximal and lateral to the capitellum, giving origin to the common extensor tendon; it is the last elbow centre to ossify. The capitellum is the larger rounded articular surface facing the radial head.
lateral epicondyle of right humerus: Small bony prominence on the radial side of the distal humerus immediately proximal to the capitellum, giving origin to the common extensor tendon; it is smaller and less projecting than the medial epicondyle and always lies on the same side as the radius.
lateral femoral condyle: Femoral condyle on the same side as the fibular head on the frontal radiograph, forming the lateral wall of the intercondylar notch; the medial condyle projects further distally and carries the adductor tubercle on its upper medial surface.
lateral femoral epicondyle: Small bony prominence on the outer surface of the lateral femoral condyle, proximal to the articular cartilage, giving origin to the lateral collateral ligament; it is smaller and smoother than the medial epicondyle, which carries the adductor tubercle just above it.
lateral malleolus: The expanded distal end of the fibula forming the lateral wall of the ankle mortise, projecting further distally and more posteriorly than the medial malleolus. If the malleolus is the shorter, medial one continuous with the tibial plafond, it is the medial malleolus instead.
lateral malleolus (distal fibula): Distal end of the fibula, lying posterolateral to the tibia and extending further distally than the medial malleolus; on a mortise view its medial surface articulates with the lateral talus, while the medial malleolus is the shorter medial tibial projection.
lateral malleolus (of fibula): Distal expanded end of the fibula forming the lateral wall of the ankle mortise; it descends roughly a centimetre lower and lies more posteriorly than the medial malleolus, which is the shorter medial tibial process.
lateral malleolus (of the fibula): Distal end of the fibula forming the lateral wall of the ankle mortise, descending roughly a centimetre lower and lying more posteriorly than the medial malleolus, which is the shorter blunt medial tibial process.
lateral malleolus/distal fibula: The slender lateral leg bone whose distal expansion forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise, descending further and lying more posteriorly than the medial malleolus. On oblique foot views its tip projects lateral to the talus, well proximal to the fifth metatarsal base.
lateral mass of c1: Paired bony pillar of the atlas lying either side of the odontoid peg on the open-mouth view, carrying the superior facet for the occipital condyle and the inferior facet for C2; its lateral border should align with that of the C2 body, and C1 has no vertebral body, only these masses joined by anterior and posterior arches.
lateral mass of the atlas: Bulky block of bone flanking the dens on axial CT and the open-mouth view, carrying the facet for the occipital condyle above and for C2 below; the transverse ligament attaches to its medial aspect.
lateral mass of the atlas (c1): Rectangular block of bone flanking the dens on each side on the open mouth view, forming the upper half of the atlantoaxial joint and articulating above with the occipital condyle. Its lateral border should line up with that of C2; lateral overhang suggests a Jefferson fracture.
lateral mass of the axis (c2): On the open mouth view, the block of bone forming the lower half of the atlantoaxial joint, continuous below with the C2 body and medially with the base of the dens. The C1 lateral mass sits above the joint line, and their lateral cortical margins should align.
lateral meniscus: Not directly visible on radiographs: its position is inferred as the fibrocartilage occupying the lateral joint space between the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau, on the same side as the fibular head. The medial meniscus lies in the opposite, medial compartment.
lateral plantar artery: Larger terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery, running obliquely across the sole towards the fifth metatarsal base before arching back medially as the deep plantar arch; the medial plantar branch is smaller and runs straight along the great toe side.
lateral process of the c2 vertebra: Bone projecting laterally from C2 immediately below the lateral mass of C1, forming the lower half of the lateral atlantoaxial joint on a frontal view. The lateral margins of C1 and C2 should line up; overhang suggests a C1 ring fracture.
lateral right tibial plateau: Articular surface of the proximal tibia on the same side as the fibular head, separated from the medial plateau by the intercondylar eminence; the lateral plateau is slightly convex whereas the medial plateau is concave and deeper.
lateral scapular border: Thick cortical strut running from the inferior aspect of the glenoid neck down to the inferior angle, forming the dense line at the outer edge of the scapular blade on a frontal shoulder film. The medial border is the longer, thinner line running parallel to the spine.
lateral thoracic artery: Arises from the second part of the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor and descends along that muscle's lateral border onto the chest wall and breast; the thoracoacromial trunk instead arises more proximally and fans out short branches around the clavicle and acromion.
lateral tibial plateau: Articular surface of the tibia on the same side as the fibular head; it is slightly convex, whereas the medial plateau is concave and larger.
lateral tibial plateau of the right knee: Flatter, slightly convex articular surface of the proximal tibia on the same side as the fibular head, which is the reliable side marker on an AP radiograph; the medial plateau is larger and concave.
lateral tubercle of the talus: Posterior projection of the talus behind the tibial plafond on the lateral view, the lateral of the two tubercles separated by the groove for flexor hallucis longus; when it fails to fuse it appears as a separate corticated os trigonum.
lateral ventricle: Paired slit-like anechoic spaces either side of the midline beneath the corpus callosum, containing brightly echogenic choroid plexus in the body and atrium; the midline anechoic space between them is the cavum septi pellucidi, not a ventricle.
lateral wall of right maxillary sinus: Outer cortical margin of the antrum, running from the zygomatic recess down to the alveolar process and forming the sinus wall nearest the cheek; the medial wall is the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, adjacent to the septum.
lateral wall of the right maxillary sinu: Curved cortical line forming the outer border of the antrum, running up into the zygomatic buttress and cheek prominence. The medial wall is the straighter line bordering the nasal cavity, and the roof is the orbital floor above.
lesser sciatic notch: The smaller, shallower concavity on the posterior ischial margin below the ischial spine, between that spine and the ischial tuberosity; the greater notch above it is far larger and bounded by ilium. Converted by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments into the lesser sciatic foramen.
lesser trochanter: Small conical prominence on the posteromedial femur at the lower end of the neck, seen in profile pointing medially on the frontal radiograph and receiving iliopsoas; the greater trochanter is the much larger prominence on the lateral side.
lesser trochanter of the right femur: Small cone-shaped prominence on the posteromedial femur at the base of the neck, seen in profile pointing medially on the frontal film; it takes the iliopsoas tendon, whereas gluteus medius and minimus attach to the greater trochanter laterally.
lesser tubercle of humerus: Anterior prominence of the proximal humerus lying medial to the greater tubercle and separated from it by the intertubercular groove; it receives subscapularis. It is profiled medially on internal rotation, whereas external rotation profiles the greater tubercle laterally.
lesser tuberosity: Anteromedial prominence of the proximal humerus receiving subscapularis, separated from the laterally placed greater tuberosity by the intertubercular groove; it is profiled medially when the arm is internally rotated, whereas the greater tuberosity profiles laterally in external rotation.
lesser tuberosity of humerus: Anteriorly directed prominence on the proximal humerus lying medial to the bicipital groove and taking the subscapularis insertion; it is profiled medially on an internally rotated AP, whereas the greater tuberosity is lateral and profiled on external rotation.
lesser tuberosity of the humerus: Anteriorly facing prominence on the proximal humerus immediately medial to the bicipital groove, taking the subscapularis tendon; the greater tuberosity lies lateral to the groove and is profiled on external rotation, while the lesser is profiled on internal rotation.
lesser tuberosity of the left humerus: Anterior and medially placed prominence of the proximal humerus, separated from the greater tuberosity by the bicipital groove and receiving subscapularis. It is profiled medially on internal rotation; the greater tuberosity is the lateral prominence.
lesser tuberosity of the right humerus: Anteromedial bony prominence of the proximal humerus, the footprint of subscapularis and hence occasionally avulsed by forced external rotation; the greater tuberosity, which takes supraspinatus, lies lateral to it beyond the intertubercular groove.
lesser wing of sphenoid: One of the two thin dense lines that cross in the superolateral part of the orbit on a frontal skull film. The lesser wing is the more superior and medially directed, sweeping toward the anterior clinoid and forming the upper margin of the superior orbital fissure.
ligamentum flavum: Short paired elastic ligaments joining the laminae of adjacent vertebrae and forming the posterolateral wall of the spinal canal, seen on axial imaging as a thin low signal band deep to the lamina and just in front of the facet joint. Hypertrophy narrows the canal.
ligamentum teres: Intra-articular low-signal band from the acetabular notch to the fovea capitis of the femoral head, carrying nutrient vessels. Distinguish it from the acetabular labrum, which is a triangular fibrocartilaginous rim seated on the bony acetabular margin rather than crossing the joint.
linea aspera: Sharp cortical ridge on the posterior surface of the femoral shaft, seen on axial images as a small posterior beak of low-signal cortex where the intermuscular septa and adductor aponeurosis attach; it is a normal ridge, not periosteal reaction or an exostosis.
little finger metacarpal: Fifth and most ulnar metacarpal, the shortest of the four finger metacarpals, its base articulating with the hamate and its head with the proximal phalanx of the little finger.
liver: Largest abdominal organ, filling the right upper quadrant with its inferior margin outlined by fat on the plain film; on ultrasound it is homogeneous mid-grey and marginally more echogenic than the adjacent right renal cortex, which is the standard comparison.
liver lobe: Largest homogeneous mid-grey parenchymal organ filling the right upper quadrant beneath the echogenic diaphragm and anterior to the right kidney, its echogenicity equal to or slightly greater than renal cortex. The middle hepatic vein/gallbladder fossa plane divides it from the left lobe.
lobe of liver: The left lobe lies in the epigastric midline in front of the aorta and serves as the acoustic window to the pancreas, while the right lobe fills the right upper quadrant. The functional boundary is the plane of the middle hepatic vein, from gallbladder fossa to IVC.
lobe of the liver: Homogeneous mid-echogenic parenchyma lying in the epigastrium anterior to the stomach, pancreas and aorta, used as the acoustic window for those structures; the falciform ligament and ligamentum teres mark its boundary with the right lobe.
lobe of thyroid: Homogeneous, finely granular tissue distinctly brighter than adjacent muscle, lying lateral to the trachea and medial to the common carotid artery, joined across the midline by the isthmus. The overlying strap and sternomastoid muscles are darker.
lobe of thyroid gland: Homogeneous, finely granular, relatively reflective tissue lying lateral to the trachea and anteromedial to the carotid artery and jugular vein, deep to the strap muscles. The overlying strap and sternomastoid muscles are darker with a striated fibrillar pattern.
long head of biceps brachii muscle: Arises from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, its tendon arching over the humeral head and then descending in the intertubercular groove between greater and lesser tubercles, so find the groove to place it. The short head instead arises with coracobrachialis from the coracoid tip.
long head of biceps brachii tendon: Originates from the supraglenoid tubercle, arcs over the humeral head and then descends as a small round black dot within the bicipital groove of the proximal humerus; subscapularis tendon lies medial to it, crossing to the lesser tuberosity.
long head of biceps brachii tendon sheat: Fluid- or contrast-filled halo surrounding the dark tendon within the intertubercular groove; because it communicates with the glenohumeral joint it opacifies at arthrography, while the tendon itself is the black dot at its centre.
long head of biceps femoris muscle: Posterolateral hamstring arising with semitendinosus by a conjoint tendon from the ischial tuberosity and descending laterally towards the fibular head; semitendinosus lies posteromedially and forms a long cord-like tendon, and the short head appears only distally, arising from the femur.
long head of biceps tendon: Small round dark dot sitting within the bicipital groove between the greater and lesser tuberosities on axial images, traceable proximally through the joint over the humeral head to the supraglenoid tubercle. The subscapularis tendon nearby is a broad flat band running medially to the lesser tuberosity.
long saphenous vein: Superficial vein lying in subcutaneous fat outside the deep muscular fascia along the medial calf and thigh, ascending from in front of the medial malleolus to the saphenofemoral junction in the groin; the femoral vein lies deep to the fascia alongside the artery.
lower border of teres major: Teres major runs from the lower lateral border and inferior angle of the scapula to the medial lip of the intertubercular groove; its lower border is the landmark at which the axillary vessels become brachial, with latissimus dorsi tendon wrapping just anterior to it.
lower canine: Third tooth from the midline in the lower arch, between the lateral incisor and first premolar, with a single pointed cusp and the longest root of the lower teeth; the first premolar behind it has a bicuspid crown.
lower left 2nd premolar: Fifth tooth from the midline in the lower arch, between the first premolar and first molar, with a single root and a two-cusped crown; the tooth immediately behind it has two roots and is therefore the first molar.
lower lip: Anterior soft-tissue bulge in front of the lower incisors and mandibular alveolus on the lateral facial radiograph, separated from the upper lip above by the lucent oral fissure. Trace the skin surface down from the nose to place it correctly.
lower lobe bronchus: Air-filled tubular lucency continuing inferolaterally through the heart shadow beyond the origin of the left upper lobe bronchus; the left main bronchus is the longer, more horizontal segment above this, arising directly at the carina.
lower lobe pulmonary artery: Vessel descending from the hilum and diverging into the lower zone, forming the inferior limb of the hilar point where the upper lobe vein crosses it; on the left it is largely projected behind the heart and its hilum sits higher because the artery arches over the left main bronchus.
lower right 3rd molar (wisdom tooth): Most posterior tooth in the lower arch, eighth from the midline, lying against the anterior border of the ramus and frequently unerupted or impacted with its roots close to the inferior alveolar canal.
lower right canine: Third tooth from the midline in the lower arch, with a single pointed cusp and the longest root of the lower dentition; the lateral incisor in front is smaller and chisel-shaped, the first premolar behind has two cusps.
lower second molar: Count back seven teeth from the midline along the lower arch: the middle of the three molars, sitting immediately in front of the wisdom tooth. Lower molars carry two roots, unlike the three-rooted upper molars.
lower third molar: Most posterior tooth of the lower arch, the wisdom tooth, lying at the anterior margin of the ramus with the second molar immediately in front; frequently impacted or unerupted with its crown tilted forwards.
lumbar intervertebral disc: Soft-tissue attenuation structure between adjacent lumbar endplates, clearly less dense than bone; on a slice through the intervertebral foramen it, rather than the vertebral body, forms the anterior wall of the vertebral canal.
lumbar vertebra: Deep midline structure recognised on abdominal ultrasound by the curved bright anterior cortical surface with dense complete posterior acoustic shadowing, lying immediately behind the aorta and inferior vena cava. The shadowing is the giveaway, since no soft tissue is seen beyond it.
lumbar vertebral body: Bright curved anterior cortical interface with complete posterior acoustic shadowing, sitting immediately deep to the aorta and inferior vena cava on transverse epigastric scanning and marking the deepest visible landmark.
lumbrical muscle to ring finger: Small slender muscle arising in the palm from the flexor digitorum profundus tendon and running on the radial side of its finger towards the extensor expansion; the interossei lie deeper, between and against the metacarpal shafts.
lunate: Central bone of the proximal carpal row, between scaphoid laterally and triquetral medially, quadrilateral on the PA view. On the lateral it is the crescentic bone cupped by the distal radius while itself cradling the capitate head, becoming triangular and tilted when dislocated.
lunate bone: Central bone of the proximal carpal row, quadrangular on PA and lying between scaphoid radially and triquetral ulnarly, articulating with the distal radius above and the capitate below; on lateral it is the crescentic cup whose concavity holds the round capitate head.
lung: Everything beyond the bright diaphragmatic line is aerated lung: the beam is totally reflected, so no anatomy is visible, only a bright pleural line with reverberation artefact or a mirror image of the liver. Absence of real structure is the recognition feature.
lung (apex right lung): Air-filled signal-void space at the top of the thoracic cavity rising above the first rib and medial clavicle, bounded medially by mediastinal fat and vessels; adjacent chest wall muscle shows intermediate signal rather than void.
main bronchus: Air column arising from the carina and passing inferolaterally into the hilum; the left is longer and more horizontal with the left pulmonary artery arching over it, so the left hilum sits higher, whereas the right is shorter, wider and more vertical.
main submandibular duct: Single large smooth contrast-filled duct (Wharton's) running forwards and medially from the gland hilum to open at the sublingual caruncle beside the frenulum; it is wider, unbranched and extraglandular, unlike the fine arborising intraglandular ducts.
mandibular body: Horizontally curved tooth-bearing part of the mandible running forwards from the angle to the midline symphysis, with the mental foramen in its outer cortex. The ramus is the vertical toothless portion behind the angle.
mandibular canal: Horizontal tubular lucency with thin corticated upper and lower walls running through the mandibular body from the mandibular foramen on the medial ramus forwards to the mental foramen, carrying the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle; its parallel corticated margins separate it from a lytic lesion.
mandibular condyle: Rounded articular head topping the mandibular ramus, seated in the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone just in front of the external auditory canal and translating forwards onto the articular eminence when the mouth opens. The coronoid process is the pointed, non-articular projection anterior to it.
mandibular notch: Concave upper margin of the mandibular ramus lying between the pointed coronoid process in front and the condylar process behind; it is the gap itself, not either of the two processes that flank it.
mandibular ramus: Vertical quadrilateral plate of mandible running from the angle up to the condyle and coronoid process, carrying no teeth and pierced medially at the lingula by the inferior alveolar nerve. The body is the horizontal tooth-bearing part in front of the angle.
manubrio-sternal joint (sternal angle): Step in the anterior sternal cortex where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum, best appreciated on the lateral film. It is a secondary cartilaginous joint lying at the level of the T4–T5 disc and the aortic arch.
manubriosternal joint (angle of louis): Transverse ridge where the manubrium meets the sternal body, best seen on the lateral radiograph as a step in the anterior sternal cortex; it lies at the level of the second costal cartilage, carina and aortic arch, well above the xiphisternal junction.
manubrium: Broad quadrangular uppermost segment of the sternum, articulating with the clavicles and first costal cartilages and meeting the sternal body at the sternal angle, which lies at the level of the second costal cartilage and the T4/T5 disc; below that angle the narrower sternal body continues.
mastoid air cells: Honeycomb cluster of fine lucencies within the mastoid process of the temporal bone, immediately posterior and inferior to the external auditory canal. Their trabeculated pattern distinguishes them from the smoothly outlined middle ear cavity and petrous apex lying anterior to them.
mastoid portion of the left temporal bon: Posteroinferior part of the temporal bone behind the external auditory meatus, recognised by its honeycomb trabecular air cells and the conical process projecting below; the petrous part is denser, more uniform and lies medially.
mastoid process: Cone-shaped downward projection of the temporal bone behind and below the external acoustic meatus, its fine honeycomb lucency due to air cells; the styloid process is a thin spike lying anteromedial to it.
maxillary antrum: Large triangular lucency within the maxilla, roofed by the orbital floor, bounded medially by the lateral nasal wall and with its floor just above the upper molar roots. Do not mistake the overlying coronoid process or petrous ridge for opacity within it.
maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve: Purely sensory division supplying the midface, tracked from the trigeminal ganglion through foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa, then via the inferior orbital fissure into the infraorbital canal in the sinus roof to the infraorbital foramen. The mandibular division instead exits foramen ovale.
maxillary sinus: Pyramidal air-filled antrum within the body of the maxilla, lying below the orbital floor and lateral to the nasal cavity, the largest paranasal sinus and draining into the middle meatus. On an occipitomental view it is the large triangular lucency beneath the orbit.
maxillary sinus (or antrum): Paired pyramidal air-filled lucencies beneath the orbital floors, lateral to the nasal cavity and medial to the zygoma; on the occipitomental view the petrous ridges are thrown below them, so any asymmetric opacity is genuine sinus fluid rather than overlap.
maxillary sinus/antrum: Air-filled pyramidal lucency in the maxilla beneath the orbital floor and lateral to the nasal cavity, draining into the middle meatus. Its floor lies just above the upper molar roots, and its lateral wall runs up into the zygomatic buttress.
medial (or internal) epicondyle: Non-articular prominence on the ulnar side of the distal humerus, origin of the common flexor tendon and immediately adjacent to the ulnar nerve; ossifies about seven years, before the trochlea. If a trochlear centre is present without it, it has been avulsed into the joint.
medial and lateral (ulnar and radial) co: Radiolucent capsular thickenings on either side of the elbow, inferred from their bony attachments: the ulnar collateral runs from the medial epicondyle to the coronoid and olecranon, the radial collateral from the lateral epicondyle to the annular ligament around the radial head.
medial border of left scapula: Near-vertical line over the lateral part of the upper hemithorax; follow it up and down beyond the lung into the remainder of the scapula, and note that lung markings continue lateral to it, unlike the edge of a pneumothorax.
medial clavicle: Expanded sternal end of the clavicle articulating with the manubrium at the sternoclavicular joint; the equal distance of the two medial clavicle ends from the adjacent spinous processes is what you use to judge rotation on a frontal chest film.
medial collateral ligament (mcl): Not seen as such on radiographs; it runs along the medial joint margin from the medial femoral epicondyle down to the medial tibia several centimetres below the joint line. Chronic injury calcifies at its femoral origin (Pellegrini-Stieda); the lateral collateral ligament instead ends on the fibular head.
medial condyle of the right femur: On a lateral radiograph the condyles are superimposed: the medial one is the larger and projects further inferiorly, so its outline is the lower of the two curved articular margins. The lateral condyle carries the condylopatellar (lateral femoral) notch.
medial cuneiform: Largest cuneiform, lying at the medial side of the midfoot between the navicular behind and the base of the first metatarsal in front. On the AP view it is the most medial of the three wedge-shaped bones, abutting the intermediate cuneiform laterally.
medial epicondyle: Non-articular bony prominence projecting medially from the distal humerus beyond the trochlea, giving origin to the common flexor tendon, with the ulnar nerve running behind it. The trochlea, immediately lateral to it, is articular and forms the joint surface with the ulna.
medial epicondyle apophysis: Ossification centre on the ulnar side of the distal humerus, sitting on the metaphyseal flare above the joint line and non-articular; appears about seven years, before the trochlea. If a trochlear centre is visible with no medial epicondyle, it has been avulsed into the joint.
medial epicondyle of the left humerus: Non-articular bony prominence on the medial side of the distal humerus, proximal and medial to the trochlea, giving origin to the forearm flexors with the ulnar nerve behind it. The trochlea beside it is the grooved articular surface.
medial epicondyle ossification centre: Third centre of the CRITOL sequence, appearing on the medial side of the distal humeral metaphysis and lying outside the joint capsule. If a trochlear centre is visible but no medial epicondylar centre, suspect an avulsed epicondyle displaced into the joint.
medial femoral epicondyle of the right f: Bony prominence on the medial surface of the medial femoral condyle just proximal to the articular surface, giving origin to the medial collateral ligament, with the small adductor tubercle at its upper edge; it is larger than the lateral epicondyle, which lies on the fibular side.
medial genicular artery: Small branch leaving the medial side of the popliteal artery within the popliteal fossa and curving forwards around the medial femoral or tibial condyle to the peri-patellar anastomosis; sural branches instead pass straight backwards into the gastrocnemius bellies.
medial head of gastrocnemius: Arises from the posterior aspect of the medial femoral condyle and forms the superficial posteromedial calf, larger and extending further distally than the lateral head; semimembranosus lies deep and anterior to it at the knee, with soleus deep to it below.
medial head of the right gastrocnemius m: Superficial posteromedial muscle of the upper calf arising from the medial femoral condyle, forming one of the two rounded bellies on axial MRI; soleus lies deep to both heads and extends further distally, and the lateral head lies on the opposite side.
medial malleolus: Short blunt medial projection of the distal tibia whose lateral surface forms the medial wall of the ankle mortise against the talus; it ends more proximally than the lateral malleolus, which belongs to the fibula and lies further distal and posterior.
medial malleolus (of the tibia): Blunt medial process of the distal tibia forming the medial wall of the ankle mortise; it ends more proximally than the fibular tip, which descends about a centimetre lower and lies more posteriorly.
medial malleolus of left tibia: Short blunt process on the medial side of the distal tibia forming the medial wall of the ankle mortise; it stops higher than the lateral malleolus, which descends about a centimetre further and lies more posteriorly.
medial malleolus of the tibia: Medial bony prominence of the distal tibia projecting below the ankle joint line and articulating with the medial talar facet; in children it is the medial extension of the distal tibial epiphysis. The lateral malleolus is distal fibula and descends further.
medial prominence of tibial spine (inter: The medial of the two small bony peaks rising from the intercondylar eminence of the tibial plateau, projecting up into the femoral intercondylar notch and lying at the inner margin of the medial plateau. Do not confuse these central peaks with the peripheral tibial plateau margins.
medial tibial condyle: Medial half of the tibial plateau below the joint line, the larger of the two with a concave articular surface, lying on the side away from the fibular head; the femoral condyles are the rounded masses above the joint line.
medial tibial plateau: Articular surface of the tibia on the side away from the fibula, matching the medial femoral condyle above it; its surface is dished and concave, whereas the lateral plateau is flatter or slightly convex and overlies the fibular head.
medial tibial spine: The medial of the two peaks of the intercondylar eminence, projecting upwards from the tibial plateau between the medial and lateral articular facets. Identify the medial tibial compartment first, since the paired spines are otherwise easily transposed on a frontal view.
medial tibial spine of the right tibia: Medial of the two peaks of the intercondylar eminence rising between the tibial plateaus, identified on an AP film as the one furthest from the fibular head; sharply pointed and continuous with the tibia, not a loose body.
medial tibial spine or tubercle of inter: Medial of the two bony peaks rising between the tibial plateaus, on the side opposite the fibular head on an AP film; the cruciate and meniscal attachments lie on the intercondylar area around these spines, which should not be mistaken for loose bodies.
median antecubital vein: Short superficial vein crossing the antecubital fossa obliquely from the cephalic vein laterally to the basilic vein medially, lying on the bicipital aponeurosis; the paired brachial veins are deep, straddling the brachial artery rather than crossing obliquely.
median nerve: In the carpal tunnel it is the flattened structure lying immediately deep to the flexor retinaculum on the radial side, superficial to the flexor tendons; more proximally it runs between flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus. Its speckled fascicular texture separates it from the uniformly dark tendons.
median nerve, four flexor digitorum supe: Ten structures deep to the flexor retinaculum: the nerve is the most volar and radial, flattened with visible fascicles and slightly higher signal than the uniformly black tendons; superficialis tendons lie volar to profundus, with flexor pollicis longus most radial.
medullary cavity of the humerus: Central marrow space of the shaft, high signal on T1 from fatty marrow, ringed by the uniformly low-signal cortex; do not mistake the black cortical ring or the adjacent periosteal soft tissue for the cavity itself.
mental foramen: Small round corticated lucency in the body of the mandible below the premolar roots on an orthopantomogram, transmitting the mental nerve and vessels with surrounding fat. Its smooth round outline separate from the tooth distinguishes it from a periapical lucency, which is continuous with a root.
mental nerve: Terminal branch of the inferior alveolar nerve, identified where the mandibular canal turns upward and exits the mental foramen, a round corticated lucency near the premolar apices in the outer mandibular body; the smooth cortical rim distinguishes it from a periapical lesion.
metacarpophalangeal joint of the left ri: Joint between the head of the fourth metacarpal and the base of its proximal phalanx, on the knuckle line. Count rays from the thumb — the ring finger is the fourth; the interphalangeal joints lie further distally.
metaphysis: Flared segment of a growing long bone between the growth plate and the tubular diaphysis, with thinner cortex and prominent trabecular bone. The epiphysis lies beyond the physis, at the articular end of the bone.
metaphysis of the base of the proximal p: Flared portion of the phalangeal shaft immediately on the shaft side of the lucent growth plate at the proximal end of the little finger's proximal phalanx. The epiphysis is the separate ossific centre on the joint side of that same physis.
middle cuneiform: Wedge-shaped bone lying between the medial and lateral cuneiforms, articulating with the navicular behind and the base of the second metatarsal in front; being the shortest cuneiform, it leaves the second metatarsal base recessed between its neighbours.
middle glenohumeral ligament: Oblique anterior capsular band running from the anterosuperior labrum and glenoid neck across the front of the humeral head to blend with the deep surface of subscapularis; on arthrography contrast separates it from that tendon, and it lies above the thicker inferior glenohumeral ligament.
middle hepatic vein: Runs in the main lobar fissure between right and left lobes, separating segments 4 and 5/8, and drains superiorly into the IVC; hepatic veins have thin imperceptible walls and run between segments, whereas portal veins have bright echogenic walls and run within them.
middle phalanx 2nd toe: The short, squat middle segment of the second toe, lying between its proximal and distal phalanges; the second toe is the ray immediately lateral to the hallux. The great toe has only two phalanges, so it has no middle phalanx to confuse this with.
middle phalanx of fourth toe: Count from the great toe, which has only two phalanges; on the fourth ray the middle phalanx is the short stubby segment lying between the longer proximal phalanx and the small distal phalanx with its terminal tuft.
middle phalanx of the left 4th toe: Short squat segment between the proximal and distal phalanges of the fourth toe; the lesser toes each have three phalanges and their middle phalanx is characteristically small and often hypoplastic, unlike the longer proximal phalanx.
middle third of left clavicle: Central segment of the S-shaped bone that runs between the sternoclavicular joint medially and the acromial end laterally, at the point where it crosses the first rib; this junction of the two curves is the commonest fracture site.
nasal bone: Small thin elongated bone forming the bony bridge of the nose, projecting forwards and downwards from the frontal bone at the frontonasal suture and lying above the lucent anterior nasal aperture on the lateral view. A normal longitudinal vascular groove can mimic a fracture.
nasal septum: Midline vertical partition dividing the nasal cavities, formed by the perpendicular plate of ethmoid above and the vomer below, sitting above the hard palate between the two nasal fossae; the turbinates are the soft tissue shelves lateral to it.
nasopharynx: Air-filled space behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate, bounded posteriorly by adenoidal soft tissue overlying the anterior arch of C1 and C2 on the lateral view. The oropharynx lies below the soft palate, behind the tongue.
natal cleft: Vertical midline soft-tissue lucent stripe overlying the lower sacrum and coccyx on the frontal pelvis; being a skin fold it extends beyond the bone margins, unlike a true fracture line which is confined within the bone.
navicula: Boat-shaped tarsal bone of the medial midfoot, wedged between the talar head behind and the three cuneiforms in front; the cuboid is its lateral counterpart, lying between the calcaneus and the fourth and fifth metatarsals.
navicular: Boat-shaped medial midfoot bone lying between the talar head behind and the three cuneiforms in front, with a medial tuberosity for tibialis posterior. The cuboid is its lateral counterpart, sitting between the calcaneus and the fourth and fifth metatarsals.
navicular bone: Boat-shaped tarsal bone on the medial midfoot lying between the head of the talus proximally and the three cuneiforms distally; it is the last tarsal to ossify so may be small or irregular in young children, and an accessory os tibiale externum can sit at its medial tuberosity within the tibialis posterior tendon.
neck of femur: The obliquely oriented segment between head and trochanters; disruption of the trabecular pattern or cortical step here indicates fracture.
neck of fibula: Short constricted segment immediately below the expanded fibular head, just distal to the proximal tibiofibular joint; the common peroneal nerve winds around it, so fractures here cause foot drop.
neck of fibula (left): Short constriction immediately below the expanded fibular head, lying lateral and slightly posterior to the proximal tibia and encircled by the common peroneal nerve; the head is the knob above it and the styloid the small upward spike.
neck of pancreas: Short midline segment of gland crossing anterior to the L1/L2 vertebrae and lying directly in front of the superior mesenteric vein/portal venous confluence. That confluence is the landmark defining it, with head to the right and body to the left.
neck of radius: Short constricted segment of bone between the disc-shaped radial head above and the radial tuberosity below. A line drawn along it should pass through the capitulum; the shaft distal to the tuberosity is wider and straighter.
neck of the rib (left): Narrow bar of the rib between the head, which articulates with the vertebral body and disc, and the tubercle, which meets the transverse process; it runs backwards and laterally just in front of the transverse process.
nerve roots of the cauda equina: Lumbosacral roots descending almost vertically below the conus, seen as multiple fine low-signal strands within bright CSF and layering posteriorly in the supine patient; a single midline strand instead would be the filum terminale.
normal anterior left humeral fat pad: Thin lucent stripe lying flat against the anterior cortex of the distal humerus in the coronoid fossa on a lateral elbow film; it is normally visible and hugs the bone, becoming convex and lifted (sail sign) with an effusion, whereas any visible posterior fat pad is abnormal.
nucleus pulposus l4/5 intervertebral dis: Central portion of the second-from-lowest lumbar disc, of intermediate to high signal, ringed by the uniformly dark annulus fibrosus and bounded above and below by the L4 and L5 endplates.
nucleus pulposus of l2/l3 disc: Bright central portion of the L2/L3 disc on T2, enclosed by the low-signal annulus and separated from marrow by the thin dark endplates; count levels up from the sacrum rather than down from the top of the image.
nucleus pulposus of l5/s1 disc: Soft central part of the lowest lumbar disc, brighter than its surrounding annulus on T2, lying between the L5 body and the sloping sacral endplate at the lumbosacral angle.
nucleus pulposus of the l1/l2 disc: Central water-rich core of the disc between the L1 and L2 bodies, bright on T2 and rimmed by the uniformly dark annulus; fix the level by the conus medullaris, which normally ends at L1/L2.
nutrient vessel of l1: Linear channel running horizontally forward from the middle of the posterior L1 vertebral body toward its centre, carrying the basivertebral vein. Unlike a fracture line it is midline, horizontal and stops short of the endplates.
obturator externus: Flat muscle on the OUTER surface of the obturator membrane and adjacent pubis/ischium, sweeping posterolaterally beneath the femoral neck to the trochanteric fossa. Obturator internus is its mirror image on the inner (pelvic) surface of the same membrane.
obturator foramen: Large oval lucency in the anteroinferior pelvis bounded by the superior and inferior pubic rami and the ischium; symmetry of the two foramina is the standard check for pelvic rotation on an AP film.
obturator internus: Fan-shaped muscle lining the inner (pelvic) surface of the obturator membrane and forming the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa; its tendon turns sharply round the lesser sciatic notch to the medial greater trochanter. Obturator externus lies outside the membrane.
obturator internus muscle: Arises from the internal, pelvic surface of the obturator membrane and ring, lining the lateral pelvic wall, then turns sharply around the lesser sciatic notch to insert on the medial aspect of the greater trochanter; obturator externus lies on the outer surface of the same membrane.
obturator nerve: Arising from the lumbar plexus (L2–L4), it leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal at the superolateral corner of the obturator foramen alongside the obturator vessels, then supplies the adductor compartment. Contrast with the femoral nerve, which passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery.
occipital bone: Bone forming the back and base of the skull around the foramen magnum. On lateral or peg views its basiocciput lies directly above C1 with the odontoid peg pointing up toward the basion, and its condyles articulate with the lateral masses of the atlas.
occipital condyle: Paired oval bony prominences on the undersurface of the occipital bone flanking the anterolateral margins of the foramen magnum, articulating with the superior facets of the C1 lateral masses; the mastoid process lies considerably further lateral.
occipital lobe: Most posterior brain parenchyma, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus and above the tentorium, lying behind the splenium and occipital horn; the cerebellum lies below the tentorium and is markedly more echogenic.
occipitomastoid suture: Suture between the mastoid part of the temporal bone and the occipital bone, running downwards and forwards from the lower end of the lambdoid suture behind the mastoid; corticated serrated margins distinguish it from a fracture.
odontoid peg: Vertical tooth-like projection rising from the body of C2, resting against the back of the anterior arch of the atlas and tethered by ligaments to atlas and occiput. On the open-mouth view it should sit centrally with equal gaps to the C1 lateral masses.
odontoid peg or dens: Midline peg of bone projecting upwards from the body of C2, seen between the lateral masses of C1 on an open-mouth view and directly behind the small oval anterior arch of C1 on the lateral. The arch is a ring in front of it; the peg is solid.
odontoid process: The peg projecting superiorly from the C2 body into the anterior arch of C1, held by the transverse ligament.
odontoid process (dens) of axis (c2): Midline vertical peg arising from the upper surface of the C2 body, projected in the midline through the oral cavity on facial views, well below the maxilla and nasal septum. Its base blends with the C2 body; it is not a separate ossicle unless os odontoideum is present.
odontoid process (dens) of c2 vertebra (: On the frontal open-mouth or facial view it sits centrally between the two lateral masses of C1 with symmetric spaces either side; trace it downwards and it becomes continuous with the C2 body, which teeth shadows never do.
olecranon: Posterior beak of the proximal ulna, best profiled on the lateral view where it caps the trochlear notch; its ossification centre is the O of CRITOL, appearing around nine years, after the trochlea and before the lateral epicondyle.
olecranon fossa: Shallow depression on the posterior aspect of the distal humerus that receives the olecranon in full extension, appearing on the AP radiograph as a rounded lucency just above the trochlea; it houses the posterior fat pad, which becomes visible only with an effusion. Its anterior counterpart is the coronoid fossa.
olecranon fossa (left): Hollow on the posterior aspect of the distal humerus between the two epicondyles, seen on AP as a lucent oval just proximal to the trochlea, into which the olecranon locks in full extension; the coronoid fossa is the smaller anterior depression.
olecranon fossa left humerus: Hollow on the posterior distal humerus between the epicondyles, projected on AP as a lucent oval just above the trochlea; it is often thinned or even fenestrated as a normal variant, so do not call this apparent lucency a lesion or fracture.
olecranon of the left ulna: Large hook-like posterior process of the proximal ulna forming the point of the elbow, seating in the olecranon fossa on extension. The coronoid process is the smaller anterior beak at the front of the trochlear notch.
olecranon of the ulna: Large beak-like posterior process of the proximal ulna forming the point of the elbow and seating in the olecranon fossa on extension; on the lateral view it is the most posterior bony prominence. The coronoid process is its anterior counterpart, the two forming the trochlear notch.
olecranon of ulna: Posterior prominence of the proximal ulna that fits into the olecranon fossa in extension and forms the palpable point of the elbow; triceps inserts here, whereas biceps inserts anteriorly on the radial tuberosity.
olecranon ossification centre: Crescentic ossific fragment capping the posterior tip of the olecranon on the lateral view, separated from the ulna by a lucent physis; appears about nine years (the O of CRITOE) and is frequently bilateral, unlike an avulsion fracture.
olecranon process: Proximal projection of the ulna forming the point of the elbow and the posterior half of the trochlear notch, receiving triceps and seating in the olecranon fossa in extension; the coronoid process is the smaller anterior lip of the same notch.
olecranon process of the ulna (left): Beak-shaped posterior projection at the very top of the ulna forming the posterosuperior lip of the trochlear notch and seating in the olecranon fossa on extension; the coronoid process is its anterior counterpart on the same notch.
olecranon process of ulna: Curved posterior eminence at the top of the ulna forming the point of the elbow, fitting into the olecranon fossa of the humerus in extension. The coronoid process is the anterior eminence of the same hook.
oral vestibule opposite to the second up: Contrast-filled recess between cheek and upper alveolus level with the second upper molar, the opening of the parotid (Stensen's) duct where the sialography cannula sits; the submandibular duct instead opens beneath the tongue.
orbital floor: Thin curved cortical line forming both the base of the orbit and the roof of the maxillary antrum; a blowout fracture disrupts it with soft tissue hanging into the sinus. It lies behind and above the inferior orbital rim, which is the thicker anterior margin.
os acromiale: Accessory ossicle at the anterior acromion resulting from failure of fusion of its secondary ossification centre, separated by a smooth, transversely oriented, fully corticated lucent line and best seen on an axillary view; the rounded corticated margins distinguish it from an acromial fracture.
os peroneum: Round corticated accessory ossicle lying lateral or plantar to the cuboid near the calcaneocuboid joint, within the peroneus longus tendon; its smooth complete cortex separates it from an avulsion fragment, and it lies proximal to the os vesalianum at the fifth metatarsal base.
os subfibulare: Small accessory ossicle sitting just distal to the tip of the lateral malleolus, with smooth, complete corticated margins on all sides. That continuous cortex separates it from an avulsion fragment, which has a sharp uncorticated edge and a matching donor defect on the fibular tip.
os tibiale externum: Well-corticated accessory ossicle lying against the medial aspect of the navicular tuberosity within the tibialis posterior insertion; its smooth rounded cortex and smooth lucent cleft separate it from an avulsion fracture, whose margins are irregular and uncorticated.
os trigonum: Well-corticated accessory ossicle lying immediately behind the posterior process of the talus on the lateral ankle radiograph, representing an unfused lateral tubercle. Its smooth cortex all the way round distinguishes it from a fracture of the posterior process, which has a sharp uncorticated edge.
os vesalianum: Rounded, fully corticated accessory ossicle lying just proximal to the fifth metatarsal tuberosity within the peroneus brevis tendon; the normal apophysis is a thin sliver lying parallel to the shaft, and an avulsion fracture is transverse with sharp uncorticated margins.
os vesalianum fused to base of 5th metat: Accessory ossicle at the proximal fifth metatarsal within the peroneus brevis tendon, here united with the base so it appears as a prominent bulbous or beaked tuberosity; smooth continuous cortex separates it from an avulsion fracture fragment.
osseus acetabular concavity: Echogenic curved bony socket deep to the femoral head, formed by the ilium above and running inferiorly to the triradiate cartilage; its depth against the straight iliac line gives the alpha angle, in contrast to the hypoechoic cartilaginous roof extending laterally over the head.
ossification centre of right humeral hea: Small rounded ossific nucleus capping the proximal humeral metaphysis, separated from it by the radiolucent unossified physis; because it lies within the humeral outline it should not be mistaken for the overlying acromion or a lung nodule.
ossification centre of the distal right: Flat ossific plate at the distal end of the radius, separated from the flared metaphysis by a transverse lucent physis and lying on the thumb side of the wrist; it appears earlier and is larger than the distal ulnar epiphysis. The carpal bones are separate rounded ossicles distal to it.
ossification centre of the left internal: Third centre in the CRITOL sequence, appearing about five years on the medial side of the distal humerus and lying outside the joint. The trochlear centre next to it appears only at about ten years.
ossification centre of the left medial e: Separate ossicle on the medial side of the distal humerus, proximal to and outside the joint line, appearing third in the CRITOE sequence; if a trochlear centre is present but no medial epicondylar centre is seen medially, assume it has been avulsed and displaced into the joint.
ossification centre of the navicula: Last tarsal bone to ossify, appearing as a small ossific nucleus in the medial midfoot between the head of the talus and the three cuneiforms; the cuboid, its usual confusion, lies laterally between the calcaneus and the fourth and fifth metatarsals.
ossification centre of the olecranon of: Secondary centre at the posterosuperior tip of the proximal ulna, often bipartite or fragmented, appearing late in the CRITOE sequence; its smooth corticated margins and location at the olecranon apex separate it from an avulsion fracture.
ossification centre of the proximal phal: Ossific fleck at the proximal end of the proximal phalanx of the ulnar-most digit; identify the little finger by counting its three phalanges, with hamate and pisiform marking the ulnar side of the wrist. Phalangeal epiphyses lie at the base, not the head.
ossification centre of the right capitul: Rounded nucleus at the lateral articular surface of the distal humerus, directly opposite the radial head; the first elbow centre to appear, within the first year, so its presence alone says little about age. The radial head centre lies across the joint, on the radius.
ossification centre of the right thumb m: Ossific centre at the proximal end (base) of the thumb metacarpal; the thumb is unique among metacarpals in this, as the second to fifth ossify from a centre at the head. Confirm the thumb ray by its shortness, radial position and only two phalanges.
outer dural layer (periosteum): Endosteal layer of dura applied directly to the inner table of the skull; it separates from the inner meningeal layer to enclose the dural venous sinuses, and the potential extradural space lies between it and bone.
palatine process of maxilla: Horizontal bony shelf forming the front three-quarters of the hard palate, meeting its fellow at the midline palatine suture with the palatine bone completing the palate behind; seen as a dense line above the upper teeth.
palmar aponeurosis: Thin low-signal fibrous sheet spread across the palm immediately deep to the subcutaneous fat and superficial to the flexor tendons, continuous proximally with palmaris longus; the flexor retinaculum is the thicker band further proximally, bridging the carpal bones.
palmar digital arteries: Tiny round vessels arising from the superficial palmar arch and running along the sides of the flexor tendon sheaths towards the fingers, paired with digital nerves; they lie beside the tendons rather than within them.
pancreas: Retroperitoneal gland lying transversely across the epigastrium, anterior to the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vessels and aorta, behind the stomach and left lobe of liver. It is homogeneous and iso- to hyperechoic to liver; trace the splenic vein along its posterior border to find it.
paratracheal stripe: Thin vertical soft-tissue line, normally under 3 to 4 mm, along the right lateral tracheal wall from the clavicles down to the azygos vein at the right tracheobronchial angle, formed by tracheal wall and apposed pleura with aerated lung immediately outside it.
parietal pleura: Outer pleural layer lining the inner surface of the ribs, diaphragm and mediastinum, continuous with the visceral layer at the hilum; the visceral layer covers the lung itself and dips into the fissures. Neither is visible on a radiograph unless thickened, calcified or separated by fluid or air.
parotid duct: Runs forwards across the masseter from the anterior parotid, then turns medially through buccinator to open opposite the crown of the upper second molar; it is not visible on a normal plain film or OPG unless opacified or containing a calculus.
parotid gland: The largest salivary gland, lying superficial to the masseter and mandibular ramus, with the facial nerve running through it and its duct opening opposite the second upper molar.
pars interarticularis of l1: Isthmus of bone between the superior and inferior articular processes of L1, forming the posterior boundary of the neural exit foramen on parasagittal images; the pedicle is the more anterior bar joining the arch to the vertebral body.
patella: Sesamoid bone within the quadriceps tendon, projected over the distal femur on the AP view and lying anterior to the femoral condyles on the lateral. A bipartite variant at the superolateral corner is fully corticated and rounded, unlike the sharp margins of a fracture.
patella tendon: Thick soft tissue band running from the apex (inferior pole) of the patella to the tibial tuberosity, outlined behind by Hoffa's fat pad on the lateral radiograph; the quadriceps tendon is the corresponding band above, attaching to the patellar base.
patellar ligament: Band of soft-tissue density on the lateral view running from the patellar apex down to the tibial tuberosity, outlined against the lucent infrapatellar fat pad; the quadriceps tendon is the equivalent band above the patella.
patellar tendon: Straight soft-tissue band running from the apex (inferior pole) of the patella to the tibial tuberosity, passing superficial to Hoffa's fat pad on the lateral view; the quadriceps tendon is its counterpart above, attaching to the patellar base.
pectineus muscle: Flat quadrangular muscle forming the floor of the femoral triangle, running from the pecten of the superior pubic ramus to the pectineal line below the lesser trochanter. On axial MRI it sits directly behind the femoral vessels, between iliopsoas laterally and adductor brevis medially.
pectoralis major muscle: Broad superficial sheet of the anterior chest wall arising from medial clavicle, sternum and costal cartilages and converging laterally to form the anterior axillary fold; pectoralis minor is the smaller muscle deep to it running to the coracoid.
pectoralis minor muscle: Thin flat triangular muscle deep to pectoralis major, arising from the upper ribs and converging superolaterally to insert on the coracoid process. A fat plane separates it from the thicker, more superficial pectoralis major, which inserts on the humerus instead.
pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and b: All attach to the coracoid process, the short beak-like projection arising from the anterosuperior scapula just medial to the glenoid and pointing anterolaterally; pectoralis minor inserts on it while coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps arise from its tip. The acromion, by contrast, lies more lateral and superior at the acromioclavicular joint.
pedicle: Short bar of bone joining the back of the vertebral body to the articular pillar and forming the lateral wall of the vertebral canal on axial CT; the lamina is the flatter plate running posteromedially towards the spinous process.
pedicle of c6: Short bar of bone connecting the posterior vertebral body to the articular pillar and lamina, forming the roof and floor of the neural foramen. On the lateral it is the segment bridging the posterior body line and the facet column.
pedicle of c7: Short bar of bone joining the back of the lowest cervical body to its lamina and articular pillar, forming the boundary between the C6/7 and C7/T1 neural foramina. The transverse process lies further laterally, projecting beyond the vertebral body outline.
pedicle of l1: Short stout bar linking the posterolateral vertebral body to the lamina; on the frontal radiograph it is the oval cortical ring (owl's eye) at the upper corner of the body. Confirm level from T12, the lowest rib-bearing vertebra.
pedicle of l2: Short stout bar joining the posterior L2 body to its lamina and articular processes; seen end on as the oval cortical ring in the upper half of the body on frontal films, and as the roof of the L2/3 foramen laterally. The L2 nerve root exits directly beneath it.
pedicle of l2 vertebra: Oval cortical ring seen end on lateral to the midline in the upper half of the L2 body on the frontal view. The midline density between the two pedicles is the spinous process, which angles caudally and is usually projected over the vertebra below.
pedicle of l3: Short bony bridge joining the posterior vertebral body to the lamina and articular processes, seen end-on as the paired oval corticated rings at the upper outer corners of the body on a frontal film and forming the eye of the Scotty dog on oblique views; identify the level by counting up from L5 or down from T12.
pedicle of l3 vertebra: Bony strut connecting the posterolateral corner of the L3 body to the lamina and transverse process, forming the lateral wall of the spinal canal on axial images. Confirm the level by counting down from T12, the last rib bearing vertebra.
pedicle of l4 vertebra: Bony bridge running from the posterolateral vertebral body to the lamina and articular processes; on the frontal radiograph it is the cortical ring at the superolateral corner of the body. Count up from the sacrum and L5 to confirm the level.
pedicle of t1 vertebra: Short bony bridge joining the vertebral body in front to the lamina and articular processes behind; on a frontal view it projects as an oval cortical ring beside the upper vertebral body. T1 is the first vertebra bearing a rib.
pedicle of t5: Pedicles appear on the frontal film as paired oval ring densities at the upper corners of the vertebral body, one either side of the midline spinous process. Count down from T1 to reach T5; loss of a pedicle ring suggests metastasis.
pedicle of t7: Oval ring density at the upper corner of the vertebral body on the frontal projection, one either side of the midline; count down carefully from T1, or up from the last rib-bearing vertebra, to confirm T7. The spinous process is single and central.
pedicle of the axis (c2): Short bar of bone linking the axis body to its lateral mass and posterior elements, projected below and medial to the C1-C2 articulation on the open mouth view. The transverse process lies further laterally, beyond the articular mass.
pedicle of the lumbar vertebra: Short thick strut of dense bone joining the back of the vertebral body to the facets and lamina, forming the lateral wall of the canal; a slice through the pedicles shows no neural foramen, since the foramen lies between adjacent pedicles.
pelvic brim: Continuous curved line running from the sacral promontory along the arcuate line of the ilium to the pectineal line of the pubis and symphysis, dividing false from true pelvis; the ilioischial line is a separate, more vertical medial line.
pericardial fat pad: Triangular opacity filling the cardiophrenic angle, less dense than soft tissue so the heart border and vessels remain visible through it. That low density and its typical angle location separate it from a genuine mediastinal mass.
periodontal ligament: Thin radiolucent line following the contour of the neck and root of the tooth, sandwiched between the root surface and the dense white lamina dura; if the line you have picked is white rather than black, it is lamina dura.
peroneal artery: Arises from the tibioperoneal trunk just beyond the anterior tibial origin and descends in the deep posterior compartment hugging the medial border of the fibula. Its medial neighbour, the posterior tibial artery, runs alongside the tibia to pass behind the medial malleolus.
peroneal brevis/longus tendons: Paired tendons curving behind and below the lateral malleolus in the retromalleolar groove, brevis lying deeper and inserting on the fifth metatarsal tuberosity while longus passes under the cuboid to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base. Tibialis posterior lies behind the medial malleolus instead.
peroneus brevis: Runs behind the lateral malleolus lying anterior to peroneus longus and inserts on the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal, the point usually labelled on foot radiographs; peroneus longus instead crosses the sole to the first metatarsal base and medial cuneiform.
peroneus brevis tendon: Runs behind the lateral malleolus and forwards to insert on the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal, so a transverse avulsion fragment here reflects its pull. Peroneus longus continues past this point, hooking under the cuboid to reach the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base.
peroneus longus: Lateral compartment muscle forming the superficial layer over the lateral surface of the fibula, arising from its head and upper shaft; peroneus brevis lies deep to it, closer to the bone, and becomes the more prominent muscle bulk in the lower leg.
pes anserinus: Conjoined tendinous insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the anteromedial proximal tibia, just below the medial tibial condyle and joint line. Look for the thin flat tendon bundle superficial to the medial collateral ligament, which lies deeper and runs vertically.
petrous ridge: Dense curvilinear sclerotic band formed by the superior edge of the petrous temporal bone, running from the lateral skull towards the midline and projected across the orbits or antra depending on tube angulation. Unlike the innominate line, which is a vertical line at the lateral orbital wall, it is horizontal.
physis for the 5th metacarpal: Lucent transverse growth plate at the distal end of the little finger metacarpal, separating the head epiphysis from the shaft. Metacarpals two to five have distal physes; only the thumb metacarpal has its physis at the base.
pia and arachnoid mater: Thin echogenic layer applied directly to the surface of the hypoechoic cord, outlining its margins. Anechoic CSF in the subarachnoid space separates it from the outer, more superficial echogenic dural line of the thecal sac.
pinna: Curved soft-tissue outline of the external ear projected over the mastoid and squamous temporal bone, its edge visible because air outlines it. It runs off the skull margin and lacks the corticated edges of a suture or the sharp lucency of a fracture.
pinnae of ears: Paired curved soft-tissue outlines of the external ears superimposed over the temporal region on a lateral skull film, projecting beyond the bony calvarial margin. Their soft-tissue density and ear-shaped contour distinguish them from bony sutures or vascular grooves within the vault.
pisiform: Sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon lying palmar to the triquetral, so on a PA film it is a rounded, well-corticated density superimposed on the triquetral at the ulnar side, only separated on the lateral or oblique view.
pituitary fossa: Saddle-shaped depression in the body of the sphenoid on the lateral skull film, bounded anteriorly by the tuberculum sellae and anterior clinoids and posteriorly by the dorsum sellae with its posterior clinoids, sitting directly above the sphenoid sinus.
pituitary fossa (sella turcica): Saddle-shaped midline depression on the upper surface of the sphenoid body, bounded in front by the tuberculum and anterior clinoids and behind by the dorsum sellae, sitting directly on the roof of the sphenoid sinus.
pituitary fossa or sella turcica: Midline saddle-shaped depression in the sphenoid body on the lateral projection, sitting directly above the aerated sphenoid sinus with the squared dorsum sellae as its back wall; the anterior clinoids form its anterior lip.
plantar fascia: Thick soft tissue band arising from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and running forwards along the sole deep to the heel fat pad towards the metatarsal heads. Distinguish from the Achilles tendon, which attaches to the posterior surface of the same tuberosity.
planum sphenoidale: Flat shelf of the sphenoid body between the lesser wings, forming the roof of the sphenoid sinus and the posterior floor of the anterior cranial fossa; on the lateral view it runs horizontally forwards from the tuberculum sellae.
pons: Rounded anterior bulge of the brainstem on the midline sagittal view, lying against the clivus in front of the fourth ventricle, with midbrain above and medulla below; the echogenic vermis lies behind the fourth ventricle.
popliteal artery: Continuation of the superficial femoral artery beyond the adductor hiatus, running deep in the popliteal fossa immediately behind the distal femur and knee joint before dividing at the lower border of popliteus into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk.
popliteal groove of the right femur: Shallow depression on the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle, just below and behind the lateral epicondyle, which lodges the popliteus tendon; do not confuse it with the intercondylar fossa, which lies between the two condyles.
popliteus tendon: Arises from a small pit on the outer surface of the lateral femoral condyle just below and in front of the epicondyle, then runs intra-articularly deep to the lateral collateral ligament towards the posterior tibia; the collateral ligament attaches higher, on the epicondyle itself.
portal vein: Vessel with characteristically bright echogenic walls at the porta hepatis, formed behind the pancreatic neck and running anterior to the IVC with the common bile duct just in front of it. Hepatic veins differ in having thin, non-echogenic walls and draining into the IVC.
portal venous confluence: Junction behind the pancreatic neck where the transversely running splenic vein meets the vertically ascending superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein; the splenic vein alone can be traced leftwards along the pancreatic tail, whereas the confluence sits directly behind the neck.
posterior 6th rib/right blade of scapula: Posterior rib arcs are the sharply defined, roughly horizontal arcs counted downwards from the apex, whereas anterior ribs are fainter and slope steeply downwards and medially; the scapular blade overlaps them as a broad band with a sharp vertical medial border over the lateral upper chest.
posterior arch of c1 (atlas): Thin smoothly corticated curved line lying behind the dens at the skull base, well above the other spinous processes; C1 has no body, so if the arrow is on a lone posterior ring segment just below the occiput it is the atlas, not C2.
posterior arch of c2: Posterior bony ring of the axis formed by its pedicles, laminae and large spinous process, projected below the thinner posterior arch of C1; C1's arch is a slender uniform ring without a bulky spinous process.
posterior arch of the atlas: Thin curved bar completing the C1 ring behind the cord, seen on midline sagittal images as an isolated block of bone above the C2 lamina; unlike C2 it carries only a small posterior tubercle rather than a large bifid spinous process.
posterior border of the scapula: On a lateral or swimmer's projection the scapula is seen edge-on as a long, smooth, obliquely vertical cortical line projected over the upper thorax behind the humeral head; being a projected edge it runs on well beyond the vertebral outlines, unlike a fracture line.
posterior clinoid process: Paired bony knobs capping the upper corners of the dorsum sellae and forming the posterior lip of the pituitary fossa on a lateral skull film. The anterior clinoids are their counterpart at the front of the sella, projecting backwards from the lesser wings of the sphenoid.
posterior clinoid process of the sphenoi: Paired bony spurs at the upper corners of the dorsum sellae, forming the back wall of the pituitary fossa on the lateral skull. The anterior clinoid processes point backwards from the lesser wings in front of the sella, on the far side of the fossa.
posterior epidural space: Fat-containing compartment inside the canal but outside the dura, lying between the thecal sac and the ligamentum flavum and laminae; it is bright on T1 and most capacious at L3/4 and L4/5, unlike the T1-dark CSF in front of it.
posterior fontanelle: Triangular membranous gap at the lambda, where the sagittal suture meets the two limbs of the lambdoid suture, closing in the first few months of life. The anterior fontanelle is the larger diamond-shaped gap at bregma between coronal and sagittal sutures.
posterior inferior iliac spine: Small projection at the lower end of the posterior iliac border, immediately above the greater sciatic notch and just below the posterior superior iliac spine; the anterior inferior iliac spine instead projects forward above the acetabular roof.
posterior interosseous artery: Springs from the short common interosseous trunk of the ulnar artery below the elbow, then passes backwards over the upper free edge of the interosseous membrane to supply the extensor compartment; the anterior interosseous stays in front of the membrane.
posterior junction line: Vertical line projected over the tracheal air column where the posteromedial parts of both upper lobes appose behind the oesophagus. Unlike the anterior junction line it extends above the clavicles and runs down only as far as the aortic arch.
posterior longitudinal ligament: Thin low signal band running along the posterior surface of the vertebral bodies and discs within the front of the spinal canal, narrower than the anterior longitudinal ligament and often blending with cortex and annulus; the ligamentum flavum, in contrast, lies posteriorly, bridging adjacent laminae.
posterior ninth rib: Ninth arc counted downwards from the apex among the sharply defined, roughly horizontal posterior ribs; seeing nine or ten posterior ribs above the hemidiaphragm is the standard marker of adequate inspiration on a frontal chest radiograph.
posterior right third rib: Third of the well-defined, roughly horizontal posterior rib arcs counted downwards from the first rib at the apex; anterior rib ends are less sharply defined and slope obliquely downwards and medially, so counting must stay within one plane.
posterior subtalar joint (talocalcaneal: Obliquely orientated joint line between the undersurface of the talar body and the posterior facet of the calcaneus on the lateral radiograph, lying below the ankle joint and behind the funnel-shaped lucency of the sinus tarsi; the talonavicular joint lies further anteriorly.
posterior tibial (pt) artery: Most medial of the three below-knee run-off vessels, arising from the tibioperoneal trunk and coursing down the posteromedial leg deep to soleus to pass behind the medial malleolus; the peroneal artery is the parallel vessel lying against the fibula.
posterior tibial artery: Larger terminal branch of the tibioperoneal trunk, descending in the deep posterior compartment alongside the tibia and passing behind the medial malleolus into the sole. On an AP angiogram it is the most medial calf vessel; the peroneal runs laterally along the fibula.
posterior tibial artery (pta): Most medial of the three calf run-off vessels, arising from the tibioperoneal trunk and descending deep to soleus against the posterior tibia to become superficial behind the medial malleolus; the peroneal artery runs parallel but hugs the fibula.
posterior tibial neurovascular bundle: Cluster of the tibial nerve with the posterior tibial artery and its paired veins lying on the posterior surface of tibialis posterior in the plane between the deep and superficial posterior compartments, deep to soleus; the peroneal bundle sits further laterally against the fibula.
posterior tubercle of c1: Small knob at the midline posterior end of the atlas arch, the rudimentary spinous process, seen on the lateral just below the occiput and clearly smaller than the large bifid C2 spinous process below it.
posterior wall of the maxillary sinus: Thin cortical line forming the back of the antrum and separating it from the pterygopalatine and infratemporal fossae, best appreciated where the sinus outline curves backwards. The anterior wall is the more forward line lying beneath the infraorbital rim.
presacral fat: Fatty tissue filling the hollow in front of the sacrum and behind the rectum, high signal on T2 and T1; adjacent large vessels are distinguished by their dark flow void against this bright background.
presacral space: Fat-filled space on sagittal images between the anterior cortex of the sacrum and the back of the rectum, bright on T1; do not confuse it with epidural fat, which lies inside the spinal canal behind the thecal sac.
prevertebral soft tissues: Soft-tissue stripe between the anterior margins of the vertebral bodies and the pharyngeal/tracheal air column on the lateral view; it is thin in the upper cervical region and step-widens below the cricoid where the oesophagus begins, so focal widening above suggests injury.
profunda femoris: Large branch leaving the common femoral artery posterolaterally about 4 cm below the inguinal ligament, sweeping deep behind the SFA and giving perforating branches to the posterior thigh; on angiography the SFA is the straight, branchless vessel continuing down the thigh.
profunda femoris artery: Arises from the posterolateral aspect of the common femoral artery a few centimetres below the inguinal ligament and passes deep, giving the circumflex femoral and perforating branches; the superficial femoral artery is the straighter medial continuation running down the thigh.
profunda femoris artery (pfa): Arises from the posterolateral aspect of the common femoral artery a few centimetres below the inguinal ligament, then runs deep and posterior to the SFA giving the perforating branches; the SFA is the vessel running vertically down the thigh without significant branches.
properitoneal fat stripe/line: Thin vertical lucent line running down each flank on a supine abdominal radiograph, the fat plane separating peritoneum from the lateral abdominal wall muscles. Its loss or displacement suggests peritoneal or abdominal wall pathology; ascending/descending colon lies just medial to it.
proximal diaphysis of radius: Shaft of the radius just distal to the radial neck and tuberosity, on the thumb side of the forearm; identify the radius by its disc-shaped head abutting the capitulum. The ulna is the bone that is bulky proximally, bearing the olecranon and trochlear notch.
proximal diaphysis of the ulna: Shaft of the ulna immediately distal to the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity; on the lateral elbow trace it back to the olecranon posteriorly, whereas the radius runs anteriorly to meet the capitellum.
