The ulna is broad proximally and tapers distally, the reverse of the radius.
proximal epiphysis of the distal phalanx: Small ossification centre at the base of the great toe's terminal phalanx, separated from the shaft by a smooth transverse lucent physis; all phalangeal epiphyses in the foot are proximal, and the even corticated line excludes a fracture.
proximal epiphysis of the first metacarp: Ossific centre at the base of the thumb metacarpal near the trapezium, separated from the shaft by a lucent physis; the thumb metacarpal is unique in ossifying proximally while metacarpals two to five have distal epiphyses, so a basal epiphysis confirms the thumb.
proximal epiphysis of the proximal phala: Small ossific nucleus capping the base of the thumb's proximal phalanx and separated from the shaft by a lucent physis; all phalangeal epiphyses are proximal, so do not read this unfused centre as a separate bone or a sesamoid.
proximal humeral epiphyseal plate: Undulating transverse lucency crossing the proximal humerus at the head-metaphysis junction in a child, with smooth corticated margins and a mirror-image appearance on the other side; a fracture line by contrast is sharp, irregular and non-corticated.
proximal humeral growth plate: Wavy, undulating lucent line running obliquely across the proximal humeral metaphysis just below the head, often projecting as a step or V on AP; its smooth corticated margins and typical position distinguish it from a fracture.
proximal humerus: Identified by the rounded articular head facing medially into the glenoid, the greater tuberosity laterally and lesser tuberosity anteriorly with the bicipital groove between them; below the tuberosities the bone narrows into the surgical neck and shaft.
proximal interphalangeal joint (pipj) of: Joint between the proximal and middle phalanges of the second digit, the middle of the finger's three joints; count from the metacarpal head, which forms the more proximal knuckle joint (MCPJ), and remember the thumb has no PIPJ because it lacks a middle phalanx.
proximal phalanx of little toe: First and longest of the fifth toe's phalanges, articulating with the head of the fifth metatarsal; the segments beyond it are small and frequently fused, so do not mistake a stubby distal fragment for the proximal phalanx.
proximal phalanx of right second toe: First and longest of the three phalanges of the second toe, articulating proximally with the head of the second metatarsal at the metatarsophalangeal joint; distinguish it from the much shorter, squatter middle phalanx immediately distal to it.
proximal phalanx of the left index finge: First and longest phalanx of the second digit, lying between the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. The index is the ray immediately beside the thumb, which has only two phalanges.
proximal phalanx of the thumb: First of only two phalanges in the thumb, articulating proximally with the head of the first metacarpal at the metacarpophalangeal joint, where sesamoids lie volarly; the first metacarpal is longer and its base articulates with the trapezium.
proximal phalanx of thumb: The thumb has only two phalanges, and this is the proximal one, articulating with the head of the first metacarpal at the MCP joint where the paired sesamoids lie volarly. The metacarpal is separated by having its base at the trapezium.
proximal phalynx little (fifth) left toe: Most proximal and longest phalanx of the fifth toe, articulating with the head of the fifth metatarsal; the middle and distal phalanges of the little toe are small and often fused, so the substantial segment just beyond the metatarsophalangeal joint is the proximal phalanx.
proximal radial metaphysis: Flared segment of the proximal radius between the radial head physis and the tubular diaphysis, i.e. the radial neck region; the epiphysis is the separate ossific radial head beyond the lucent physis, and the tuberosity lies just distal on the ulnar side.
proximal radioulnar joint: Articulation between the circumference of the radial head and the radial notch of the ulna, held by the annular ligament encircling the head. Distinguish it from the humeroradial joint immediately above, which is between the radial head and the capitulum.
proximal tibial epiphysis: Expanded articular end of the tibia beyond the growth plate, carrying the tibial plateaus; the metaphysis is the flared segment on the shaft side of the physis, and the tibial tuberosity is a separate anterior apophysis.
proximal tibial metaphysis: Flared, trabecular segment of the tibia lying immediately proximal to the diaphysis and just below the growth plate; the epiphysis is the ossified portion on the joint side of the physis, the metaphysis on the shaft side.
proximal tibiofibular joint: The articulation between the fibular head and the posterolateral corner of the lateral tibial condyle, sitting below the knee joint line where the fibular head overlaps the lateral tibial metaphysis on the frontal view. Not the lateral tibiofemoral compartment, which lies above it.
psoas: Long paravertebral muscle lying anterolateral to the lumbar vertebral bodies, enlarging as it descends to join iliacus and pass under the inguinal ligament to the lesser trochanter. On axial images it lies in front of the transverse processes; quadratus lumborum lies behind it.
psoas major muscle: Paired muscle lying immediately anterolateral to the lumbar vertebral bodies, arising from the T12 to L5 transverse processes and bodies and enlarging caudally as it crosses the pelvic brim to join iliacus and insert on the lesser trochanter; quadratus lumborum lies behind it, flattened against the transverse processes.
psoas muscle: On the plain abdominal film, the straight lateral margin sloping inferolaterally from the upper lumbar vertebrae towards the lesser trochanter, visible only because of adjacent retroperitoneal fat; on cross-section it is the rounded muscle immediately anterolateral to the lumbar vertebral bodies.
psoas shadow/outline: Straight or gently convex oblique line running inferolaterally from the upper lumbar vertebrae to the pelvic brim, made visible by adjacent retroperitoneal fat. Loss of the outline may indicate retroperitoneal pathology, though it can be absent in thin patients or with poor technique.
pterion: H-shaped sutural meeting point on the lateral skull wall above the anterior zygomatic arch, where frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater sphenoid wing bones converge. It is the thinnest part of the vault and overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
pubic symphysis: The narrow midline lucency at the base of the pelvic ring between the bodies of the two pubic bones, whose superior margins should lie level with one another. Distinguish from the wider, obliquely oriented sacroiliac joints posteriorly.
pubis: One of the three bones meeting at the triradiate cartilage, contributing the anterior wall of the acetabulum and passing anteromedially as the superior ramus to the symphysis; the ischium forms the posteroinferior wall and the ilium the roof.
pulmonary artery: The right main pulmonary artery crosses anterior to the carina; on the lateral film it appears as a rounded opacity anterior to the trachea.
pulmonary trunk: Short convex segment of the left cardiomediastinal border lying between the concave aorto-pulmonary window above and the left atrial appendage below; the aortic knuckle is the separate, higher bulge on the far side of that window.
pulp cavity: Central lucent chamber within the tooth extending from the crown down into the root canal, sharply outlined by the denser surrounding dentine; unlike caries it is central and symmetric, and unlike the periodontal ligament space it lies inside the root rather than around it.
pulp cavity of second left lower molar t: Central lucent chamber inside the tooth, enclosed by dense dentine and enamel and tapering into the root canals; here in the seventh tooth back from the midline in the lower jaw. Unlike a periapical lucency it lies within the tooth, not in the bone beyond the root apex.
pulp chamber: Central lucent cavity within the crown of the tooth, tapering downwards into the root canals that transmit nerves and vessels. Its deep, central position distinguishes it from caries, which erodes the outer enamel surface.
pyloric canal: Narrow muscular channel joining gastric antrum to duodenal cap, seen as a hypoechoic muscle ring around echogenic mucosa: a doughnut in transverse section, a cervix-like channel longitudinally. Measure muscle thickness and canal length here; in pyloric stenosis it fails to open after a test feed.
pylorus: Gastric outlet lying to the right of the midline and anterior to the right kidney, seen as a short tubular structure with a hypoechoic muscular wall and echogenic central mucosa joining antrum to duodenal cap; fluid-filled duodenum lacks the thick muscle ring and changes with peristalsis.
quadratus lumborum: Rectangular posterior abdominal wall muscle immediately lateral to psoas major, spanning from the iliac crest to the 12th rib and lumbar transverse processes. On coronal CT look for the flat muscle slab hugging the posterior wall beside the more rounded psoas.
quadratus lumborum muscle: Quadrilateral posterior abdominal wall muscle lying lateral to the lumbar transverse processes and directly posterior to psoas major, spanning the twelfth rib to the iliac crest. Its position behind psoas but in front of the erector spinae mass identifies it on axial imaging.
quadriceps tendon: Thick soft-tissue band descending in front of the distal femur on the lateral radiograph to insert on the base (superior pole) of the patella, with the suprapatellar recess and fat deep to it; the patellar tendon is the corresponding band below the patella.
radial artery: Lateral terminal branch of the brachial artery arising at the level of the radial neck and running down the radial side of the forearm to lie superficially at the wrist; unlike the medial ulnar artery it gives no common interosseous branch just beyond its origin.
radial collateral ligament: Thin low-signal fan running from the lateral epicondyle down to blend with the annular ligament around the radial head, deep to the common extensor tendon; the overlying extensor tendon is thicker and continues into muscle rather than encircling the radial head.
radial head: Disc-shaped, slightly concave proximal end of the radius articulating with the capitulum; a line along the radial shaft and neck should always intersect the capitulum. The coronoid process of the ulna lies medial to it and projects anteriorly.
radial nerve: At the elbow it lies anterior to the lateral epicondyle in the groove between brachialis and brachioradialis, dividing into a superficial sensory branch and the posterior interosseous nerve which enters supinator; the median nerve is medial, beside the brachial artery.
radial nerve, deep brachial artery(s), d: Neurovascular bundle lying in the spiral groove against the posterior humeral shaft, between the medial and lateral heads of triceps; the brachial artery, veins and median nerve run anteromedially, medial to biceps and brachialis.
radial neurovascular bundle (radial arte: Small vessels and nerve on the radial side of the anterior forearm, deep to brachioradialis and lateral to flexor carpi radialis; the ulnar bundle lies deep to flexor carpi ulnaris medially, and the median nerve runs centrally between superficialis and profundus.
radial styloid: Distal lateral (thumb-side) projection of the radius extending beyond the radiocarpal joint line and articulating with the scaphoid; the ulnar styloid is the corresponding smaller ulnar-sided process arising from the ulnar head.
radial styloid epiphysis: Pointed lateral projection of the distal radial epiphysis on the thumb side of the wrist, lying distal to the transverse lucent physis and extending further distally than the ulnar styloid. The scaphoid is separate, rounded and lies beyond the radiocarpal joint.
radial styloid process: Distal lateral, thumb-side projection of the radius which articulates with the scaphoid and extends further distally than the ulnar styloid. The ulnar styloid is on the little-finger side, shorter and more pointed.
radial tuberosity: Oval cortical bulge on the anteromedial aspect of the proximal radius just distal to the neck, giving attachment to the biceps brachii tendon; projected obliquely it can mimic a lucent lesion, and the bicipital aponeurosis attaches more medially to forearm fascia.
radial tuberosity (left): Oval prominence on the medial (ulnar) aspect of the proximal radius just below the neck, giving attachment to the biceps tendon; when rotated away from the beam its thin cortex mimics a lucent lesion, and it lies distal to the radial head and neck.
radius: Lateral, thumb-side forearm bone, narrow proximally at the disc-shaped head and broad distally where it articulates with the scaphoid and lunate; the ulna is medial, bulky proximally at the olecranon and tapers to the styloid, appearing shorter than the radius at the wrist.
ramus of mandible: Vertical quadrilateral plate of mandible rising from the angle to the condylar and coronoid processes, projected lateral to the maxillary sinus on facial views; the body is the horizontal tooth-bearing part running forwards from the angle.
ramus of right mandible: Vertical limb of the mandible running from the angle upwards to the condyle and coronoid process; the tooth-bearing horizontal portion in front of the angle is the body, not the ramus.
rectum: Gas and faeces containing bowel lying in the midline directly in front of the sacrum, following the sacral curve in the presacral space. Its fixed midline presacral position separates it from the more mobile, higher and more variable sigmoid loops.
rectum (gas filled): Midline gas-filled tubular lucency in the presacral space lying immediately anterior to the lower sacrum and coccyx and continuous with the sigmoid above; unlike sigmoid or small bowel gas it is fixed, midline and does not move out of the sacral hollow.
rectus abdominis muscle: Paired vertical strap muscles either side of the midline linea alba lying just deep to subcutaneous fat, so on epigastric ultrasound this is the muscle layer immediately under the probe, anterior to the left lobe of liver; the three flat oblique muscles lie further laterally.
rectus abdominus: Paired superficial hypoechoic muscle band lying immediately deep to subcutaneous fat on either side of the midline linea alba, wrapped in an echogenic fascial sheath. It is the near-field structure the beam crosses before reaching any intra-abdominal viscus.
rectus abdominus muscle: Superficial paired hypoechoic muscle belly with an echogenic fascial sheath, lying just under the subcutaneous fat either side of the midline linea alba, immediately beneath the transducer and anterior to all intraperitoneal structures.
rectus femoris: Anterior midline muscle of the thigh on axial section, lying superficial to vastus intermedius, and arising by a direct head from the anterior inferior iliac spine. Sartorius, from the anterior superior iliac spine, is the much smaller strap muscle crossing obliquely superficial and medial to it.
rectus femoris - straight head: Arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine, the bony prominence on the ilium immediately above the acetabular roof; do not confuse with the anterior superior iliac spine higher up at the anterior end of the iliac crest, which gives origin to sartorius and tensor fascia lata.
rectus femoris muscle: Most anterior quadriceps muscle, lying in the anterior midline of the thigh directly superficial to vastus intermedius on axial sections; sartorius, its usual mimic, is the much smaller superficial strap lying anteromedially and moving medially as it descends.
renal artery: Arises from the aorta just below the superior mesenteric artery and runs to the right renal hilum passing POSTERIOR to the inferior vena cava; that retrocaval course is the giveaway. The right renal vein lies anterior to the artery and drains directly into the IVC.
renal cortex: Outer band of renal parenchyma between the capsule and the pyramids, extending inwards between them as columns of Bertin; iso- or slightly hypoechoic to liver and spleen. The medullary pyramids are distinctly more hypoechoic and triangular, ringed around the bright central sinus fat.
renal vein: Crosses the midline in the angle between the aorta behind and the superior mesenteric artery in front to reach the IVC, just beneath the pancreatic body; the splenic vein by contrast lies anterior to the SMA along the back of the pancreas.
reparative 'filling' in left lower molar: Uniformly metal-dense, sharply marginated opacity confined to the crown of a molar and brighter than surrounding enamel; its non-anatomical geometric outline and lack of a pulp cavity within it identify it as a restoration rather than bone or tooth.
right ventricle: The most anterior cardiac chamber, crescent-shaped with a thinner wall than the left ventricle, which bulges into it.
s1 nerve: Traversing root descending in the lateral recess behind the L5/S1 disc and in front of the S1 superior articular process; a posterolateral disc herniation at this level compresses this root, not the already-exited L5.
sacral ala: Flat wing-like expansion of the upper sacrum lateral to the S1 body, forming the sacral side of the sacroiliac joint and the posterior part of the pelvic brim; the L5 transverse process lies above it and is separated by a clear lucent gap.
sacral ala (or wing): Flat triangular lateral mass of the upper sacrum, lying between the S1 body medially and the sacroiliac joint laterally; its superior surface slopes down from the promontory and forms part of the posterior pelvic brim.
sacral alum: Broad wing of bone lateral to the S1 body, forming the upper lateral corner of the sacrum and the medial side of the sacroiliac joint. The iliac bone lies on the far, lateral side of that joint line.
sacral foramen of s3 vertebra: One of the paired arcuate lucencies within the sacral body, counted as the third pair downwards from S1; the anterior sacral foramina line up in curved rows and transmit the sacral nerve rami, unlike the obliquely oriented sacroiliac joint laterally.
sacral promontory: Anteriorly projecting upper edge of the S1 vertebral body at the lumbosacral junction, forming the posterior landmark of the pelvic inlet; on the lateral view it is the anterosuperior corner of the sacrum immediately below the L5/S1 disc, not the L5 body above it.
sacro-iliac joint: Obliquely oriented joint between the sacral ala medially and the ilium laterally; on frontal projections it appears as two roughly parallel lucent lines because the anterior and posterior joint margins are projected separately.
sacroiliac joint: Obliquely oriented lucent cleft between the auricular surface of the sacrum and the ilium in the posterior pelvis; its obliquity projects the anterior and posterior margins as two roughly parallel lines on a frontal film, which should not be read as erosion.
sacrum: Broad triangular fused bone below the L5-S1 disc, curving posteriorly and articulating with both iliac bones, with the coccyx continuing from its tip. Unlike the lumbar vertebrae above, its segments have no disc spaces, only transverse fusion lines.
sagittal suture: Single serrated midline lucency running front to back between the two parietal bones, from bregma anteriorly to lambda posteriorly where it meets the lambdoid sutures. Its strictly midline course separates it from the paired coronal and lambdoid sutures, which run obliquely.
sartorius: Thin flat strap muscle spiralling from the ASIS to the medial knee, so on serial axial images it shifts from anterolateral proximally to anteromedial distally, forming the roof of the adductor canal; gracilis is the similarly thin muscle lying medial throughout.
sartorius and tensor fascia latae: Oblique soft-tissue lines descending from around the anterior superior iliac spine across the hip on the frontal pelvis, sartorius running inferomedially and tensor fasciae latae inferolaterally; being soft tissue they extend beyond the edges of the bone they overlie.
sartorius muscle: Long thin strap muscle running from the anterior superior iliac spine obliquely across the thigh to the pes anserinus, forming the lateral border of the femoral triangle. On axial images it is the small superficial muscle lying anterolaterally proximally and becoming progressively more medial distally.
scapho-lunate (sl) ligament. this short: Short low-signal band bridging the proximal poles of scaphoid and lunate on coronal images, at the radial end of the proximal carpal row; the lunotriquetral ligament is its counterpart on the ulnar side of the lunate.
scapho-lunate joint space: Narrow lucency between scaphoid and lunate in the proximal carpal row on the PA view; it should be parallel and no wider than the other intercarpal spaces. Widening indicates scapholunate ligament disruption.
scaphoid: Boat-shaped bone at the radial end of the proximal carpal row, obliquely orientated with a narrow waist and distal tubercle, forming the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. It lies radial to the lunate and its distal pole abuts the trapezium and trapezoid.
scaphoid bone: Boat-shaped bone at the radial end of the proximal carpal row, the largest of that row, articulating with the radius proximally and having a proximal pole, waist and distal pole. The lunate lies immediately medial to it and is crescentic rather than elongated.
scaphoid tubercle: Palmar prominence at the distal pole of the scaphoid, lying just distal to the radial styloid and proximal to the trapezium at the base of the thenar eminence; on PA it projects as a dense corticated ring or oval over the distal scaphoid, not a separate ossicle.
scapholunate ligament: Short low-signal band bridging the proximal margins of scaphoid and lunate on the coronal image, roofing the scapholunate interval; its mirror image on the ulnar side of the lunate is the lunotriquetral ligament.
scapula blade: Thin flat triangular body of the scapula seen as a faint plate of bone between its medial and lateral borders; the scapular spine, its usual mimic, is a denser bar lying more posteriorly and running continuously into the acromion.
scapula blade or body: Thin triangular plate of bone projected over the posterolateral upper ribs, relatively lucent because it is so thin, bounded by the thick lateral border running down to the inferior angle and by the spine passing laterally to the acromion.
scapular spine: Dense oblique bar of bone crossing the upper scapular body from the medial border upwards and laterally to become the acromion; it is denser and more posterior than the thin flat scapular blade, and its continuity with the acromion is the giveaway.
sciatic nerve: Flat ovoid band with fascicular internal texture emerging below piriformis and lying on the posterior surface of obturator internus and quadratus femoris deep to gluteus maximus, roughly midway between ischial tuberosity and greater trochanter; adjacent vessels lack fascicles and show flow voids.
second metacarpal: Index-ray metacarpal, second from the radial side and the longest, its base keyed into a notch to articulate with the trapezoid; the thumb metacarpal is shorter and more abducted, with its epiphysis at the base rather than the head.
second rib: Second in the sequence counted down from the short sharply curved first rib that arches from T1 over the lung apex; it forms a longer, flatter arc whose anterior cartilage meets the sternum at the manubriosternal angle.
secondary ossification centre of right f: Unlike the lesser metatarsals, which ossify at their heads, the first metatarsal has its secondary centre at the base; after fusion a residual corticated lucent cleft at the proximal end is a normal finding frequently misread as a fracture.
secondary ossification centre of the cap: First elbow centre to appear (the C of CRITOE, around one year), a small rounded ossicle at the lateral aspect of the distal humerus lined up with the radial head; the trochlear centre appears years later, lies medially and is often fragmented.
secondary ossification centre of the med: Ossicle on the medial side of the distal humerus, proximal to and outside the joint line, appearing third in CRITOE; if a trochlear centre is visible without a medial epicondylar centre in position, the epicondyle has been avulsed and may lie within the joint.
segment 4 of the liver: Left medial segment lying between the fissure for the ligamentum teres/falciform ligament laterally and the middle hepatic vein and gallbladder fossa on its right, subdivided into 4a above and 4b below the portal venous plane. Segments 2 and 3 lie lateral to the fissure.
segment 8 of the liver: Right anterior superior segment, lying above the plane of the right portal vein and between the middle hepatic vein medially and the right hepatic vein laterally, just under the dome. Segment 5 is the same column below the portal venous plane.
sella turcica: The saddle-shaped depression of the sphenoid housing the pituitary, bounded by the anterior and posterior clinoid processes.
sella turcica (pituitary fossa): Saddle-shaped midline depression in the body of the sphenoid on the lateral skull film, sitting directly on the roof of the sphenoid sinus, bounded in front by the anterior clinoid processes and behind by the squared dorsum sellae.
sella turcica or pituitary fossa: Saddle-shaped hollow in the body of the sphenoid on the lateral skull film, bounded in front by the tuberculum sellae with the anterior clinoids and behind by the dorsum sellae with the posterior clinoids; it houses the pituitary gland.
semimembranosus muscle: Posteromedial hamstring lying deep and anterior to semitendinosus, with a broad flat proximal tendon from the ischial tuberosity and insertion on the posteromedial tibial condyle; semitendinosus is the more superficial muscle whose tendon becomes rounded and cord-like distally.
semitendinosus muscle: Posteromedial hamstring lying superficial (posterior) to semimembranosus on axial thigh images. In the distal thigh it is recognised by its long thin tendon while semimembranosus still has bulky muscle belly; biceps femoris occupies the posterolateral position.
sesamoid bone: Small rounded ossicle with a complete smooth cortex lying within a tendon adjacent to a joint, typically at the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint or beneath the first metatarsal head. The intact corticated margin all round separates it from an acute avulsed fragment.
sesamoid bone (in flexor hallucis brevis: One of the two small oval ossicles lying beneath the head of the first metatarsal, embedded in the medial and lateral heads of flexor hallucis brevis, projected over the metatarsal head on a dorsoplantar view. No other metatarsal head has a constant paired sesamoid.
sesamoid bone at left thumb metacarpopha: Small round or ovoid ossicle with a complete smooth cortical rim projected over the palmar aspect of the first metacarpal head, usually one of a pair; the intact corticated margin all the way round separates it from an avulsion fragment.
sesamoid bone in flexor hallucis brevis: Small rounded, well-corticated ossicle projecting over the plantar aspect of the first metatarsal head, embedded in a head of flexor hallucis brevis; smooth rounded margins separate a normal or bipartite sesamoid from a fracture, which has sharp irregular edges.
sesamoid bone on the thumb: Small smoothly corticated ossicle projected over the palmar aspect of the first metacarpophalangeal joint within the thenar tendons. Its complete rounded cortex separates it from an avulsion fragment, which has a sharp uncorticated edge.
sesamoid bones in left flexor hallucis b: Paired round ossicles lying directly plantar to the head of the first metatarsal, embedded in the two tendons of flexor hallucis brevis; their constant position under that head separates them from accessory ossicles such as the os peroneum lateral to the cuboid.
sesamoid bones in right flexor hallucis: Paired small oval corticated ossicles projected over or just beneath the head of the first metatarsal, embedded in the two tendons of flexor hallucis brevis; their fixed position under the first metatarsal head separates them from accessory ossicles elsewhere in the foot.
shaft of humerus: Tubular diaphysis with thick parallel cortices and a medullary canal, extending distally from the surgical neck just below the tubercles. The scapular blade projected across it is a thin flat plate with faint margins and no medullary cavity.
shaft of ulna: Long straight bone on the medial, little-finger side of the forearm, broad proximally at the olecranon and tapering towards the wrist. The radius is the mirror image, narrow proximally and flaring distally to form the wrist joint.
shenton's line: Smooth continuous arc traced along the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus and continued along the inferomedial margin of the femoral neck; a step or break in this curve indicates a displaced femoral neck fracture or dislocated or dysplastic hip.
short saphenous vein: The only sizeable vessel running subcutaneously in the posterior midline of the calf, superficial to the gastrocnemius fascia, ascending from behind the lateral malleolus to join the popliteal vein; deep calf veins instead run in pairs beside arteries within the muscle compartments.
situs inversus: Mirror-image arrangement with the cardiac apex and aortic knuckle on the right and the gastric air bubble under the right hemidiaphragm; check the side marker to be sure the film has not simply been displayed reversed.
soft palate: Soft-tissue band sloping posteroinferiorly from the back of the hard palate towards the oropharynx and ending in the uvula, outlined by nasopharyngeal air above and oral air below on a lateral view; adenoidal tissue, by contrast, lies on the posterosuperior nasopharyngeal wall.
soleus: Broad flat muscle of the superficial posterior calf lying deep to gastrocnemius, arising from both the soleal line of the tibia and the posterior fibular head, and blending with gastrocnemius into the Achilles tendon; unlike gastrocnemius it does not cross the knee joint.
soleus muscle: Broad flat superficial posterior compartment muscle lying deep to gastrocnemius, arising from the posterior tibia and fibula and extending much further distally, so below the level where the gastrocnemius bellies end it is the only large muscle in front of the Achilles tendon.
sphenoid sinus: Aerated lucency within the body of the sphenoid, lying directly beneath the pituitary fossa and behind the posterior ethmoid air cells, above the roof of the nasopharynx; the posterior ethmoids that mimic it lie anterior and slightly higher.
spinal column: Curved bright midline interface deep to the aorta and inferior vena cava with dense posterior acoustic shadowing that obliterates all detail beyond it, marking the anterior vertebral body surface and the posterior limit of the ultrasound image.
spinal cord: On neonatal longitudinal ultrasound a hypoechoic tubular band within the canal containing a bright central echo complex, tapering distally to the conus medullaris. Below that level only the fine parallel strands of the cauda equina are seen, which is how the two are separated.
spinal cord in the spinal canal: Ribbon of intermediate signal running within the CSF filled thecal sac from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris at L1/L2, widest at the cervical enlargement. Surrounding CSF separates it out by being bright on T2 and dark on T1.
spinal nerve root (exiting nerve root): Root that has left the sac and passes anterolaterally beneath the pedicle of its own numbered vertebra, a dark oval in the upper foramen surrounded by fat; the traversing root of the level below remains medially in the lateral recess.
spinal nerve root (left): Low-signal nerve surrounded by bright foraminal fat, running anterolaterally and downwards after leaving the thecal sac; formed by the union of dorsal and ventral roots, with the ganglion normally lying within the exit foramen.
spine of left scapula: Dense oblique line crossing the upper left hemithorax, running superolaterally from the medial scapular border towards the acromion. Trace it beyond the lung margin into the shoulder soft tissues to separate it from a pleural line.
spine of scapula: Transverse bony ridge crossing the posterior surface of the scapula and widening laterally into the acromion; on MRI it is the landmark separating supraspinatus in its fossa above from infraspinatus below.
spine of the left scapula: Dense oblique ridge crossing the upper scapula from its medial border upwards and laterally towards the acromion, projected as a sharp line over the upper zone; unlike a pleural line or apical companion shadow it can be traced beyond the lung edge into the soft tissues.
spine of the right scapula: Dense linear ridge running obliquely and laterally across the scapular body, continuing into the acromion which forms the posterior fork of the Y. The anterior fork, closer to the ribs, is the coracoid process.
spine of the scapula: Dense oblique ridge crossing the upper posterior scapular body and widening laterally into the acromion. On a frontal film it appears as a linear band across the blade; the superior border is a thin smooth edge without this ridge density.
spinous process: Superficial midline echogenic structure of the posterior arch, lying between the skin surface and the thecal sac; the incompletely ossified arches of infancy are what allow the cord to be imaged at all. Echogenic lines deeper than it are meninges, not bone.
spinous process l5 vertebra: Seen end-on in the midline of a frontal pelvic radiograph as an oval or teardrop density within the body of the lowest lumbar vertebra, immediately above the sacrum. The transverse processes are the separate wings projecting laterally on either side.
spinous process of atlas: Small posterior tubercle at the back of the C1 posterior arch on the lateral view, rudimentary in size; the large bifid spinous process immediately below it belongs to C2 and is far bulkier.
spinous process of c2: Large bifid spinous process lying behind and just below the odontoid peg, the first prominent posterior bony process below the skull base on the lateral cervical film. C7 also has a long spinous process but is the lowest one, at the cervicothoracic junction, and is not bifid.
spinous process of c4: Short, frequently bifid posterior spur arising from the C4 laminae behind the spinolaminar line; count down from C2, whose spinous process is the first large one. It is far shorter than the long C7 spinous process.
spinous process of c7: Longest and non-bifid cervical spinous process, the palpable vertebra prominens at the base of the neck; confirm the level because C7 transverse processes point downwards whereas thoracic transverse processes point upwards and T1 carries the first rib.
spinous process of c7 (vertebra prominen: Longest, most posteriorly projecting and usually non-bifid cervical spinous process at the cervicothoracic junction; identify it by counting along the spinolaminar line down to the vertebra just above the first rib-bearing body, T1.
spinous process of l1 vertebra: Midline teardrop shaped density projected posteriorly from the L1 laminae, distinct from the paired oval pedicles either side of it. Because lumbar spinous processes angle caudally, the L1 process is usually projected over the L1/2 disc or the top of L2.
spinous process of l2: Most posterior midline bony projection on the sagittal image, running back and slightly down from the fused laminae and containing fatty marrow; the lamina is the flatter bar just anterior to it forming the canal's back wall.
spinous process of l3: Broad posteriorly directed midline process, seen end-on as a vertical teardrop density in the middle of the vertebral body on the frontal view and as a stout, near-horizontal bar on the lateral; lumbar processes lie at the level of their own body, unlike caudally angled thoracic ones. Count up from L5 to confirm the level.
spinous process of l3 vertebra: Broad, roughly horizontal quadrangular plate projecting posteriorly in the midline from the L3 laminae, seen as the midline teardrop density on frontal films. Lumbar spinous processes are much more horizontal than the steeply downsloping thoracic ones.
spinous process of l4: Broad, almost horizontal quadrangular plate projecting backwards in the midline from the junction of the laminae; on the frontal view it is the midline teardrop density. Count upwards from the sacrum, since L5 is the lowest free lumbar vertebra.
spinous process of l5: Midline vertically oriented oval or teardrop density projected over the centre of the vertebral body on the AP radiograph, between the pedicles. Identify L5 by counting up from the sacrum: it is the last mobile segment, with a short blunt spinous process.
spinous process of t1: Midline posterior bony process of the first thoracic vertebra, identified by tracing the first rib back to its vertebra rather than by counting downwards. It is easily confused with the C7 spinous process, which is the last one without a rib-bearing vertebra.
spinous process of t12 vertebra: Posterior midline process of the last rib-bearing vertebra, found by tracing the twelfth rib back to its body; at this level the spinous processes are shorter and more horizontal than the steeply overlapping mid-thoracic ones.
spinous process of t2: Midline posterior bony process seen end-on as an oval or teardrop density between the pedicles on a frontal film, counted down from T1 using the first rib; because thoracic spinous processes angle caudally, its tip projects over the vertebral level below its own body.
spinous process t1 vertebra: Single midline vertical density projected over the vertebral body between the paired pedicle rings; pedicles are paired and lateral, the spinous process central. T1 is the first vertebra bearing a rib, below the downward-pointing transverse processes of C7.
splenic artery: Largest branch of the coeliac axis, running leftwards along the superior border of the pancreas in a tortuous course, so only short segments appear on any one image. The common hepatic artery is the branch running to the right towards the porta hepatis.
splenic vein: Long transverse vessel running along the posterior surface of the pancreatic body and tail, a reliable landmark for finding the pancreas, joining the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein; the splenic artery, in contrast, is tortuous and runs along the superior pancreatic border.
splenic vein and superior mesenteric vei: The two tributaries uniting behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein: the splenic vein runs transversely from the left along the posterior border of the pancreas, while the superior mesenteric vein ascends vertically, to the right of its artery and in front of the uncinate process.
sternoclavicular joint: Articulation between the expanded medial end of the clavicle and the upper lateral corner of the manubrium, one either side of the midline at the top of the mediastinum; symmetry of the two relative to the spinous processes indicates a rotation-free film.
sternocleidomastoid muscle: Superficial hypoechoic muscle lying anterolateral to the thyroid lobe, directly over the internal jugular vein and common carotid artery. It is thicker and more lateral than the strap muscles, which lie flat in front of the gland.
sternomastoid: Bulky superficial hypoechoic muscle lying anterolateral to the thyroid lobe, capping the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein. The strap muscles are much thinner ribbons sitting directly in front of the gland, closer to the midline.
stomach: Gas- and fluid-containing viscus in the left upper quadrant directly beneath the left hemidiaphragm, often showing rugal folds and a rounded fundal air bubble; distinguish from splenic flexure gas, which is more lateral, tubular and haustrated.
stomach bubble: Rounded lucency directly under the left hemidiaphragm, continuous with the gastric shadow and usually with an air-fluid level on an erect film; gas in the splenic flexure lies lower, is more angular and shows haustral markings.
stomach bubble/gas within the gastric fu: Lucent gas collection lying immediately beneath the left hemidiaphragm, showing an air-fluid level on an erect film; colonic gas at the splenic flexure sits lower and shows haustral folds, while free intraperitoneal gas would outline both sides of the bowel wall.
strap muscle: Thin hypoechoic ribbon of muscle immediately anterior to the thyroid lobe and isthmus, sandwiched between gland and subcutaneous fat. Thinner and more medial than sternomastoid, which is bulkier and lies anterolaterally over the carotid and jugular vein.
styloid process: Thin pointed spike of bone projecting downward and forward from the undersurface of the petrous temporal bone just anterior to the mastoid, passing medial to the mandibular ramus. It anchors the stylohyoid ligament, whose ossification makes it appear abnormally elongated toward the hyoid.
styloid process 5th metatarsal: Blunt proximolateral projection at the base of the fifth metatarsal, pointing backwards beyond the cuboid articulation and giving attachment to peroneus brevis; an avulsion fracture line here runs transversely, whereas the childhood apophysis lies parallel to the shaft.
styloid process of right ulna: Short conical spike projecting distally from the posteromedial aspect of the ulnar head, on the little-finger side of the wrist; the radial styloid lies on the thumb side and extends noticeably further distally.
styloid process of the fibula: Small pointed upward spike on the top of the fibular head, just lateral to the proximal tibiofibular joint near the biceps femoris and arcuate ligament attachments; a fabella is instead a separate rounded ossicle behind the lateral femoral condyle.
styloid process of the fibular head: The small pointed projection rising from the posterosuperior aspect of the fibular head above its tibial articulation, at the posterolateral corner of the knee. Avulsion of this tip is the arcuate sign; the biceps femoris tendon and fibular collateral ligament attach to the adjacent fibular head.
styloid process of ulna: Short pointed projection from the posteromedial aspect of the ulnar head, on the little-finger side of the wrist, anchoring the triangular fibrocartilage complex and ulnar collateral ligament. The radial styloid lies on the thumb side and projects considerably further distally.
stylomastoid foramen: Small round opening on the inferior skull base lying between the base of the styloid process and the mastoid process, transmitting the facial nerve; the jugular foramen is much larger and lies anteromedial to it.
subarachnoid space: CSF-containing layer between arachnoid and pia that follows the brain surface down into the sulci and, in the spine, surrounds the cord and cauda equina to about S2; a subdural collection by contrast does not extend into the sulci.
subclavian artery: On the right, arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the sternoclavicular joint and arches over the lung apex and first rib, giving branches to chest wall and shoulder; it becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the first rib, which is the landmark separating the two.
subclavian vein: Continuation of the axillary vein from the outer border of the first rib, lying anterior and slightly inferior to the subclavian artery with scalenus anterior between them; it meets the internal jugular behind the sternoclavicular joint.
subscapularis: Muscle filling the anterior costal surface of the scapula between the blade and the chest wall, its tendon passing in front of the humeral head to the lesser tuberosity. Infraspinatus, by contrast, lies on the posterior scapular surface and inserts on the greater tuberosity.
subscapularis (muscle/tendon): The only cuff muscle on the front of the scapula, filling the subscapular fossa and passing anterior to the humeral head to insert on the lesser tuberosity; serratus anterior lies further forward, plastered against the ribs.
subscapularis muscle: Fills the subscapular fossa on the costal surface of the scapula, sandwiched between scapula and chest wall, its tendon crossing in front of the humeral head to reach the lesser tuberosity. Infraspinatus is its mirror image on the posterior scapular surface.
subscapularis tendon: Anterior cuff tendon with a striated, multi-fascicular look, running from the costal surface of the scapula across the front of the humeral head to the lesser tuberosity; the long head of biceps tendon lies just lateral to it in the groove.
subtalar joint: The talocalcaneal articulation immediately below the tibiotalar joint on a lateral view, separating the undersurface of the talar body from the superior calcaneal facets, and allowing inversion/eversion. Do not confuse with the talonavicular joint, which lies further anteriorly beyond the talar neck.
superficial and deep palmar arches: Two transverse arterial arcades across the palm on a hand angiogram: the superficial arch is the more distal one, chiefly from the ulnar artery and giving off the common palmar digital arteries, while the deep arch lies more proximally at the metacarpal bases and derives mainly from the radial artery.
superficial circumflex iliac artery: Small branch from the lateral aspect of the proximal common femoral artery just below the inguinal ligament, running superolaterally in the superficial fascia towards the ASIS; the superficial epigastric branch instead heads medially and upwards towards the umbilicus.
superficial femoral artery: Continuation of the common femoral artery beyond the origin of profunda femoris, descending medially through the adductor canal to become the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus. On angiography it is the long smooth vessel with few branches; the profunda lies lateral and branches repeatedly.
superficial femoral artery (sfa): Direct continuation of the common femoral artery, running vertically down the medial thigh in the adductor canal with no significant branches, becoming the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus; the profunda is the branching vessel that dives posterolaterally.
superior angle of right scapula: Uppermost medial corner of the scapula where the vertebral and superior borders meet, projected over the upper thorax and traceable into the rest of the scapular outline; a cervical rib differs in arising from the C7 transverse process, which points caudally unlike that of T1.
superior articular facet of c2: Flat lateral shoulder of the axis forming the lower half of the lateral atlantoaxial joint on the open-mouth view; the C1 lateral mass lies above the joint line and should align flush with the C2 facet's outer edge.
superior articular facet of l5: Process ascending from the L5 arch to form the anterolateral half of the L4/5 facet joint, its articular surface facing posteromedially; the L4 inferior process is the piece lying behind and medial to it.
superior articular process of c7 vertebr: Process ascending from the C7 articular pillar, its facet directed posterosuperiorly to receive the inferior articular process of C6; it lies anterior to that process at the joint. Confirm the level by the long non-bifid C7 spinous process.
superior articular process of l4: Upward-pointing process at the pedicle-lamina junction that articulates with L3 above; on the oblique lumbar radiograph it is the ear of the Scotty dog, with the pedicle as the eye and the pars interarticularis as the neck.
superior articular process of l4 vertebr: Projects upwards from the pedicle-lamina junction carrying a concave facet that faces backwards and medially to grip the inferior articular process of L3; on the oblique radiograph it forms the Scotty dog's ear.
superior articular process of l5: Process projecting upward from the junction of the L5 pedicle and lamina to meet the inferior articular process of L4; the pars interarticularis, the site of spondylolysis, is the bone immediately below it. On oblique views it forms the ear of the Scotty dog.
superior articular process of the verteb: Process ascending from the arch of the vertebra below to form the anterolateral half of the facet joint; it also makes the back wall of the lateral recess, where the traversing root can be trapped.
superior cornu of thyroid cartilage: Slender horn projecting upwards from the posterior border of the thyroid lamina towards the hyoid, to which it is joined by the thyrohyoid ligament; the greater cornu of the hyoid lies higher and points backwards from the hyoid body.
superior endplate of l2: Dense cortical line forming the top surface of the L2 body and the lower margin of the L1-L2 disc space. The parallel line immediately above it, on the far side of the disc, is the inferior endplate of L1.
superior glenoid labrum: Triangular dark fibrocartilage capping the upper glenoid rim on coronal oblique images, continuous with the long head of biceps anchor; the inferior labrum sits at the opposite pole and articular cartilage over the glenoid face is brighter and thinner.
superior glenoid tubercle: Small bony prominence at the upper margin of the glenoid, the anchor of the long head of biceps tendon and continuous with the superior labrum; the coracoid process is a much larger hook projecting anteriorly, giving origin to the short head.
superior labrum: Dark triangular fibrocartilage at the top of the glenoid where the long head of biceps anchors, the site of SLAP tears; the biceps tendon itself continues laterally over the humeral head, and a sublabral recess may undercut the labrum here.
superior mesenteric artery: Anterior aortic branch arising about a centimetre below the coeliac axis and running caudally parallel to the aorta, surrounded by echogenic or high-signal fat; on axial images it is the round vessel behind the pancreatic neck with the left renal vein and third part of duodenum passing between it and the aorta. The coeliac axis, above it, is short and divides immediately.
superior orbital fissure: Elongated triangular lucency at the orbital apex between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid, transmitting cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and VI with the superior ophthalmic vein. On a frontal skull view the foramen rotundum is the small round lucency just below its medial end.
superior pubic ramus: Bar of bone running from the pubic body superolaterally to the acetabulum, forming the upper margin of the obturator foramen and part of the pelvic brim; the inferior ramus passes down and back from the body to the ischium, closing the foramen below.
superior sagittal sinus: Triangular, largely echo-poor channel at the very apex of the midline on the coronal view, lying immediately deep to the vault where the falx attaches; colour Doppler confirms venous flow. The falx itself continues inferiorly from it as a thin echogenic line.
superior ulnar collateral artery: Slender branch from the medial side of the brachial artery around mid-arm, descending with the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle to join the anastomosis about the elbow; the profunda brachii arises higher and swings laterally and posteriorly around the humerus.
superior vena cava: Forms the straight or gently convex upper right mediastinal border above the right atrium, running vertically just lateral to the trachea and right paratracheal stripe; the right atrium takes over as border-former lower down at a distinct change in contour.
supinator: Muscle that wraps as a collar around the proximal radius, in direct contact with the bone just distal to the radial tuberosity; brachioradialis and the extensor mass lie more superficially and never hug the radial shaft circumferentially.
supinator muscle: Muscle that wraps around the proximal radius, in direct contact with the bone and reaching anteriorly around it; brachioradialis is the most lateral superficial muscle anteriorly and lies away from the radial shaft.
suprascapular notch (containing suprasca: Indentation on the superior border of the scapula just medial to the base of the coracoid, bridged by the transverse scapular ligament with the nerve under it and vessels over it; the spinoglenoid notch lies further laterally between spine and glenoid.
suprascapular vein: Small vein accompanying the suprascapular artery along the superior border of the scapula at the suprascapular notch; artery and vein pass above the transverse scapular ligament whereas the suprascapular nerve passes beneath it.
supraspinatous muscle/tendon/subacromial: Soft-tissue gap between the top of the humeral head and the undersurface of the acromion, through which supraspinatus passes to the greater tuberosity; narrowing with a high-riding humeral head suggests cuff tear. The glenohumeral joint space lies medially, against the glenoid.
supraspinatus: Muscle occupying the supraspinous fossa above the scapular spine, deep to trapezius, its tendon passing beneath the acromion to the superior facet of the greater tuberosity; infraspinatus lies below the spine and deltoid is superficial and lateral.
supraspinatus muscle: Rotator cuff muscle filling the supraspinous fossa above the scapular spine, its tendon passing under the acromion and coracoacromial arch to the superior facet of the greater tuberosity; infraspinatus, its usual confusion, occupies the larger fossa below the spine.
supraspinatus muscle (musculotendinous p: Point medial to the acromion where the feathered muscle filling the supraspinous fossa gives way to uniformly dark tendon; the portion actually passing under the acromion is pure tendon, so muscle fibres must still be visible here.
supraspinatus tendon: Uniformly dark, fan-shaped tendon running laterally from the musculotendinous junction through the subacromial space to the superior facet of the greater tuberosity; it is the tendon, not the muscle belly, that passes beneath the acromion.
supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres mino: The four rotator cuff muscles: supraspinatus above the scapular spine, infraspinatus below it and teres minor at the lateral border, all inserting on greater tuberosity facets, plus subscapularis on the costal surface inserting on the lesser tuberosity.
surgical neck of humerus: The waisted region of the proximal humerus just distal to the greater and lesser tuberosities, where the head region meets the shaft and most fractures occur. The anatomical neck is higher, a narrow groove at the margin of the articular surface above the tuberosities.
surgical neck of the humerus: Constriction of the proximal humerus just below the greater and lesser tubercles where metaphysis meets shaft; the common fracture site, with the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels at risk. The anatomical neck is higher, immediately beneath the articular head.
surgical neck of the right humerus: Constricted zone where the proximal humerus narrows into the shaft, just below the greater and lesser tubercles — the common fracture site. The anatomical neck is the subtle line higher up at the margin of the articular head.
sustentaculum tali: Horizontal medial eminence, the talar shelf, arising from the anterosuperior calcaneus to support the talar neck and give ligamentous attachment; on the lateral radiograph it is the dense beak projecting forward beneath the talar head.
sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus: Horizontal shelf projecting medially from the anterosuperior calcaneus that supports the talar neck; on the lateral radiograph it is the dense beak-like projection beneath the talar head, grooved on its undersurface by flexor hallucis longus.
sylvian fissure: Echogenic branching cleft running laterally on each side between frontal and temporal lobes on coronal neonatal cranial ultrasound, made conspicuous by the pulsatile middle cerebral artery within it; the interhemispheric fissure containing the falx is the midline one.
symphysis menti: Midline of the mandibular body at the chin, where the two halves fuse in infancy. On the orthopantomogram it is the point at the very front of the mandibular arch between the lower central incisor roots, at the bottom centre of the image.
symphysis pubis: Midline cartilaginous joint uniting the two pubic bodies at the front of the pelvic ring, seen as a narrow vertical lucency between parallel cortical margins. On a well-centred AP pelvis it should lie in the midline in line with the sacral spinous processes.
t11/12 intervertebral disc: Thoracolumbar junction disc, narrower than the lumbar spaces below; identify it by tracing the twelfth rib to T12 and taking the space immediately above, or by counting up from the conus at L1/L2.
t11/t12 disc space: The space immediately above the T12 body: identify T12 as the lowest rib bearing vertebra and count one space upward. The space below T12, between it and the first non rib bearing vertebra, is T12/L1.
t12 vertebral body: Lowest rib bearing vertebra, confirmed by tracing the 12th rib back to its costovertebral joint. On the lateral film it is the last thoracic body, sitting immediately above L1 at the thoracolumbar junction.
t4: Count vertebral bodies down from the first rib-bearing vertebra. The T4–T5 level is confirmed by the landmarks lying at it: the manubriosternal joint, the aortic arch and the carina, which is quicker than counting alone on a lateral film.
talar dome: Convex superior articular surface of the talar body sitting within the ankle mortise beneath the tibial plafond; the talar head is the more distal rounded part directed anteromedially that articulates with the navicular.
talar dome/talus: Convex superior articular surface of the talar body, capped by smooth cortex and articulating with the tibial plafond inside the mortise; the neck and head continue forward from it and the subtalar joint lies beneath.
talonavicular joint: Articulation between the rounded talar head and the concave proximal surface of the navicular, forming the medial half of the midtarsal joint; the lateral half is the calcaneocuboid joint, and the two should line up in a smooth continuous arc.
talus: Bone with no muscular attachments whose body sits in the ankle mortise beneath the tibial plafond, narrowing at the neck into a head that articulates with the navicular, and resting on the calcaneus at the subtalar joint.
talus (head of talus): Rounded anterior end of the talus, projecting forward from the constricted neck to sit in the concavity of the navicular; distinguish it from the navicular itself, which lies beyond that joint line and is flatter and boat-shaped.
talus (neck of talus): Constricted segment linking the talar body and dome behind to the rounded head in front, best appreciated on the lateral where it forms the roof of the sinus tarsi; the body is the broader block articulating under the tibia.
temporal lobe: Parenchyma lying below and lateral to the Sylvian fissure on the coronal view, sitting on the floor of the middle cranial fossa; brain above the fissure at this level is frontal lobe, not temporal.
temporal process of the right zygomatic: Backward-projecting process of the zygoma that meets the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to complete the zygomatic arch, so it forms the anterior half of that thin curved strut; temporalis passes deep to the arch to reach the coronoid process.
temporomandibular fossa: Concavity on the undersurface of the temporal bone that receives the mandibular condyle, lying immediately in front of the external acoustic meatus and bounded anteriorly by the articular eminence, over which the condyle translates on mouth opening.
temporomandibular joint: Articulation between the rounded mandibular condyle and the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone, seen at the upper end of each ramus at the outer edges of an orthopantomogram. The condyle sits in the fossa when closed and translates forward onto the articular eminence on opening.
temporomandibular joint (tmj): Lucent joint space between the mandibular condyle and the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone, sitting immediately anterior to the external acoustic meatus; find the rounded condylar head first, then the curved fossa capping it.
temporoparietal (squamosal) suture: Runs roughly horizontally along the lateral skull vault where the squamous temporal bone overlaps the parietal, above the external auditory canal. Sutures are symmetric with serrated, corticated margins, whereas a fracture is sharp, lucent and follows no anatomical line.
temporosquamal suture: Arched suture curving above the external auditory meatus between the squamous temporal bone and the parietal bone; unlike a fracture it has corticated, gently serrated margins and a mirror image on the opposite side.
tendon of biceps brachii muscle: Uniformly dark, cord-like tendon descending through the antecubital fossa and passing posterolaterally to insert on the radial tuberosity, with the bicipital aponeurosis sweeping medially over the flexor mass. The brachialis tendon lies deeper and inserts on the ulnar coronoid instead.
tendon of extensor carpi ulnaris muscle: Occupies the sixth dorsal compartment, sitting in its own shallow groove on the dorsoulnar aspect of the distal ulna and held down by the ECU subsheath, making it the most ulnar dorsal tendon. The usual confusion is with flexor carpi ulnaris, which lies volar and runs to the pisiform.
tendon of flexor digitorum profundus: Deep finger flexor: within the carpal tunnel it lies dorsal to superficialis, and in the digit it passes through the split superficialis tendon to insert on the base of the distal phalanx, whereas superficialis stops at the middle phalanx.
tendon of flexor digitorum superficialis: Volar tendon of each flexor pair, superficial to the profundus tendon at the wrist and palm; at the proximal phalanx it divides into two slips that pass around profundus and insert on the base of the middle phalanx.

Volar member of the paired flexor tendons lying in line with the third ray, superficial to the profundus tendon; at the proximal phalanx it splits into two slips that pass around profundus to insert on the middle phalanx.
tendon of flexor pollicis longus: Single tendon at the radial side of the carpal tunnel, adjacent to the scaphoid and trapezium and running in the same deep plane as the profundus tendons, which are four in number; it continues alone to the thumb.
tendon of long head of biceps brachii: Runs from the supraglenoid tubercle across the top of the humeral head, then descends in the intertubercular (bicipital) groove between the greater and lesser tubercles. Not visible itself on a radiograph — locate the groove between the two tubercles.
tendon of right flexor pollicis longus: Single round tendon at the radial edge of the carpal tunnel, adjacent to the scaphoid and trapezium and in the same deep plane as the profundus tendons; the other tendons at this level come in groups of four.
tendon of the subscapularis muscle: Converging striated tendon crossing the front of the humeral head to the lesser tuberosity, seen on axial sections just medial to the biceps tendon in the groove; it is the only cuff tendon lying anterior to the joint.
tendons of right flexor digitorum profun: Four tendons forming the deepest layer of the carpal tunnel, lying directly against the volar surface of the carpal bones, deep to the superficialis tendons; flexor pollicis longus lies in the same deep plane but is single and most radial.
tensor fasciae latae: Small elongated muscle at the anterolateral hip, arising from the iliac crest just behind the ASIS and lying superficial and anterior to gluteus medius and minimus before inserting into the iliotibial tract; sartorius is the comparable small muscle lying more anteromedially, over the femoral vessels.
teres major muscle: Arises from the dorsal surface of the lower lateral border and inferior angle of the scapula and passes to the medial lip of the intertubercular groove, forming the lower posterior axillary fold; teres minor lies above it and is a rotator cuff muscle.
teres minor muscle: Smallest and most inferior rotator cuff muscle, arising from the lateral border of the scapula below infraspinatus and inserting on the inferior facet of the greater tuberosity, separated from infraspinatus by a fat plane on sagittal images. Teres major lies below it, is not a cuff muscle and passes anteriorly to the humerus.
the antero-inferior glenoid rim: Anterior margin of the lower half of the glenoid fossa, facing the axilla; the site of a bony Bankart lesion after anterior dislocation and best profiled on an apical oblique or West Point view. Its paired lesion is the Hill-Sachs defect on the posterosuperior humeral head.
the long head of biceps tendon runs thro: On axial images the tendon is a round black dot in the groove between the greater and lesser tuberosities, roofed by the transverse humeral ligament; traced proximally it arcs over the humeral head to the supraglenoid tubercle.
thenar eminence: Muscle mass at the radial base of the palm overlying the first metacarpal, comprising abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis; the hypothenar eminence is the corresponding ulnar mass over the fifth metacarpal.
third ventricle: Narrow slit-like anechoic midline cavity lying between the two thalami, below the level of the lateral ventricles; the cavum septum pellucidum sits higher, between the frontal horns and above the fornices.
thoracic vertebral body: Roughly heart-shaped body on axial CT, smaller than a lumbar body, with costal facets at its posterolateral corners for the rib head and pedicles projecting straight backwards; lumbar bodies are larger, more kidney-shaped and lack costal facets.
thumb metacarpal: Shortest and stoutest metacarpal, lying anterior and separate from the other metacarpals and rotated out of plane with them; trace its base to the trapezium at the saddle joint, which distinguishes it from a proximal phalanx or from the second metacarpal.
thymus: Anterior mediastinal soft tissue widening the upper mediastinum in infants, often with a straight lateral sail-shaped edge and a wavy border indented by adjacent ribs; unlike a true mass it causes no tracheal displacement and blends with the cardiac silhouette.
thyroid cartilage: Largest laryngeal cartilage, forming the anterior laryngeal prominence at about C4 to C5 and visible on radiographs only when calcified; the hyoid is the separate U-shaped bone above it and the cricoid the complete ring immediately below.
thyroid isthmus: Thin band of thyroid tissue crossing the midline directly anterior to the trachea and joining the two lobes, lying deep to the strap muscles. It shows the same finely granular reflective texture as the lobes, with bright tracheal air and shadowing immediately deep to it.
tibia: Larger, medial bone of the leg with a triangular cross-section and a subcutaneous anteromedial surface; the fibula is the much smaller bone lying posterolateral to it, the two joined by the interosseous membrane.
tibial diaphysis: Tubular shaft between the two metaphyses, with thick cortex and a narrow medullary canal; the metaphysis is the flared segment adjacent to the growth plate and the epiphysis is the ossified articular end beyond the physis.
tibial epiphysis: Ossified segment of the distal tibia on the joint side of the physis, forming the tibial plafond and medial malleolus and articulating with the talar dome; the bone proximal to the lucent physeal line is metaphysis.
tibial physis (or epiphyseal plate): Transverse lucent band across the distal tibia separating the flared metaphysis above from the ossified epiphysis below; the true ankle joint space lies further distally, between the tibial epiphysis and the talar dome.
tibial plateau: Flat horizontal articular surface at the top of the tibia formed by the medial and lateral condyles either side of the intercondylar eminence, lying beneath the femoral condyles; the fibular head is lateral and clearly below its level.
tibial sesamoid bone: Medial of the two hallux sesamoids beneath the first metatarsal head, tibial meaning medial, lying nearer the body midline within the medial head of flexor hallucis brevis; the fibular sesamoid sits on the side towards the second metatarsal.
tibial tuberosity: Bony prominence on the anterior surface of the proximal tibial metaphysis a short distance below the joint line, seen in profile on the lateral view, giving insertion to the patellar tendon; in adolescents its apophysis is normally irregular or fragmented.
tibialis anterior: Largest and most medial muscle of the anterior compartment, lying immediately lateral to the sharp anterior border of the tibia; extensor digitorum longus lies lateral to it and extensor hallucis longus is squeezed between the two lower in the leg.
tibialis anterior muscle: Largest and most medial muscle of the anterior compartment, lying immediately lateral to the tibia against its anterolateral surface; extensor digitorum longus lies lateral to it, while tibialis posterior sits deep, between tibia and fibula on the interosseous membrane.
tibialis posterior: Deepest muscle of the leg, lying directly on the interosseous membrane between the tibia and fibula, with flexor digitorum longus medial and flexor hallucis longus lateral to it; its tendon later passes behind the medial malleolus.
tibialis posterior muscle: Deepest posterior compartment muscle, lying directly on the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula and deep to soleus; flexor digitorum longus lies medial to it against the posterior tibia, and its tendon is the most anterior of the medial ankle tendons.
tibio-talar joint: Horizontal lucent joint space between the tibial plafond above and the convex talar dome below, continuing around the malleoli as the mortise; the subtalar joint is the separate space beneath the talus, above the calcaneus.
tibioperoneal trunk: Short common stem continuing from the popliteal artery after the anterior tibial artery has branched off laterally, dividing shortly afterwards into the posterior tibial and peroneal arteries. On the angiogram it is the single medial vessel between those two branch points.
tibioperoneal trunk (posterior tibial ar: Medial run-off vessel arising from the popliteal artery beyond the anterior tibial origin, named tibioperoneal trunk until the peroneal branches off and posterior tibial thereafter; APP mnemonic: Anterior tibial lateral, Peroneal middle, Posterior tibial most medial.
tibioperoneal trunk (tpt): Short common stem continuing from the popliteal artery after the anterior tibial has branched off, before it divides into the peroneal and posterior tibial arteries; it is the brief single medial trunk between the two-vessel and three-vessel levels of the run-off.
tibioperoneal trunk or right posterior t: Continuation of the popliteal artery once the anterior tibial has branched off, called the tibioperoneal trunk until the peroneal artery arises and the posterior tibial beyond that; it is the medial vessel, running deep to soleus towards the medial malleolus.
tongue: Soft tissue mass filling the oral cavity between the hard palate above and the body of the mandible below, outlined behind by air in the oropharynx on the lateral skull radiograph.
trace of synovial fluid within gleno-hum: Thin bright T2 rim between the humeral head and glenoid cartilage, a normal finding; a true effusion distends the capsule and axillary recess, while subacromial-subdeltoid bursal fluid lies outside the joint, above the cuff.
trachea: Midline air column from the cricoid at C6 to the carina at about T4/5, normally deviating slightly to the right at the aortic arch on a frontal chest film. On ultrasound it is the anterior midline neck structure deep to the thyroid isthmus, shadowing densely because of contained air.
transverse colon: Gas-filled bowel sagging across the upper abdomen with thick, widely spaced haustral folds that do not cross the whole lumen. Small bowel valvulae conniventes are thin, closely spaced and traverse the entire lumen; small bowel also lies centrally, colon peripherally.
transverse foramen of c1: Round lucency within the broad transverse process of the atlas, lateral to its lateral mass, transmitting the vertebral artery, which then loops medially over the posterior arch. The C1 transverse processes are the widest in the cervical spine, projecting beyond those of C2.
transverse humeral ligament: Thin dark band bridging the greater and lesser tuberosities on axial images, roofing the intertubercular groove and holding the biceps tendon within it; its fibres are inseparable from the distal subscapularis tendon.
transverse part of the ilio-femoral liga: Low-signal capsular thickening on the anterior hip, arising near the anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular rim and running laterally to the upper intertrochanteric line. The descending limb runs more vertically and medially; the pubofemoral ligament lies inferomedially.
transverse process: Projects laterally from the junction of pedicle and lamina; in the thoracic spine it carries the costal facet for the rib.
transverse process of c 7: Lowest cervical bony process projecting laterally beyond the vertebral body outline, immediately above the first rib. Unlike the T1 transverse process, which is directed upward and laterally, the C7 process points downward and laterally.
transverse process of c6: Bony bar projecting laterally from the side of the C6 vertebra, perforated by the foramen transversarium that transmits the vertebral artery; the uncinate process is different, hooking upwards from the lateral edge of the body's upper surface.
transverse process of c7: Cervical transverse processes point downwards and laterally, unlike thoracic ones which point upwards; C7's sits just above the first rib at the thoracic inlet. A downward-directed process carrying an extra ossified strut indicates a cervical rib.
transverse process of l3: Slender bar of fatty-marrow bone extending laterally from the L3 arch into psoas; for level, remember the aorta usually divides at L4 and the IVC forms at L5, so seeing both intact vessels implies L3 or above.
transverse process of l3 vertebra: Longest of the lumbar transverse processes, a thin spike projecting laterally at pedicle level from the junction of pedicle and lamina. Confirm the level by counting up from L5, whose transverse processes are short and stout.
transverse process of l4: Thin bony spike projecting laterally at pedicle level from the junction of pedicle and lamina, not from the body itself. Distinguish it from the 12th rib, which is longer, curved and arises at T12, and from the shorter stouter transverse process of L5.
transverse process of t1: First upward-angled transverse process below the cervical spine on a frontal film: thoracic transverse processes point cranially, whereas the C7 processes immediately above point caudally. The presence of the first rib articulating with it confirms the level.
transverse process of t2: Short blunt bony process projecting laterally from the vertebral arch at the T2 level, overlapping the medial end of the corresponding posterior rib; unlike a rib it is stubby and does not arc laterally around the chest wall.
transverse process of t3: Thoracic transverse processes project upwards and laterally from the vertebra, whereas cervical ones point downwards, which is how a cervical rib is identified. Count down from T1 at the thoracic inlet to localise T3.
transverse process of t6: Thoracic transverse processes project laterally from the vertebral column as small, symmetric bony densities; count ribs or vertebral bodies down to localise T6. Their symmetry and bony density stop them being mistaken for mediastinal pathology.
transverse process of the c7 vertebra: Lies at the thoracic inlet just above the first rib and points downwards and laterally, the opposite of the upward-directed thoracic transverse processes; an extra bony strut arising from such a downward-pointing process is a cervical rib.
transverse process of the lumbar vertebr: Thin flat spike of bone projecting laterally from the junction of pedicle and arch into the psoas, giving attachment to the intertransverse muscles; unlike a rib it makes no articulation with the vertebral body.
transverse venous sinus: Curvilinear groove on the inner table of the occipital bone sweeping laterally and forwards from the internal occipital protuberance towards the sigmoid sinus; it is a broad band with corticated edges, unlike a fracture, which is sharper and non-corticated.
trapezium: Most radial bone of the distal carpal row, recognised by its saddle-shaped articulation with the base of the thumb metacarpal. The trapezoid lies immediately ulnar to it and takes the second metacarpal, so trace the metacarpal proximally to decide between them.
trapezium bone: Most radial bone of the distal carpal row, identified by tracing the thumb metacarpal proximally to its saddle joint; a groove on its palmar aspect carries flexor carpi radialis. The scaphoid lies proximal to it and the trapezoid immediately ulnar.
trapezius muscle: Large superficial triangular muscle of the upper back and neck, arising from occiput, ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes and inserting on the lateral clavicle, acromion and scapular spine. On axial images it is the outermost posterior layer, superficial to supraspinatus and the scapula.
trapezoid: Smallest bone of the distal carpal row, wedged between the trapezium radially and the capitate ulnarly and articulating distally with the base of the second metacarpal. Tracing the second metacarpal proximally separates it from the trapezium, which takes the thumb metacarpal.
trapezoid and conoid components of the c: Not visible as a density; they occupy the gap between the coracoid process below and the undersurface of the lateral clavicle above, conoid posteromedial and trapezoid anterolateral. Judged by coracoclavicular distance, unlike the acromioclavicular ligament which spans the joint itself.
triangular fibrocartilage: Low signal triangular structure spanning the ulnar side of the wrist from the sigmoid notch of the distal radius to the base of the ulnar styloid, separating the distal ulna from the lunate and triquetral; it is the main stabiliser of the distal radioulnar joint and is not visible on radiographs.
triangular fibrocartilage complex: Dark triangular fibrocartilage on the coronal image with its base on the ulnar margin of the distal radius and apex at the ulnar styloid, cushioning the ulnar head from lunate and triquetrum; the scapholunate ligament is the shorter band lying between carpal bones.
triangular fibrocartilage. this fibrocar: Low-signal triangular disc on coronal images running from the ulnar border of the distal radius to the base of the ulnar styloid, separating the distal radioulnar joint from the ulnar carpus; fluid signal crossing it indicates a tear.
triangular fibrocartilaginous complex: Triangular low-signal disc with its base on the ulnar border of the distal radius and its apex at the ulnar styloid, roofing the ulnar carpus on coronal images and separating the distal radioulnar joint from the radiocarpal joint.
triangular fibrocartilaginous disc: Dark triangular band on coronal images running from the ulnar corner of the distal radius (sigmoid notch) to the base of the ulnar styloid, roofing the ulnar carpus and separating the ulnar head from the lunate and triquetrum.
