Its uniformly low signal on all sequences separates it from adjacent bright fluid or hyaline cartilage.
triceps brachii muscle: Fills the entire posterior compartment of the arm and is the only muscle behind the humerus on axial MRI, its long, lateral and medial heads converging on a tendon inserting into the olecranon; biceps and brachialis lie anteriorly.
triceps brachii tendon: Posterior low-signal band on sagittal elbow images running down the back of the humerus to insert on the olecranon; the biceps tendon is the anterior equivalent and passes forward to the radial tuberosity.
triceps muscle: Fills the posterior compartment of the arm behind the humerus, its long head arising from the infraglenoid tubercle and descending between teres minor and teres major; deltoid is the superficial muscle capping the shoulder laterally.
triceps tendon: Broad low-signal band on the posterior aspect of the distal humerus converging to insert on the tip of the olecranon; on sagittal images follow it distally to the olecranon rather than anteriorly to the radial tuberosity like the distal biceps tendon.
triquetral: Proximal carpal row bone on the ulnar side, articulating with the lunate radially and lying just distal to the ulnar styloid across the triangular fibrocartilage; on a PA radiograph the pisiform is superimposed on it as a denser oval.
triquetrum: The ulnar-most bone of the proximal carpal row, lying beneath the pisiform on a lateral view.
triradiate cartilage: Y-shaped lucency at the centre of the acetabulum on a paediatric pelvic radiograph, where ilium, ischium and pubis converge. It marks the acetabular floor, and should not be confused with the femoral neck physis, which lies lateral to the joint within the proximal femur.
triradiate cartilage of the acetabulum: Y-shaped lucency in the floor of the acetabulum where ilium, ischium and pubis converge in the immature pelvis; symmetry with the opposite side and smooth sclerotic margins distinguish it from a fracture, and it sits far above the ischiopubic synchondrosis.
triradiate cartilage of the left acetabu: The Y-shaped lucency in the medial floor of the immature acetabulum where the ilium, ischium and pubis converge, with smooth corticated margins and a mirror-image appearance on the opposite side. Its symmetry and typical Y configuration distinguish it from an acetabular fracture.
triradiate cartilage or 'y' cartilage of: Y-shaped lucency in the acetabular floor where ilium, ischium and pubis meet in the immature pelvis; look for the same appearance and smooth sclerotic margins on the opposite hip, which excludes fracture.
trochlea: Spool or pulley-shaped medial articular surface of the distal humerus that receives the trochlear notch of the ulna. Distinguish it from the medial epicondyle, which is non-articular and lies further medially, and from the rounded capitulum laterally.
trochlea (left): Medial articular condyle of the distal humerus, spool- or pulley-shaped with a central groove, articulating with the trochlear notch of the ulna; the capitellum lies laterally, is a simple rounded ball and takes the radial head.
trochlea epiphysis: Ossific centre medial to the capitellum at the articular surface facing the trochlear notch of the ulna, often irregular or multi-centric; appears about nine years. Unlike the medial epicondyle it lies at the joint line rather than on the medial metaphyseal flare.
trochlea of distal humerus: Spool- or pulley-shaped medial articular surface of the distal humerus which grips the trochlear notch of the ulna, lying medial to the rounded capitulum. The medial epicondyle is further medial and non-articular, projecting off the metaphysis rather than the joint surface.
trochlea of humerus: Grooved, pulley-shaped medial articular surface of the distal humerus lying within the trochlear notch of the ulna, which is bounded by the coronoid process anteriorly and the olecranon posteriorly; the capitulum is lateral and rounded, articulating with the radius.
trochlea of the humerus: Medial, spool-shaped articular surface of the distal humerus with a central groove, sitting within the trochlear notch of the ulna; the capitulum is the rounded lateral condyle articulating with the concave radial head.
trochlea of the left humerus: Medial, spool- or pulley-shaped articular surface of the distal humerus that grips the trochlear notch of the ulna; its lateral neighbour the capitellum is a rounded ball articulating with the radial head.
trochlea ossification centre: Ossific nucleus appearing about nine years at the medial articular surface of the distal humerus, facing the trochlear notch of the ulna and often irregular or multi-centric. It sits at the joint line, unlike the medial epicondyle, which is non-articular and more proximal.
trochlear notch of ulna: C-shaped concave articular surface of the proximal ulna between the olecranon behind and the coronoid in front, gripping the humeral trochlea; the radial notch is a much smaller separate facet on its lateral aspect that takes the radial head.
tubercles of intercondylar eminence/tibi: Two small pointed peaks rising from the centre of the tibial plateau between the medial and lateral articular surfaces, projecting into the femoral notch; they belong to the tibia below the joint line, unlike the femoral condyles above it.
tuberosity of base of right 5th metatars: Beak-like projection at the proximal-lateral corner of the fifth metatarsal base, insertion of peroneus brevis; in children its apophysis runs parallel to the shaft, unlike a transverse avulsion fracture, and unlike the separate corticated os peroneum lying lateral to the cuboid.
tuberosity of radius: Blunt bony prominence on the anteromedial aspect of the proximal radius just distal to the neck, facing the ulna, and the insertion of the biceps brachii tendon. It should not be confused with the ulnar coronoid process, which is on the opposite bone and forms part of the joint.
tuberosity of right radius: Oval prominence on the medial (ulnar) side of the proximal radius just distal to the neck, giving attachment to the biceps tendon; when projected obliquely its thin cortex creates an apparent lucency that should not be mistaken for a lytic lesion.
tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal: The prominence projecting proximally and laterally from the base of the fifth metatarsal, beyond the cuboid articulation, receiving the peroneus brevis tendon. In children the normal apophysis lies parallel to the shaft, whereas an avulsion fracture line is transverse.
tuft of the distal phalanx of the left g: The expanded, spade-shaped distal end of the terminal phalanx of the hallux, the most distal osseous structure of the big toe and the part underlying the nail bed. The base of the same phalanx, at its opposite end, articulates with the proximal phalanx at the interphalangeal joint.
twelfth rib: Lowest and shortest rib, arising at the T12 level and angling laterally and downward with no anterior costal attachment. Do not mistake it for the L1 transverse process, which is shorter, arises more posteriorly at pedicle level and points transversely rather than obliquely.
ulna: Medial forearm bone, broad proximally where the olecranon and trochlear notch grip the humeral trochlea, tapering to a small distal head and styloid. The radius is its mirror image: narrow head and neck proximally, broad and articular distally at the wrist.
ulna styloid: Small pointed projection from the posteromedial aspect of the distal ulna on the little-finger side, ending more proximally than the radial styloid, and the attachment of the apex of the triangular fibrocartilage. The radial styloid is larger and lateral.
ulnar artery: Larger medial terminal branch of the brachial artery arising at the level of the radial neck, running medially in the forearm with the ulnar nerve deep to flexor carpi ulnaris and entering the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum; unlike the radial artery it gives off the common interosseous just beyond its origin.
ulnar nerve: Small ovoid fascicular structure lying in fat within the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, then passing between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris. The median nerve is anterior, running medial to the brachial artery in the antecubital fossa.
ulnar nerve and artery (the structure la: Contents of the canal between the pisiform and the hook of hamate, lying superficial (volar) to the flexor retinaculum and so outside the carpal tunnel, with the nerve ulnar to the artery; the median nerve lies deep to the retinaculum.
ulnar nerve, ulnar artery and vein: Small bundle lying superficial (volar) to the flexor retinaculum between the pisiform and the hook of hamate, therefore outside the carpal tunnel, with the nerve on the ulnar side of the artery; carpal tunnel contents lie deep to the retinaculum.
ulnar styloid: Short conical spike projecting distally from the posteromedial aspect of the ulnar head, giving attachment to the triangular fibrocartilage. It sits on the little-finger side and normally ends more proximally than the radial styloid, which extends further distally on the thumb side.
ulnar styloid process: Short conical spike projecting distally and posteromedially from the ulnar head on the little-finger side of the wrist; the radial styloid is the thumb-side counterpart and normally extends further distally than the ulnar one.
uncinate process of c5: Upward-pointing hook at the lateral margin of the upper surface of the C5 body, meeting the body above at the uncovertebral joint of Luschka; the transverse process projects laterally rather than upwards and lies further out.
uncinate process of pancreas: Sharp beak of pancreatic head projecting posteriorly and to the left behind the superior mesenteric vein, sandwiched between that vein anteriorly and the aorta/IVC posteriorly. Its position behind the vein separates it from the bulk of the head, which lies to the right of the vein.
uncinate process of the pancreas: Posteroinferior hook of the pancreatic head extending leftwards behind the superior mesenteric vein and anterior to the aorta and IVC. If the pancreatic tissue lies posterior to the vein rather than to its right, it is the uncinate process.
uncinate process/head of pancreas: Hook-shaped posteroinferior extension of the pancreatic head that passes behind the superior mesenteric vein and in front of the aorta and IVC. Trace the head round the right side of the vein to its sharp left-pointing tip lying posterior to the vessels.
uncovertebral joint c5–c6: Small cleft at the lateral corner of the C5-C6 disc space on the frontal view, where the uncinate process rising from the superolateral margin of C6 meets the bevelled inferolateral edge of the C5 body. The facet joints lie further posterolaterally and are seen as separate obliquely oriented lines.
unfused calcaneus secondary ossification: Dense, often fragmented crescent of bone applied to the posterior surface of the calcaneus and separated from it by a lucent line; this posterior apophysis appears around age 5 and fuses at puberty, so it is normal, not a fracture.
unfused epiphysis left medial malleolus: Triangular ossified epiphysis at the medial corner of the distal tibia, separated from the metaphysis by a smooth, uniformly wide corticated lucency; the even width and intact cortical margins identify a normal open physis rather than a Salter-Harris fracture.
upper central incisor: First tooth either side of the midline in the upper arch, with the widest crown of the incisors and a single straight root; the narrower tooth immediately lateral to it is the lateral incisor.
upper left lateral incisor: Second tooth from the midline in the upper arch, narrower and shorter than the central incisor beside it and single-rooted; count outwards from the midline pair so it is not mislabelled as the canine.
upper lobe pulmonary vein: Vessel descending obliquely across the lateral part of the left hilum and crossing in front of the lower lobe artery, the angle of that crossing being the hilar point. Veins head towards the left atrium and have no accompanying bronchus, unlike arteries.
upper lobe segmental bronchus (end on): Small ring shadow, a lucent circle with a thin soft-tissue wall, projected near the right hilum where a segmental bronchus runs parallel to the beam, usually paired with its accompanying artery as a solid dot. The central lucency separates it from a true nodule.
upper right 1st molar: Sixth tooth from the midline in the upper arch and the first of the three molars, immediately behind the second premolar; upper molars have three roots that often project up towards the maxillary sinus floor.
urinary bladder: Midline extraperitoneal viscus lying immediately behind the pubic symphysis, containing uniformly high T2 signal urine within a thin dark muscular wall; unlike a fluid-filled bowel loop it has no folds or gas, and in males the prostate sits at its base.
uterus: Pear-shaped midline pelvic organ on the sagittal study, lying behind the bladder and in front of the rectum, with T2 zonal anatomy of bright endometrium, dark junctional zone and intermediate myometrium.
vallecula: Air-filled recess between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, seen on the lateral soft-tissue neck film as a lucent pouch immediately anterior to the epiglottic outline and above the level of the pyriform sinuses, which lie lower and more posterolateral.
vastus intermedius: Quadriceps muscle lying directly on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft, deep to rectus femoris and sandwiched between vastus medialis and vastus lateralis; rectus femoris is the more superficial oval muscle with a central tendon.
vastus intermedius muscle: Deepest quadriceps muscle, lying directly against the anterior and lateral surface of the femoral shaft, deep to rectus femoris; rectus femoris is the more superficial anterior muscle sitting in the midline with a central tendon.
vastus lateralis: Largest quadriceps muscle, occupying the lateral thigh against the femur and deep to the iliotibial tract; tensor fasciae latae is the much smaller muscle seen only proximally, anterolateral to the greater trochanter, feeding into that tract.
vastus lateralis muscle: Largest quadriceps component, filling the anterolateral thigh lateral to the femur deep to the iliotibial tract and tensor fascia lata, arising from the greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera; the lateral intermuscular septum separates it from biceps femoris behind.
vastus medialis: Anterior compartment muscle applied to the medial aspect of the femoral shaft that forms the anterior (anterolateral) boundary of the adductor canal, with the adductors behind it and sartorius roofing the canal medially; adductor longus and magnus lie posteromedially.
vastus medialis muscle: Bulky muscle on the anteromedial aspect of the femur forming the anterolateral wall of the adductor canal and extending further distally than the other quadriceps towards the medial patella; the adductors lie behind it and strap-like sartorius lies superficial and medial.
venous valve: Focal transverse waist in a contrast-filled vein with slight bulging of the sinuses just beyond it, giving a fine linear defect and a local widening; unlike thrombus it is a thin line at a fixed point rather than a persistent elongated filling defect.
ventricle: Anterior chamber that contributes nothing to the frontal cardiac silhouette, where the right border is right atrium and the left border left ventricle; on the lateral radiograph it is the chamber abutting the lower retrosternal space.
vertebral body: Deepest structure on transverse epigastric ultrasound, a brightly echogenic anterior surface with dense posterior acoustic shadowing lying immediately behind the aorta and IVC, serving as the anchoring landmark for the retroperitoneal vessels.
vertebral body of c6: Count down from the dens: C6 is the second last cervical body and often the lowest one clearly seen before the shoulders obscure the film. C7 below it carries the long, non-bifid spinous process of the vertebra prominens.
vertebral body of l4: Count upward: the body sitting on the lumbosacral disc is L5, and L4 is the next one above it. On frontal films this level lies close to the intercristal line joining the iliac crests.
wharton's duct (submandibular duct): Long contrast-filled duct running forwards and upwards from the hilum of the submandibular gland along the floor of the mouth to open at the sublingual caruncle beside the frenulum. Stensen's parotid duct instead runs horizontally across masseter to open opposite the upper second molar.
wormian bone: Small island of accessory bone lying within a suture line, most often the lambdoid, and corticated on every margin; a fracture fragment lacks that complete cortical outline and its lucency crosses rather than follows the suture.
xiphoid process: Small, often incompletely ossified or bifid tip projecting inferiorly from the lower end of the sternal body, best appreciated on the lateral view; when calcified it can project over the epigastrium on the frontal film and mimic a mass or ingested foreign body.
zygoma: Quadrilateral cheekbone forming the prominence of the cheek and the inferolateral orbital margin, articulating with the frontal bone above, the maxilla medially and the temporal bone behind via its temporal process. The zygomatic arch is only that slender posterior bar, not the whole bone.
zygomatic arch: Slender bony bridge formed by the temporal process of the zygoma meeting the zygomatic process of the temporal bone, running from the lateral orbital margin backwards to just above the external auditory meatus. It arches over the coronoid process and ramus of the mandible.
zygomatic process of left frontal bone: Downward projection of the frontal bone forming the upper part of the lateral orbital margin and ending at the frontozygomatic suture; below that suture the rim is the frontal process of the zygoma.
zygomatic process of the frontal bone: Downward projecting lateral corner of the frontal bone forming the upper part of the lateral orbital margin, ending at the frontozygomatic suture. Everything above the suture is frontal bone; below it is the frontal process of the zygoma.
zygomatic process of the right frontal b: Stout downward projection of the frontal bone forming the upper lateral orbital margin and ending at the frontozygomatic suture, above which the bone is frontal and below which it is zygoma. It continues medially into the supraorbital rim.
zygomaticofrontal suture: Corticated lucent line at the superolateral orbital rim where the zygoma meets the frontal bone, obliquely orientated and symmetrical with the opposite side. Its smooth sclerotic margins and bilateral symmetry separate it from a fracture through the lateral orbital rim.
